Conclusion

5. The issue of taxability of works contract moved through several phases and it was always difficult for the Courts to reach to a definite conclusion regarding this issue. Even after series of cases and reasoning by the Courts, they were unable to categorically define the term 'works contract'. But it can be said that these cases helped a lot in forming some concrete concept regarding the works contract. The analysis of situation makes us realize that L&T's judgments contributed to a great extent to establish the status of taxability of works contract in India. But various principles and conditions laid down in the case resulted in conflicts.

The dominant nature test was ruled out in L&T judgment but the application of the same led to conflicts, which can be demonstrated with the help of two cases, i.e., International Hospital case and Pro Ltd. case. In the case of International Hospital v. State of U.P. 22the petitioner was the owner of superspecialty hospital where the implants were used during the course of surgical procedures. It was not considered as sale and, hence, not to be taxed. It was held that the patients visited the hospital for the surgical process; any implantation was an intrinsic and integral part of such process. Tax could not be imposed on such implantation, as the essential nature of transaction was the performance of medical procedure which in essence was outside the ambit of sale.23 But, in the case of State of Karnataka v. Pro Ltd. 24the challenge was made to the constitutional validity of the power of the State to levy tax on the processing and supply of photographs, photo prints and photo negatives. It was held by the Apex Court that after 46th Amendment that the State was given the power to levy taxes on works contracts by fictionally dividing it into sale and supply part but there will be no application of dominant intention rule. The photographic service was considered as sale and hence taxable. Therefore, there was inconsistency in the application of the said rule.

Under these circumstances, it may be expected that the GST regime (expected to be implemented in India by April, 2016) will contribute positively to the taxation of works contracts. The basis of the expectation lies in the uniform applicability of GST regime across the States which will help to avoid conflicts. Having said that it would be curious to see how the new regime will shape the taxation of works contracts in India.

Concept of the Works Contract

3. The determination of composite transactions as works contracts has been one of the most litigated topics under the indirect tax regime, proving to be a cumbersome ordeal for businesses over the years. From being not taxed at all, to the levy of tax on sale portion, and finally levy on service portion, works contracts disputes have come a long way. However, the journey of the works contracts seems to be far from concluded, particularly given the fundamental changes that the GST regime is bound to being in.

The establishment of a nexus between the sphere of works contracts with the proposed GST necessitates an overview of the developments that shaped the principles associated with the taxability of works contracts. Prior to the 46th Amendment to the Constitution of India, on perusal of various authorities12, it becomes apparent that works contracts could not have been liable to be taxed under the State tax laws; State Legislatures did not have competence to charge sales tax under Entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution on an indivisible contract of sale of goods had components of labour and service and was not within the domain of the Assessing Officer to dissect an indivisible contract to distinguish between the two constituent elements. Further, whether a particular contract was a works contract or a contract for sale of goods was dependent on the dominant intention, as reflected, inter alia, from the terms and conditions of the contract. There existed no strait-jacket formula to determine the nature of the contract, given its dependence on the facts and circumstances of each case.

Post 46th Amendment, with the insertion of sub-section (29A) under Article 366 of the Constitution, it became evident13 that the Courts started interpreting works contracts in a Constitutional backdrop. Cases which involved transfer of property along with an element of service in the context of work rendered, stood treated as works contracts.

It is pertinent to note that several principles of significance have been laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the judgments rendered in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka14 and Kone Elevator India Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in both these cases, has made a departure from the traditional understanding of the term "works contract" as had been laid down in preceding adjudications.

3.1 What Is A Works Contract ?: The term "works contract" as envisaged in Article 366(29A)(b), opined the Supreme Court, is amply wide and cannot be confined to a particular understanding of the term, or to a particular form. The term encompasses a wide range and many varieties of contracts. The Parliament had such wide meaning of "works contract" in its view at the time of 46th Amendment. Accordingly, the expression "tax on the sale or purchase of goods" in Entry 54, List II, Schedule VII, read with the definition clause (29A) includes the transfer of property in goods whether as goods or in the form other than goods involved in the execution of works contract. 10.11-4 Taxability of BOT projects

Really this is a grant of right to enjoy fruits of the immovable property for specified period. It is 'profit a prendre' i.e. grant of benefit arising out land. It is not 'works contract'.

This is not a construction contract given by Government. The 'concessionaire' (by whatever name called) is constructing the roads etc. for himself and not for Government.

This should not be taxable either under Vat or service tax.

10.3-8 Works contract if contract for construction is made with prospective buyer

In K Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka AIR 2005 SC 2350 = (2005) 5 SCC 162 = 2 STT 178 = 141 STC 298 = 3 STR 337 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

Section 2(1)(vi) of Karnataka Sales Tax Act stated that 'works contract' includes any agreement for carrying out for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, the building, construction, manufacture, processing, fabrication, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property.

Section 5B of the Act provided for tax on transfer of property in goods, whether as goods or in some other form, in the execution of works contract.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some wok on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

22.6 Distinction between construction service and works contract service

There is no doubt that construction contract is also a 'works contract'. However, under GST, distinction has been made between 'works contract service' and 'construction of complex'.

The distinction is that in case of works contract, a customer (recipient of supply of service) approaches the supplier of service (contractor) to undertake construction as per his requirements. In almost all the cases, the land is owned by or taken on lease by customer. The contractor enters into contract with customer and then undertakes construction with his own material. If the material is supplied by recipient himself (customer), then it is not works contract. It is simple contract for work.

In construction of complex, the builder or developer normally does not have any identified customer. Even if he has some identified customers before commencement of construction, he is undertaking construction activity on his own and not on basis of contract with customer. The land never belongs to the customer.

SERVICE PORTION OF WORKS CONTRACT

16.1

Background

Works contract is composite contract of goods and services. Sales tax (Vat) is on goods involved in works contract. Sales tax can be imposed on value of goods involved in works contract and service tax can be imposed on value of services.

'Service portion in the execution of a works contract' is 'declared service' - section 66E(h) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

A tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract is deemed sale of goods under Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India. [As inserted by 46th Amendment to Constitution in 1982]

Earlier, in State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley - (1958) 9 STC 353 (SC) = 1959 SCR 379 = AIR 1958 SC 560, it was held that tax cannot be levied on works contract. This was because the Constitution did not define 'sale' and hence the term 'sale' has the same meaning as given in Sale of Goods Act. To get over the difficulty created by this judgment, Constitution was amended in 1982 by 46th Amendment and concept of 'deemed sale' was introduced to cover transfer of property in goods involved in works contract.

In Builders' Association of India v. UOI - (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member constitution bench), it has been observed : 'After the 46th amendment, the works contract which was indivisible one, is by a legal fiction altered into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services. After 46th amendment, it has become possible for States to levy tax on value of goods involved in a works contract in the same way in which the sales tax was leviable on the price of goods and materials supplied in a building contract which had been entered into two distinct and separate parts.

Distinction between a divisible contract and an indivisible contract came to an end after forty sixth Amendment to Constitution - National Organic Chemicals Industries Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 54 VST 271 (Bom HC DB).

In State of Karnataka v. Transglobal Power Ltd. (2015) 77 VST 509 (Karn HC DB), it has been held that if contract is divisible, it cannot be a works contract.

16.1-1 Constitutional Validity of service tax on works contract

Constitutional Validity of service tax on works contract has been practically upheld in Association of Leasing and Financial Services v. UOI (2011) 2 SCC 352 = 7 taxmann.com 740 = 29 STT 316 = 35 VST 549 (SC 3 member bench) (though issue in that case was constitutional validity of service tax on lease).

In G D Builders v. UOI (2013) 42 GST 594 = 40 taxmann.com 415 = 68 VST 183 (Del HC DB), it was held that service tax can be imposed on works contract even prior to 1-6-2007. However, service tax can be levied only on service portion. Service tax cannot be imposed on value of goods - followed in YFC Projects v. UOI (2014) 44 GST 334 = 43 taxmann.com 219 = 68 VST 153 (Del HC DB).

Works contract not taxable prior to 1-6-2007 - In CCE v. Larsen and Toubro Ltd. (2015) 52 GST 1 = 60 taxmann.com 354 = 84 VST 403 (SC) = (2016) 1 SCC 170, it has been held that service tax cannot be imposed by works contract services prior to 1-6-2007. It was held that prior to 1-6-2007, there was no machinery provision for assessment of works contract service. In absence of machinery provision, the tax is vague and would be open to assessing authority to arbitrarily assess subject. Hence, the levy is non-existent.

In many states, contract with builder is for total value including value of land or undivided share of land. However, in some Southern States, two agreements are executed - one for undivided share of land and other for construction. Builders in those states where not including value of undivided share of land while calculating 40% of total value of contract.

Now, a retrospective amendment has been made w.e.f. 1-7-2010 to clarify that 'total amount' will include value of undivided share of land.

Now, valuation done in Northern States and Southern States is on equal footing.

However, the policy of Central Government has been consistent that no retrospective amendment shall be made. This amendment is against that declared policy of Central Government, though it cannot be said to be unfair.

Concept of fair market value - The concept of 'fair market value' will be highly relevant in cases where the customer supplies some material (like cement and steel) at lower than the fair market value. For example, if fair market value of cement is Rs. 350 per bag and the customer supplies cement to contractor free of cost, then Rs. 350 per bag will be added to 'total amount'. If the customer supplies the bag @ Rs. 250 per bag (and not free) Rs. 350 will be added to 'total amount' and deduction of Rs. 250 will be allowed. In effect. Rs. 100 per bag will be added to 'total amount' and then the percentage (40%/60%/70% as the case may be).

If fair market value of material supplied by service receiver is Rs. one lakh and if it is supplied free, then Rs. one lakh will be added to 'total amount'. If the material is supplied at Rs. 60,000 plus Vat of Rs. 3,000 (total Rs. 63,000), then Rs. 1,00,000 will be added to 'total amount' and Rs. 63,000 will be deducted. In effect, Rs. 37,000 will be added to 'total amount' and then the percentage (25%/30%/40%/60% as applicable) will be applied for calculating service tax payable.

Mere labour contract is not works contract - Geogy George v. State of Kerala (2014) 50 taxmann.com 391 = 71 VST 510 (Ker HC DB).

Pure service contract to carry out seismic survey without transfer of any goods is not a works contract - Asian Oilfield Services v. State of Tripura (2015) 81 VST 536 (Tripura HC DB).

16.1-8 Works contract if contract for construction is made with prospective buyer

In K Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka AIR 2005 SC 2350 = (2005) 5 SCC 162 = 2 STT 178 = 141 STC 298 = 3 STR 337 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

Section 2(1)(v-i) of Karnataka Sales Tax Act stated that 'works contract' includes any agreement for carrying out for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, the building, construction, manufacture, processing, fabrication, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property.

Section 5B of the Act provided for tax on transfer of property in goods, whether as goods or in some other form, in the execution of works contract.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some work on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

It was held that the developer would be liable to pay tax on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract.

10.10-3 State cannot artificially treat Inter-State works contract as local sale

Rajasthan Sales Tax Act had made provision that deemed sale in execution of works contract will be deemed to have taken place within State if goods were in the State at the time of its incorporation in works contract, irrespective of where agreement was entered into or whether goods moved from one State to another as result of contract. This provision was held ultra vires powers of State Legislature in Triveni Engineering v. State (2001) 124 STC 17 (Raj HC DB). - followed in Black Stone Rubber v. State of Rajasthan (2001) 124 STC 99 (Raj HC DB). - same view in Black Stone Rubber v. State of Rajasthan (2001) 124 STC 130 (Raj HC DB).

Similarly, explanation 4(c) to section 2(xxi) of Kerala General Sales Tax Act provided that transfer of property in goods involved in works contract (whether as goods or in some other form) shall be deemed to have taken place in the State, if the goods are within the State at the time of such transfer. This would be so irrespective of the place where works contract is made, whether assent of the other party is prior or subsequent to such transfer. In Siemens Ltd. v. State of Kerala (2001) 122 STC 1 (Ker HC DB), the 'explanation' was read down (instead of declaring it as unconstitutional) to hold that the explanation will not apply if sale is as per sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST Act. It was held that if execution of works contract is inter-state, it cannot be intra-State merely on the basis of situs of goods at the time of transfer.

In Siemens Ltd. v. State of Kerala (2001) 122 STC 1 (Ker HC DB), the 'explanation' was read down (instead of declaring it as unconstitutional) to hold that the explanation will not apply if sale is as per sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST Act. It was held that if execution of works contract is inter-state, it cannot be intra-State merely on the basis of situs of goods at the time of transfer. This decision was followed in Siemens India Ltd. v. State of Kerala (2003) 132 STC 418 (Ker HC DB). In this case, dealer had two separate contracts - one for supply of goods and other for erection and commissioning of equipment. It was held that if goods were supplied inter-state under the contract for supply of goods, it will not be part of works contract within the State.

However, in J.D.P. Associates v. State of Tamil Nadu (2003) 131 STC 334 (TNTST), goods were purchased from out of State. These were used in the execution of works contract. It was held that the taxable event in the execution of works contract takes place when goods are incorporated in the work, which happened after receipt of goods in State. Hence, sales tax in Tamil Nadu will be payable on goods involved in works contract.

In State of Kerala v. Unitech Machines (2010) 3 GST 73 = 32 VST 80 (Ker HC DB), the dealer purchased goods from outside Kerala under C form and used them in works contract. It was held that works contract tax is payable on entire value including material purchased from outside the State.

10.9

Valuation rules to determine sale price of works contract

So far, no specific provision was made in CST and hence 'sale price' was required to be determined on basis of definition of 'sale price' as contained in section 2(h) of CST Act. As per this definition, freight or delivery or the cost of installation is not includible when separately charged.

This definition is not sufficient to determine 'sale price' when the contract is an indivisible contract which comprises of both goods and services. In sales tax laws or VAT laws of many States, there is provision of 'composition scheme' to pay sales tax on gross value of contract on some ad hoc basis. So far, there was no similar provision in CST Act.

Now, proviso to section 2(h) (inserted w.e.f. 13th May 2005) provides that in case of transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of works contract, the 'sale price' of such goods shall be determined in the prescribed manner by making such deductions from the total consideration for the works contract as may be prescribed and such price shall be deemed to be the sale price for the purposes of section 2(h).

Thus, now 'sale price' in case of sale of 'goods involved in works contract' will be determined on the basis of rules that may be made by Central Government.

State valuation rules can apply if Central Government has not made rules - So far, Rules have not been framed by Central Government. In Mahim Patram P Ltd. v. UOI (2007) 7 STT 136 = 7 STR 110 = 6 VST 248 (SC), it has been held that in absence of rules, valuation can be made on basis of State Rules. It was also held that only because rules have not been framed under Central Act would not per se mean that no tax is leviable - followed in CVAT v. State of Haryana (2009) 1 GST 113 = 23 VST 10 (CSTAA).

In Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Orissa (2007) 12 VST 31 (Ori HC DB), assessment of tax on works contract was held invalid as no rules were framed. Assessment was done only on basis of departmental circulars. However, it was held that fresh assessment can be made after rules are framed.

State of MP (2007) 6 VST 1 (MP HC FB) * Jaihind Projects Ltd. v. State of MP (2007) 8 VST 1 (MP HC DB). * Builders' Association of India v. There was no provision for ascertainment of value and nature of goods supplied during execution of works contract, nor for determination of value of goods supplied in the course of inter state sale. The provision was held invalid - view confirmed in State of Chhattisgarh v. VTP Constructions (2008) 2 SCC 578 = 12 VST 14 (SC).

Works Contract - Divisible

Works contract can be divided into two separate contracts by legal fiction as provided in sub-clause (b) of clause (29A) of article 366 of the Constitution; (i) contract for the sale of goods involved in the said works contract, and (ii) for supply of labour and service. This division of contract can be made only if the works contract involved a dominant intention to transfer the property in goods and not in contracts where the transfer in property takes place as an incident of the contract of service. What is pertinent to ascertain what was the intention of the contract. [see Rainbow Colour Lab v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2000) 2 SCC 385]. The Supreme Court in Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CC (2001) 4 SCC 593 doubted this saying :

"The conclusion arrived at in Rainbow Colour Lab v. State of MP (2000) 2 SCC 385, in our opinion, runs counter to the express provision contained in article 366(29A) as also of the Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Builders Association of India v. Union of India (1989) 2 SCC 645".

The Supreme Court in BSNL v. Union of India [2006] 152 Taxman 135 agreed. However, the Supreme Court in C. K. Jideesh v. Union of India (2005) 8 SCALE 784 had held that aforesaid observations in Associated Companies Ltd.’s case were merely obiter and that Rainbow Colour Lab’s case was still good law.

Conclusion (E) of the judgment (para 92 of SCC and STC and para 81 of STT ) reads as follows, 'The aspect theory would not apply to enable the value of service to be included in the sale of goods or the price of goods in the value of service'.

In Builders Association of India v. UOI (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member Constitution bench), it was held that sales tax cannot be imposed on full value of contract. Thus, tax on works contract can be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

Service tax and Vat are mutually exclusive - In Imagic Creative Pvt. Ltd v. CCT (2008) 2 SCC 614 = 12 STT 392 = 12 VST 371 (SC), it has been held that service tax and Vat (sales tax) are mutually exclusive. State of Rajasthan (1993) 66 Taxman 229 = 1993 AIR SCW 2621 = (1993) 1 SCC 364 = 88 STC 204 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) it was held that value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. It was held that value of goods involved in the execution of a works contract will have to be determined by taking into account the value of entire works contract and deducting therefrom the charges towards labour and services, which cover—

(a)

Labour charges for execution of the works

(b)

Amount paid to a sub-contractor for labour and services

(c)

Charges for planning, designing and architect's fees

(d)

Charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of works contract

(e)

Cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of works contract, the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract

(f)

Cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services

(g)

Other similar expenses relatable to supply of labour and services and

(h)

Profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services.

The amounts deductible under these heads will have to be determined in the light of the facts of a particular case, on the basis of the material produced by the contractor. Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are not taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, Legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract.

Calculation of value of property in goods involved in works contract, transferred works contract - In Vat, the dealer can pay Vat (or sales tax) either on value of material on actual basis or under composition scheme. If Vat or sales tax has been paid or payable on actual value of material, that amount will be deductible from total value of works contract to calculate value of taxable service.

The actual words used in the rule as follows - Where value added tax (Vat) has been paid or payable on the actual value of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract, then, such value adopted for the purposes of payment of value added tax or sales tax, shall be taken as the value of transfer of property in goods transferred in the execution of the works contract for determining the value of works contract service under this clause [Rule 2A(i)(c) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006].

However, if the dealer has paid under composition scheme (i.e. at flat rate without separately calculating value of material), the value of material will have to be calculated on basis of actuals. Note that 'value' includes profit relating to goods also.

Vat or sales tax paid will not form part of value for service tax - Gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include value added tax or sales tax, as the case may be, paid, if any, on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

16.3-2 Composition scheme for payment of service tax

Though service tax is legally payable only on value of service and Vat/sales tax is payable on value of goods, in a composite/indivisible contract, it is difficult to find value of goods and services. Hence, both under service tax and State Vat, a provision has been made for payment of tax under composition scheme.

In a composition scheme, tax can be paid on some ad hoc basis at the option of the tax payer.

In State of Kerala v. Builders Association of India 104 STC 134 = (1997) 2 SCC 183 = AIR 1997 SC 3640 = 1997 AIR SCW 977, the position was that a convenient, hassle-free and simple method, which was 'rough and ready method' was evolved by State Government for collection of sales tax on Works Contract. This was optional to assessee. It was held that Legislature can evolve such alternate, simplified and hassle-free methods of assessment, making it optional to assessee. - . - In the field of taxation, legislation must be allowed greater 'play in joints'. Allowance must be made for 'trial and error' by the legislature. - - Contractor who has opted to the alternate method of taxation cannot complain. Having voluntarily, and with the full knowledge of the alternate method of taxation, opted to be governed by it, a contractor cannot be heard to question the validity of relevant sub-sections or the rules - followed in Karnataka State Construction Corporation v. State of Karnataka (2004) 138 STC 75 (Kar HC DB) * Indian Oil Corp v. Prasanna Welding Industries (2007) 7 VST 101 (Gau HC).

In Mycon Construction v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 2156 = 127 STC 105 (SC), it was held that a simplified composition scheme instead of regular assessment, can be evolved, if it is on optional basis. Validity of such provision has been upheld.

Government can make a provision allowing contractors option to opt for composition by paying a sum based on total consideration of contract. - Mytcon Construction v. State of Karnataka (1998) 111 STC 322 (Karn HC).

16.3-4 Illustration

Question - The contract for industrial construction is for Rs. 8,00,000 which includes value of services plus material which is to be supplied by contractor. Service tax paid on input services is Rs. 10,300 and excise duty paid on inputs used for construction is Rs. 41,200, Calculate service tax under composition scheme and also under normal scheme assuming service tax rate of 12.36%, if (a) the contract is covered under State works contract tax and (b) the contract is not covered under works contract service.

Answer - Under composition scheme, value of material supplied by customer free of cost is required to be added. In that case, total value of contract (including material and services supplied free by customer, but excluding value of land) is Rs. 10,00,000. The contractor can opt to pay duty @ 40% on total value i.e. on Rs. 4,00,000, if he is covered under State Works contract tax. Service tax payable will be 12.36% of Rs. 4,00,000 i.e. Rs. 49,440.

The contractor can avail Cenvat credit of Rs. 10,000.

If value of land is not shown separately, then service tax will be payable @ 40% of gross amount which will include value of land plus value of material and services supplied free by customer.

If the contract is covered under State Works Contract Tax, the service tax payable is 4.944% of Rs. 10,00,000 i.e. Rs. 49,440. He can avail Cenvat credit of Rs. 10,320. Thus, net tax payable is Rs. 39,120.

Supply of Ballast to the Railways—Whether it amounts to "sale" or "works contract"?

Their Lordships of the Andhra Pradesh High Court after perusing the material filed by the parties held that the contract in question were only for sale of ballast and not for work and labour and that the contractors were rightly assessed on the turnover of supply of ballast. [Anumolu Seshagri Rao & Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, (1973) 32 STC 51 (A.P.)]

it was held that a contract has to be characterized according to dominant nature (i.e. whether sale or service). The whole contract must be treated as a sale where the dominant intention of the contract is a sale even if some incidental or ancillary services were provided and vice versa. However, dominant nature test would be irrelevant in case of deemed sale of goods under works contract [Though dominant nature is not relevant, the fact remains that contract has to be a works contract i.e. contract for work]. In Vanguard Rolling Shutters v. CST - (1977) 39 STC 372 (SC) = AIR 1977 SC 1505, it was observed that it is difficult to lay down any rule of universal application to decide whether a contract is a works contract or contract for sale of goods. If the contract is primarily for supply of materials at prices agreed and the work or service is incidental to the execution of contract, it will be contract for sale. On the other hand, where contract is primarily a contract of work and labour and materials are supplied in execution of such contract, it is a works contract.

The goods belonged to Government of India but were entrusted to HAL for manufacture of aircraft to be delivered to Air Force. It was held that it is a works contract. It was observed that in contract for work, person producing has no 'property' in the thing produced as a whole, even if part or even whole of material used by him may have been his property. In contract of sale, the thing produced as a whole has individual existence as sole property of the party who produces it sometime before delivery and the property therein passes only under the contract relating thereto to the other party for a price.

The applicant states that the Railway is considering all service buildings as business/commerce establishments and rate charged is 18 per cent (even for original works) and works related to all welfare buildings (i.e., only colonies) are charged at 12 per cent.

The applicant is seeking advance ruling as regards applicability of GST rate for works contract services doing original works with Railways.

HELD: The applicant is executing two types of works wherein, in one set of work the applicant is executing works contract for construction of new buildings and in the second set of work, it is executing works contracts not involving new construction. The correspondence of the applicant with the Railways revealed that in Zonal Works, majority of the works, it is executing are like provision of compound wall to Railway properties, laying of tiles for buildings, plumbing with new pipelines, provisions of new GLR and OHT, Staff recreation like parks, new rain water harvesting structures, painting, renovation of old structures etc. The applicant has claimed before the Railway Authorities that these are all original works as they involve new asset creation or bringing life to unused structures of Railways and these come under the works contract services as per CGST Act. [Para 9]

The issue is basically divided into two categories. One that results in the new buildings and the other repair and reconstruction of the old structures. [Para 10]

The scope of work includes awarding contracts on behalf of DVC for construction of railway infrastructure. The work includes construction of a private siding between Joychandipahar and Bero stations in Adra division of SE Railway, enabling carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS. The Applicant is responsible for passing the bills of the vendors and contractors after necessary scrutiny, and making the payments from a specially designated escrow account in which DVC deposits the requisite amount, and making deduction of statutory taxes and deposit of the same, issuance of tax deduction certificates etc.

HELD: According to Serial No. 3(v)(a) of Notification No. 11/2017-CT (Rate) dated 28/06/2017, as amended from time to time, the composite supply of works contract as defined under section 2(119) of the GST Act, supplied by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to railways, including monorail and metro, is taxable at the rate 12 per cent. Original work, as defined under para 2(zs) of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) dated 28/06/2017, means all new construction involving (i) all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable, and (ii) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise. The term 'railways' is not defined in the GST Act. It, however, is defined under section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989, meaning a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. [Para 4]

It is evident from the above discussion that the scope of work, as outlined in the Applicant's agreement with DVC, is that of works contract, as defined under section 2(119), fit to be called an 'original work' within the meaning ascribed to the term in para 2(zs) of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) dated 28-06-2017, and pertains to 'railways', provided it is meant for public carriage of passengers or goods. It sought advance ruling on the following questions:

1.

What tax rate to be charged by the applicant to main contractor on works contract services pertaining to railways original works contract.

2.

Whether to charge tax rate of 12 per cent GST or 18 per cent GST.

The Authority for Advance Rulings ruled that

-

The tax rate to be charged by the applicant to the main contractor would be at the rate of 6 per cent of CGST and 6 per cent of SGST.

-

The tax rate to be charged would be 12 per cent.

On appeal to Appellate Authority for Advance Ruling by revenue:

HELD: There is no dispute that the services provided by the sub-contractor to its main contractor are composite supply of works contract. The main issue to decide is that the works contract services provided by the applicant are covered under item (v) of Sr. No. 3, describing the construction services, under the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended by the Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 or otherwise. A plain reading of Sr. No. 3, clause (v) reveals that 'composite supply of WCS supplied by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to, railways attracts a tax rate of 6 per cent each of CGST and SGST. The applicant has submitted that they have been sub-contracted by the main contractor to supply WCS and in turn the main contractor is supplying WCS to the railways. From the submissions made by the applicant it appears that the WCS provided by them is the same or a part of the main contract entered into between the main contractor and the railways. It also appears that works contract service is civil works performed by the sub-contractor for the railways and the property in goods (materials used in the supply of Works Contract Service) also gets transferred to the railways directly. In such a case as per the abovementioned clause (v) of Notification No. 20/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 22-10-2017, the works contract service provided by the sub-contractor to the main contractor would be supply of works contract pertaining to railways and, therefore, chargeable to tax at the rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent of CGST and SGST each). However, the benefit of 12 per cent tax rate would be available to the applicant only if the Works Contract services provided by them are Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, supplied by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to railways. Thus, in respect of Sr. No. 3 of Notification No. 11/2017 dated 28-6-2017 as amended up till today, even the sub-contractor providing services of composite supply of works contract in respect of original works pertaining to railways would be covered for concessional rate of GST at the rate of 12 per cent as given under Sr. No. 3 of Notification No. 11/2017 as amended referred above. [Para 5]

The tax rate to be charged by the sub-contractor to the main contractor would be at the rate of 6 per cent of CGST and SGST each, in the present case. The tax rate to be charged would be 12 per cent in the present case. [Para 6]

The courts generally held that the phrase 'public carriage of passengers or goods' cannot be construed in such manner as to exclude from the ambit of 'railways' the sidings built and owned by organizations other than the government. [Para 6] Article 366(20) of the Constitution excludes from the ambit of 'railway' only (a) a tramway wholly within a municipal area and (b) any line of communication wholly situate in one State and declared by Parliament by law not to be a railway. The Parliament excludes by law, apart from the tramways, the lines of rails mentioned under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989, being rails built solely for the purpose of recreation. The term 'public carriage', therefore, cannot be given any meaning that may add more exclusion than specifically provided under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. DVC - a public sector undertaking - is the owner of the railway siding being built. It is meant for carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS. The purpose of the carriage of goods is, therefore, not recreation, but producing public goods like electricity. It is, therefore, not excluded under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. The construction of the private siding that the applicant refers to, therefore, pertains to 'railways'. In view of the foregoing, it was to be ruled that construction of a private railway siding for carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS, as described in the agreement between the applicant and DVC, is a composite supply of works contract taxable at the rate of 12 per cent under Serial No 3(v)(a) of Notification no 11/2017-CT(Rate) dated 28-06-2017. [Para 7]

[Para 8] The revenue has challenged the ruling given by the Advance Ruling Authority by contending that the activities carried out by the sub-contractor will not fall under item (v) of Sr. No. 3 of the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended by the Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018, since there is no specific inclusion of works contract services provided by sub-contractor to main contractor. It further submitted that items (ix) and (x) inserted in the amending Notification No.1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 provide for the concessional rates of 12 per cent and 5 per cent GST to those sub-contractors, who are providing works contract services to the main contractor providing services, specified in item (iii) or item (vi) and item (vii) of the Sr. No. 3 of the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended by the Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 to the Central Government, State Government, Union territory, a local authority; a Governmental Authority or a Government Entity. Thus the amendment carried out in the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 does not provide the concessional rate of GST to the sub-contractor providing composite supply of the works contract to the main contractor who is given works contract by railways. It further argued that the works contract services provided by the sub-contractor to the main contractor should be covered under the residuary entry (xii) of the Notification dated 28-6-2017. The applicant vehemently countered this argument by deposing that the description of the activities covered under item (v) of Sr. No. 3 of the Notification No. 11/2017 -Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended by the Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 are services specific due to the presence of the clause 'pertaining to'. Thus there is no relevance for the provider or recipient of the services in the instant case. If the services fulfil the criteria of the activities/services having description contained the above item (v), then it is immaterial that who is providing services to whom. [Para 9]

There is no merit in the above mentioned contention of the revenue as from the plain reading of item (v) of Sr. No. 3 of the Notification dated 28-6-2017, it is very much clear that any supply of works contract pertaining to the railways including monorail and metro is subject to concessional rate of 12 per cent GST. In the instant case, though the applicant is providing works contract services to its main contractor who has entered into works contract agreement with railways, the composite supply of works contract being carried out by the applicant is ultimately going to the use of railways without being subjected to any change or modification. Thus the said works contract, though undertaken by the sub-contractor, is undoubtedly pertaining to the railways and no one else. Thus the condition specified under item (v) of Sr. No. 3 of Notification dated 28-6-2017 is completely fulfilled. Therefore, the services provided by the sub-contractor would attract concessional rate of 12 per cent GST. [Para 10]

As regards the revenue's contention that there is no specific mention of sub-contractor providing services in Sr. No. 3(v) as provided in items (ix) and (x) which were incorporated into the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 by the amending Notification No. 1/2018-Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018. There was no need to include such sub-contractors in item (v) of the Notification dated 28-6-2017 as there was no confusion whether the sub-contractor will be eligible to such concessional rate of GST, since the activities described under item (v) of Sr. No. 3 of the Notification dated 28-6-2017 are services specific. The service provider and the service recipient are immaterial for the determination of beneficiary of this concessional rate of GST. That is, if the works contract services provided by the main contractor or sub-contractor are pertaining to the railways, the concessional rate of 12 per cent GST is allowed to the person who carries out such works contract pertaining to railways. The only condition in (a) of item (v) is that,

HEADNOTE: Classification of services - Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Supply and installation - Heading No. 9954 [Construction services] - Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited (DFFCCIL) has awarded a contract to one 'A' (main contractor) for performance of works relating to design, construction, supply, installation, testing and commissioning of electrification, signaling, telecommunication and associated works of double track railways lines under construction for Bhaupur-Khurja section - 'A' (main contractor) has subcontracted performance of certain works and services of main contract to applicant - Whether contract work of applicant to main contractor is covered under Entry No. 3(v) of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 and liable to tax at 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST or 12 per cent IGST) with effect from 22-8-2017 - Held, yes [Paras 4.10 and 5][In favour of assessee]GST: Where Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited has awarded a contract to one 'A' (main contractor) for performance of works relating to railways and 'A' has sub-contracted performance of certain works and services of main contract to applicant, contract work of applicant to main contractor is covered under Entry No. 3(v) of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017

FACT: The Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited (DFFCCIL) has awarded a contract to one 'A' (main contractor) for performance of the works relating to the design, construction, supply, installation, testing and commissioning of electrification, signaling, telecommunication and associated works of double track railway lines under construction for Bhaupur-Khurja section.

'A' (main contractor) has subcontracted the performance of certain works and services of the main contract to the applicant consisting supply and installation, testing and commissioning of automatic signaling equipment of indoor and outdoor, LC gates required as per the requirement of DFFCCIL under the main contract.

The applicant sought advance ruling in respect of the following questions:

(a)

What is the rate of tax for the subcontractor who executes the works contract work like supply of goods or services or both pertaining to Railways based on the order received from the main contractor who got the work order directly from Railways.

(b)

Does the rate of tax of 6 per cent as per Sl. No. 3(v) of the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax, dated 28-6-2017, as amended, applicable to subcontractors or not.

(c)

If the answer to the question No. (b) is yes, then from which date it is applicable.

HELD: The contract of the applicant with the main contractor should satisfy the following conditions to get covered under Entry No. 3(v) of the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017:

(a)

The contract must be a composite supply of works contract.

(b)

The works must be a construction, erection, commissiong or installation of original works.

(c)

It must pertain to Railways. [Para 4.4]

In the instant case, the contract is for supply and installation, testing and commissioning of automatic signaling equipment of indoor and outdoor, LC gates and involves excavation of pits, casting and plastering and other parts which involve construction, erection, commissioning and installation of original works. Hence the second condition is satisfied.

As the contract is related to an immovable property, the entire contract is covered under the definition of works contract under section 2(119). Hence the first condition is also satisfied. [Para 4.5]

The main issue is whether this is a contract pertaining to Railways. The main contractor has obtained the contract from Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited and then subcontracted to the applicant. The work is related to supply and installation, testing and commissioning of automatic signaling equipment of indoor and outdoor, LC gates as per the requirement of DFCCIL. [Para 4.6]

Since the works related to railways network, the contract can be said to be pertaining to Railways. The term pertaining to Railways is more expansive and includes other establishments other than Indian Railways. Hence the contract is pertaining to Railways. [Para 4.8]

HEADNOTE: Classification of services - Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Works contract - Heading No. 9954 [Construction services] - Section 2(119) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017/Section 2(119) of the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 - Works contract - Applicant has constructed residential complexes for Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) - Whether since control over BDA rests with Govt. of Karnataka, BDA is a Government entity - Held, yes - Whether activity undertaken by applicant involves supply of both goods and services and is in relation to an immovable property and, hence, is a 'works contract' within meaning of section 2(119) - Held, yes - Whether transaction of applicant would be a supply of works contract services covered under clause (a) of Entry No. 3(vi) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, taxable at rate of 12 per cent GST - Held, yes [Paras 10.8, 10.9.2  11]GST : Where applicant has constructed residential complexes for Bangalore Development Authority (BDA), activity undertaken by applicant is supply of works contract service to a Govt. entity covered under Entry No. 3(vi) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, taxable at rate of 12 per cent GST

FACT: The applicant is engaged in the business of Civil Construction and Works Contract Services. The applicant has applied for the civil construction work tender with Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) with respect to construction of residential complexes/row of residential houses.

The said project is allotted to the applicant and the same has been executed by the Company through appointing various contractors.

The applicant has sought advance ruling in respect of the question as to whether the activity undertaken by the applicant is covered under section 2(119); whether Bangalore Development Authority is a Government Authority as per the provisions of GST Law and the rate of tax applicable to the transaction of the applicant and more so whether the transactions are covered under entry 3(vi) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 (as amended).

According to applicant, its activity of construction of residential house and residential complex with respect to following BDA projects (to Government Authority) are squarely covered under the definition of Works Contract and their activity will be considered as supply of services.

The applicant submits that as per the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), the activity undertaken by the applicant to BDA i.e., Government Authority is liable for GST at 6 per cent CGST and 6 per cent SGST.

HELD: For a works contract to be covered under Entry No. 3(vi) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 the following conditions needs to be satisfied:

(a)

The recipient of services must be a Government Entity and in this case, Bangalore Development Authority;

(b)

The works contract services supplied by the applicant must be in relation to the works covered under (a), (b) or (c) of Entry 3(vi);

(c)

The recipient of such services must have procured these services in relation to a work entrusted to it by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or local authority. [Para 10.6]

Bangalore Development Authority is an authority established by the State Government under the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 and it is entrusted with the activity of development of the City of Bangalore and areas adjacent thereto and for matters connected therewith. [Para 10.7]

The control over the entity rests with the Government of Karnataka and, hence, the Bangalore Development Authority satisfies both the conditions and, hence, is considered as a Government Entity within the meaning of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 28-6-2017. [Para 10.8]

The applicant is constructing a Housing Project at two places in and around Bangalore. The Bangalore Development Authority in its tender has stated that it has taken up construction of housing in and around Bangalore City as designed by the Government of Karnataka. Since this is a residential project for general public, the same is not covered under clause (b) or (c) of Entry 3(vi). [Para 10.9.1]

The applicant in its written submissions has stated that it is also eligible for benefit of Sl. (a)

The applicant is constructing a Housing Project at two places in and around Bangalore. The Bangalore Development Authority in its tender has stated that it has taken up construction of housing in and around Bangalore City as designed by the Government of Karnataka. Since this is a residential project for general public, the same is not covered under clause (b) or (c) of Entry 3(vi). [Para 10.9.1] The projects of the applicant are involving the supply of both goods and services and is in relation to an immovable property and, hence, is a 'works contract' within the meaning of section 2(119) of CGST Act. This works contract is for a construction of a civil structure and since it is a residential real estate project, the works is predominantly for use other than commerce, industry or any other business or profession and, hence, it is covered under clause (a) of the Entry No. 3(vi) of the Notification, subject to the conditions. [Para 10.9.2]

Regarding the issue as to whether the recipient has procured the said services in relation to a work entrusted to it by the State Government, it is observed that the Bangalore Development Authority Act, which is passed by the State Legislature, has entrusted the activity of development of the City of Bangalore and areas adjacent thereto and for matters connected therewith to the BDA and the Authority has to obtain the sanction of the Government of Karnataka for every scheme they propose to implement. Hence, the condition is also satisfied. [Para 10.9.3]

Hence the services provided by the applicant to the Bangalore Development Authority in relation to the construction of two housing complexes referred to in the application are covered under entry no. 3(vi)(a) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 (as amended) and is liable to tax at 6 per cent under the CGST Act, 2017. Similarly, the services provided is covered under entry no. 3(vi)(a) of Notification (11/2017) No. FD 48 CSL 2017 dated 29-6-2017 (as amended) and is liable to tax at 6 per cent under the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017. [Para 10.9.4]

Thus, activity undertaken by the applicant as enumerated in the application is covered under section 2(119) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act and is a works contract services. Bangalore Development Authority is a Government Entity as per the provisions of the GST Law. The transaction of the applicant would be a supply of works contract services covered under clause (a) of Entry No. 3(vi) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 (as amended) and not under Entry No. 3(ii) or 3(iv) or 3(v) of the said notification. [Para 11]

Previously, under the Notification dated 28-6-2017, composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 was attracting duty at the rate of 18 per cent under Heading 9954 (Construction Services) at Sl. No. 3.

Vide Notification No. 20/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 22-8-2017, the entries against serial number 3 for item (iii) in column (3) and the entries relating thereto in the Notification No. 1/2018- Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018, were substituted with (v) Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 , supplied by way of construction, erection, commissioning or installation of original works pertaining to,- (a) railways, excluding monorail and metro; attracting the duty rate at the rate of 12 per cent.

Later, vide Notification No. 1/2018- Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018, the Notification No. 8/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), was amended and the word `excluding' was substituted by 'including' also classifying that the Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 provided by a sub-contractor to the main contractor providing services specified in item (iii) or item (vi) above to the Central Government, State Government, Union territory, a local authority, a Governmental Authority or a Government Entity would attract duty at the rate of 12 per cent.

Since, in the instant case, the composite supply of work contract is being provided by a sub-contractor to the main contractor i.e. Government Authority, the same shall be covered under the above amendment carried out vide the above notification dated 25-1-2018, the same shall now attract duty at the rate 12 per cent.[Para 9.4]

In view of the above, both the members unanimously rule as under;

(i)

A contract shall be treated as Composite Contract under GST if it involves making of supply of goods and services which are inter-connected and inter­-dependent on each other even though BOQ mentions separate value of goods and services.

(ii)

A pre-GST period contract shall be treated as Composite Contract in GST if it satisfies the condition of Composite Supply.

(iii)

A contract for designing, installation and setting up of Automatic Fare Collection System for Lucknow Metro Project will amount to Work Contract.

(iv)

GST will be charged at the rate of 12 per cent in terms of Notification No. 1/2018- Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 being composite services supplied to a Government entity procured by the said entity in relation to work entrusted to it by the Central and State Government.[Para 10]

, Staff recreation like parks, new rain water harvesting structures, painting, renovation of old structures etc. The applicant has claimed before the Railway Authorities that these are all original works as they involve new asset creation or bringing life to unused structures of Railways and these come under the works contract services as per CGST Act. [Para 9]

The issue is basically divided into two categories. One that results in the new buildings and the other repair and reconstruction of the old structures. [Para 10] The rate of tax applicable in terms of Entry No. 3(v) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is 6 per cent under CGST. [Para 10.1]

Entry 3(v) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is related to works contract services supplied to Railways, which is construction or erection or commissioning or installation of original works. The entire dispute is regarding what are 'original works'. [para 10.2]

The term 'original works' has been defined in clause (zs) of para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 10.3]

On examination of definition of 'original work', it is seen that only 'additions or alterations made to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are made to make them workable' are treated as original works and not all repairs and maintenance services. [Para 10.4]

The works carried out by the applicant are analyzed and it is found that they involve two types of works - one being new construction and other being repairs of old structures. In as far as construction of new structures are concerned which are constructed where nothing existed before would definitely fall under the realm of 'original works'. [Para 10.5]

But in case of constructions which are made where the structures already existed, the same can be classified as (a) where the additions and alternations are made to the abandoned structures on land or damages structures on land to make them workable; (b) repairs of already existing structures which are in working condition and (c) construction services on structures not on land.

It is pertinent to note that only those works contract services covered under (a) are to be treated as 'original works' and not those covered under related to (b) and (c). The meaning of the words 'structures on land' needs to be analysed as only these qualify for the reduced rate of tax. [Para 10.6]

Both the contextual meaning in relation to railways is that the structure should be something which is built from parts, i.e., a building, or other constructed ones. Secondly, these constructed structures should be on land to be covered under the scope of the entry. All these point to the scope of the entry that the structures which are directly on the land are included. Further, these structures must be damaged to the extent that the same cannot be used and the activity of works contract services, if executed to make these unusable structures reusable, would cover under this entry for reduced rate of tax. [Para 11]

All repairs made to buildings do not constitute 'original works'. It is only those services executed to make an unusable building usable again is covered under 'original works'. [Para 13]

The Railways Department is a Central government Department and, hence, it is clear that the services provided to them if it is for a purpose other than for business, then the same would be covered under entry 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. However, the services of repairs, maintenance, renovation and alterations of residential complex meant for use of the Railway employees are covered under entry 3(vi) of the Notification and, hence, eligible for tax at 6 per cent CGST. [Para 14]

As regards the question of rate of tax, it is submitted by the applicant that the contract is a single contract and it consists of multiple works. On the question whether this contract amounts to a composite supply or mixed supply or a bunch of separate supplies, it is seen that the same cannot be a composite supply of works contracts as there is no principal supply and the works are not naturally bundled. It cannot be a mixed supply also because the valuations of each of the supply of works are valued separately and they would amount to separate contracts. Hence, there is no common price for all the contracts. Hence, it can be decided that each of the works mentioned in a schedule is a separate contract in itself and this is bolstered by the fact that the works are not in the same place and also are different in nature. [Para 15]

Now coming to the issue of construction of Directors Bungalow and construction of staff-faculty quarters. It is seen that the applicant has been awarded construction of Directors Bungalow, 40 nos. staff quarters, 84 nos. Faculty Quarters in the IIT Campus, Bhubaneswar. It is also observed that the civil construction of residential quarters is not the primary work entrusted to IIT, Bhubaneswar. Accordingly, why the benefit of concessional rate at the rate of 12 per cent GST should be available to this particular works contract awarded to the applicant? The intention of the Legislature has been to allow concessional rate to such work which has been entrusted to a Government entity for public interest in general, but extrapolating and extending this concessional rate to any or all activities of IIT, Bhubaneswar will not only be unwarranted but also defeat the very purpose of concessional rate. Hence, construction of Directors Bungalow and construction of staff/faculty quarters is out of purview of exemption provided under Notification No. 11/2017-C.T. The works are supply and installation of lines and equipments meant for telecommunication, signalling in the CMRL project and not related to any civil engineering work. Therefore, the supply of the applicant to Siemens is covered under SAC 9954, more specifically under SAC 995461 and the first requirement of the entry stands satisfied. [Para 11.1]

The second criteria to be satisfied is that the supply should be a 'Composite Supply'. In the case at hand from the purchase order furnished by the applicant, it is seen that there is supply of goods (equipments, goods, etc.) and services (installation, testing, etc.) for a particular cost center/Line and the work is considered to be done on that basis. Thus, there is a natural bundle of goods and services per cost center/Line and the supply is construed to be made when the entire supply of the line/cost center is made. Hence, the supply of the applicant is a composite supply and this criterion is satisfied. [Para 11.2]

The next criterion to be examined is whether the said composite supply is a 'Works Contract' as defined under section 2(119).

From the definition, a work shall be treated as Works Contract if that work is done for land or earth or for immovable property and there is transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract. Immovable property cannot be moved. It cannot be separated from the land or earth. If it is detached it shall have to destroy. In the case at hand, the 'Employer's Requirements, Particular Specifications-4B Telecommunication General Specification' - gives the outline summary of the various systems and sub-systems which are applicable to the Telecommunication scope and the outline description of the works said to be the works of the applicant. On going through same, it is observed that the work involves installation of the individual systems at platforms, stations, other select locations along the corridor and is integrated at the Operation Control Corridor (OCC) at Koyambedu and the Telecommunications Infrastructure implementation is to be synchronized with the civil construction phases. Further the scope of works of the applicant like Public Address and Voice Alarm System, CCTV System, Passenger Information Display System, Office Telephone System, etc. requires installation on specific locations, namely ceiling and the like and these goods once installed, may not necessarily be damaged while removing. The applicant has not established with documents that the works contracted to them are to be executed on immovable property as required under definition of 'Works Contract' given above. The applicant has stated that in the Pre-GST regime, under Service Tax, the applicant being a supplier of Works Contract Service relating to infrastructure project of railways, in capacity of sub-contractor was exempted from service tax and had claimed the benefit of entry 3(v) of Notification 11/2017 - C.T. Schedule II of the CGST Act clearly mentions that the following are supply of services :

a.

construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly,

In view of this, the applicant contends that scope of the activity of works contract cannot be restricted to an activity undertaken only in relation to immovable property and the scope can be extended to the services rendered in relation to plant and machinery also. Firstly the term 'works contract' is clearly defined in section 2(119). The definition is self explanatory and leaves no doubt that it is in relation to an immovable property only. Secondly, in section 17(5), the term 'plant and machinery' is also defined. Here the machinery, apparatus and equipment is secured to the earth by way of a foundation or structural support. This foundation or the structural support is meant to impart stability to the machine while working. It, however, does not impart the machine/equipment the same degree of permanence that a building acquires when built on its foundation. Here the equipment is fitted on the foundation and the same can be removed and relocated without damaging it. The same does not hold true for a building or an immovable property. Therefore, the inference drawn from the provisions of section 17(5) are erroneous.

In the second question the applicant seeks to know the rate of tax applicable on the activities proposed to be undertaken by them. Further, section 2 of CGST Act, 2017 and MPGST Act, 2017 defines works contract as a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of such contract; The composite supply of works contract as defined at section 2 of CGST Act, 2017 and MPGST Act, 2017 is treated as supply of service in terms of serial No. 6, Schedule II of CGST Act, 2017 and MPGST Act, 2017. [Para 7.9]

In the instant case, the applicant had awarded work to the successful bidder for Supply of Materials and Erection respectively. Therefore, the contract entered by the applicant squarely falls under the works contract and falls under entry No. (ii) of Sl. No. 3 of the table of Notification No. 11 of 2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended from time to time and corresponding notifications under MPGST Act, 2017 the applicable rate of tax is 18 per cent (9 per cent under Central tax and 9 per cent State tax). [Para 7.10]

Thus it is ruled as follows:

The applicant is not entitled for the benefit of concessional rate of GST at rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent under Central tax and 6 per cent State tax) for the said projects in terms of Notification No.24 of 2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 21-9-2017 read with Notification No. 31/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 13-10-2017.

2.

The applicable rate of tax is 18 per cent (9 per cent under Central tax and 9 per cent State tax).

3.

This ruling is valid subject to the provisions under section 103(2) until and unless declared void under section 104(1) of the GST Act. [Para 8]

By relying upon the above principles i.e. l) mode of object of annexation 2) mode of annexation whether the plant was installed merely to make it wobble free or it is affixed to the earth. Also, it needs to be seen whether 'the setting up of the plant itself is not intended to be permanent at a given place. The plant can be moved and is indeed moved after the project for which it is set up is completed.' [Para 52] Now, that the above judgments have been discussed, it is to be seen whether the present issue i.e. composite supply of a goods and services would be termed as immovable property or not. In order to answer this question, the nature of a contract as well as documents submitted by the appellant in relation to execution of the project have to be gone through. It is seen from the nature of contract which envisages installation, which involves civil works to erect the structure for execution of the project in its entirety. It is an entire system comprising of a variety of different structures which are installed after a lot of prior work which involves detailed designing, ground work. Appellant has also submitted few photographs of the project which clearly shows that the structure is attached to the earth with the help of civil work. The photographs indicate the magnitude of the work done. Further foundations in cement concrete, cement concrete walls as well as cement concrete structures are constructed during the execution of the project. The mode of annexation shows that the groundwork, being the necessary foundation, is an important part of the project. The object of annexation, as said earlier, cannot be to make it movable from one place to the other. It simply cannot be equated to the Asphalt mix (the issue in Solid & Concrete Engg. case) which was intended to be moved from one place to other. Hence considering the scope of the work and the facts revealed by the photographs, it can be very well said that completion of the installation, erection of the total project is resulting into immovable property. Hence the total project assigned to the appellant is nothing but composite supply of works contract as envisaged under section 2 (119). [Para 53]

Further in additional submission the appellant has relied on the Order of Advance Ruling Authority in case of NR Energy Solutions India (P.) Ltd., In re [2019] 106 taxmann.com 245 (AAR - Maharashtra) and sub-mitted that the Advance Ruling Authority had taken divergent view and held that supply of Relay & Protection Panels and Substation Automation System (SAS), complete design, manufacture, packing, insurance, transport and delivery to sites, training, installation, testing and commissioning of protection panels with SAS compatible to IEC 61850 protocol, to control and operate the 220 KV, 132 KV & 33 KV feeders, Power Transformers and equipment cannot be treated as works contract. From the order of the Advance Ruling Authority in case of NR Energy Solutions India (P.) Ltd. (supra) it can be seen that the terms of the contract are Ltd. to supply and installation of Relay & Protection Panels and Sub-station Automation System (SAS) which is a small part of system compare to the whole contract awarded to appellant. The appellant cannot equate the contract of supply and installation of certain part of the system with the whole contract in the present case of on shore and off shore supply of goods and services for complete execution of +320KV, 2 X 1000MW VSC based HVDC Terminals and DC XLPE Cable system between Pugalur and North Trichur. Hence ratio of advance ruling in case of NR Energy Solutions India (P.) Ltd. (supra) is not applicable to instant case. [Para 57]

Accordingly, it is held that from the conjoined and harmonious reading of various clauses of Third contract and Fifth contract awarded to the appellant and their interdependency under the whole contract comprising of six contracts, it can be safely concluded that the agreement for setting up for + 320KV, 2 X 1000MW VSC based HVDC Terminals and DC XLPE Cable system, between Pugalur and North Trichur associated with HVDC Bipole link between Western region (Raigarh, Chhattisgarh) and Southern region (Pugalur, Tamil Nadu - North Trichur, Kerala) is a composite works contract as defined under section 2(119) of GST Act and taxable at the rate of 18 per cent and hence:

i.

The transportation services provided by the appellant being part of the whole works contract will be taxable at the rate of 18 per cent as works contract services and will not be eligible for the exemption as provided in Serial No. 18 of the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 and Notification No. 12/2017-State Tax (Rate), dated the 29-6-2017.

ii.

Order passed by the Maharashtra Advance Ruling Authority in Siemens Ltd. In re [2019] 106 taxmann.com 178 is confirmed. [Para 58]
