The Electricity Distribution Companies are procuring these services from the applicant in relation to a work entrusted to it by the State Government, which is supply of electricity to consumers and the fifth condition is also satisfied.[Para 11.7]

The contract is for construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion of original works. The contract is a new construction involving erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures and hence the third condition is also satisfied.[Para 11.8] The issue under detailed discussion is whether the works are meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. The Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in selling of electricity to the consumers and are collecting consideration and electrical energy is considered as 'goods'. Hence the Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in the sale of goods or in general, supply of goods to the consumers for consideration. The Explanation clause inserted which provides that for the purposes of this item, the term 'business' shall not include any activity or transaction undertaken by the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority in which they are engaged as public authorities does not apply as they are not activities undertaken by the Central Government or State Government or a local authority.[Para 11.9]

Further, from the definition of business as defined in clause (17) of section 2 of the CGST Act, it is clear that any activity of trade, commerce, manufacture, etc. or any other similar activity is included in the definition of business and it is immaterial whether it is done for a pecuniary benefit, and any activity done in connection with or incidental or ancillary to such activity is also included in the scope of 'business'.[Para 11.11]

The Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in the supply of goods as already explained and hence they are involved in the business of supplying goods. They also receive consideration for the supply of electricity. The predominant activity of the Electricity Distribution Companies is to supply Electricity and the works executed by the applicant are used for this only predominant activity and hence are original works meant predominantly for use for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. Hence, the contracts in question do not satisfy the fourth condition required for them to be covered under the Entry No.3(vij(a) of Notification No.11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) as amended from time to time.[Para 11.12]

In view of the foregoing, it is ruled that the services provided by the applicant to the Electricity Supply Companies (wholly owned Government of Karnataka Undertakings) by way of construction erection, commissioning, installation, completion, etc, are not covered under entry 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No.12/2017- Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, or under entry 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No.8/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, as amended from time to time and consequentially are not eligible to be taxed at a lower rate of 12 per cent GST and hence are liable to be taxed at 18 per cent GST.[Para 12]

Sl. No. 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is the relevant entry which prescribes GST rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST+6 per cent SGST) in respect of services provided to the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory, a local authority, a Government Authority or a Government Entity by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of civil structure or any other original works meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. Thus to attract rate of tax at 12 per cent under Sl. No. 3(vi)(a), the specified service should primarily be provided to the Central Government/State Government/Union Territory/local authority/Government Authority/Government Entity and must be used for other than commercial, industrial, or any other business or professional activity.

Now it is required to examine the question whether the contractee in the instant case, i.e., TSSPDCL falls under the specified categories of recipient viz. Central Government/State Government/Union Territory/local authority/Governmental Authority/Government Entity on not. The phrase 'Government Entity' is defined under the Explanation appended to Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. The same reads as:

'Government Entity' means an authority or a board or any other body including a society, trust, corporation.

(i)

Set up by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature; or

(ii)

Established by any Government,

with 90 per cent or more participation by way of equity or control, to carry out a function entrusted by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or a local authority.

It is apparent from the schedule concerning 'shareholding of promoter' of the annual accounts of TSSPDCL that 100 per cent shares of the company were held by the Governor of Telangana. This clear indicates that the Government of Telangana have 100 per cent control over TSSPDCL. Thus TSSPDCL is evidently covered under the definition of 'Government Entity'.

The next issue to be decided in this regard is whether the impugned services supplied by the applicant are for the works which are used for other than commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. As per the details furnished by the applicant, the works undertaken are for execution/implementation of various projects for (i) Capacitor Bank Works in Nalgonda etc., (ii) HVDS-High Voltage Distribution Systems in Suryapet used for agricultural feeders. The applicant further stated that the Government of Telangana is reimbursing the money to TSSPDCL on behalf of the customers for agricultural services rendered. Thus TSSPDCL is not rendering any non-commercial services inasmuch as it is getting reimbursed for its activity on behalf of its customers. Therefore, this activity cannot be termed as other than commercial/business purposes.

The impugned works undertaken are for business/commercial purposes. Therefore, the benefit of concessional rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST) is not applicable to the services supplied by the applicant. Further the services supplied by the applicant are subjected to 18 per cent (9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST) in terms of Sl. No. 3(xii) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

Ruling

The applicant is not entitled for the benefit of concessional rate of GST at 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST) in respect of the works quoted in application in terms of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 2-6-2017 or any other concessional rate.

Whether a particular person is a Governmental Authority or a Government Entity is to be decided in terms of the definition adduced under Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 by applying the facts of each case.

The impugned works are used for commercial/business activities in view of the facts and circumstances and accordingly the same are taxable under GST Act.

The applicable rate of tax is 18 per cent (9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST) for the services referred to by the applicant. [Para 8]

The question is whether the transaction is covered under Sl. No. 3(vi) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.[Para 7.4]

As per entry No.3(vi) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, composite supply of works contract as defined in section 2(119) of the CGST Act, 2017, provided to the Government Entity by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of a civil structure or any other original works meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession is liable to tax at the rate of 6 per cent under the CGST Act. Similar notification also exists under the Karnataka Goods and Services Tax Act and also under the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act (wherein the tax rate is 12 per cent IGST).[Para 7.5]

The applicant is undertaking a contract of works contract of construction of a civil structure or any other original works for the Airport Authorities of India. The Department of Personnel and Training, Government of India has shown in the company profile that the shareholding of the Government of India in the Airport Authorities of India is 100 per cent and hence the AAI is a Government Entity.[Para 7.6]

Further, the issue is whether the constructed works is a civil structure or any other original works. The runway and the apron etc. are structures which bear the load of the aircraft and provide a stable surface for the aircraft to operate. These are, therefore, civil structures. As per the AAI letters submitted by the applicant it is clear that the applicant is engaged in the extension of the runway and construction of new aprons and allied areas. Extension of the runway requires a new construction to be carried out and so does the apron and other areas. Therefore the applicant is engaged in construction of new civil structures. The term 'original works' is not defined in the Act, but the definition is provided in the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, to mean all new constructions;

(i)

all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable;

(ii)

erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise.

The applicant is, therefore, engaged in construction of new civil structures. The activities carried out by the applicant are covered under the relevant serial number of the Notification. [Para 7.7]

The next issue is whether these works are meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession? In this regard, the original works done by the applicant are for use by the Airports Authority of India for supplying services to the Airway operations and hence is in the course of business. The airlines that use the runway and the aprons etc. constructed by the applicant work with a view to earn profits. They are engaged in commerce and business. Entry at Serial number 3(vi)(a) specifically provides that works be 'meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession'. As the works carried out by the applicant are used in the process of commerce and business, the applicant does not qualify for the works to be classified under Serial number 3(vi)(a). Hence the works contract performed by the applicant cannot be considered as covered under Serial No. 3(vi) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, liable to tax at 6 per cent, but are more appropriately covered under Serial No.3(ii) of the of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, liable to tax at 9 per cent.[Para 7.8]

An explanation has been inserted to the above entry by Notification No. 17/2018 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 26-7-2018, which provides that for the purposes of this item, the term 'business' shall not include any activity or transaction undertaken by the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority in which they are engaged as public authorities. Even with this insertion, the activities or transactions undertaken by the Central Government, State Government and a Local Authority, in which they are engaged as public authorities alone are to be excluded from the scope of 'business' for the purposes of this entry. This Explanation does not exclude a Government Entity and hence the situation remains unchanged even by the aforesaid insertion of explanation so far as the activity of the applicant is concerned. [Para 7.9]

The transaction of the applicant is verified where in applicant got work orders from the Principal contractor for the construction of 2 and 3 BHK Housing projects on behalf of Bangalore Development Authority.

Further on verification of the records it is observed that Bengaluru Development Authority has issued work orders to main contractor Gowri Infra Engineers Private Limited (GIEPL) to construct 2 and 3-BHK Housing Project on lump sum turnkey basis based on Tender's Own design under Two cover System. [Para 11.3]

The main issue is the rate of tax applicable to the transaction of the applicant and more so whether the transactions are covered under entry 3(vi) of the Notification No.11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 (as amended). The applicant himself has clearly stated that his transactions are not covered under entry No. 3(ii) of the said notification and hence they are not considered as the same is also agreed by this Authority. [Para 11.4]

The Entry No.3(vi) of the Notification No.11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 (as amended by Notification No.24/2017- Central Tax (Rate), dated 21-9-2017), reads as under:

'(vi) Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, provided to the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory, a local authority, a Governmental Authority or Government Entity by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of -

(a)

a civil structure or any other original works meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession;

(b)

a structure meant predominantly for use as (i) an educational, (ii) clinical, or (iii) an art or cultural establishment; or

(c)

a residential complex predominantly meant for self-use or the use of their employees or other persons specified in paragraph 3 of Schedule III of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017.'

and the condition stated in the Column (5) of the Notification is 'Provided that where the services are supplied to a Government Entity, they should have been procured by the said entity in relation to a work entrusted to it by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or local authority, as the case maybe.'[Para 11.5]

The Government Entity is defined in clause (x) of paragraph 4 of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, (as amended) to mean an authority or a board or any other body including a society, trust, corporation,

(i)

set up by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature; or

(ii)

established by any Government,

with 90 per cent. or more participation by way of equity or control, to carry out a function entrusted by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or a local authority. [Para 11.6]

For a works contract to be covered under this entry, the following conditions needs to be satisfied:

(a)

The recipient of services must be a Government Entity and in this case, Bangalore Development Authority;

(b)

The works contract services supplied by the main contractor must be in relation to the works covered under (a), (b) or (c);

(c)

The recipient of such services must have procured these services in relation to a work entrusted to it by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or local authority. [Para 11.7]

Regarding the first question, Bangalore Development Authority is an authority established by the State Government under the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 and it is entrusted with the activity of development of the City of Bangalore and areas adjacent thereto and for matters connected therewith. [Para 11.8]

It is very clear from section 3(3) of the BDA Act that the control over the entity rests with the Government of Karnataka and hence the Bangalore Development Authority satisfies both the conditions and hence is considered as a Government Entity within the meaning of the Notification No.11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 11.9]

all new constructions

Definition of 'Railways' as per section 2(31) of The Railway Act, 1989 as below: (31) "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods, and includes—

(a)

Needless to mention here that there is no stipulation in the said entry claimed for exemption supra, that this work must be executed to the Railways but it is sufficient that it must be "pertaining to Railways", meaning therein that the supplier and the recipient is immaterial. (ii) Composite Supply:

As per Sec. 2(30) of CGST Act of 2017, 'Composite Supply' is a kind of supply made by a taxable person to a recipient that includes two or more taxable supplies of goods or services or both, or their combination, that are naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction to each other in the ordinary course of business out of which one constitutes to be a Principal Supply.

That, in their case, the supply is a composite that includes taxable services of construction service (labour) and taxable goods (construction material) for execution of the works. Both the taxable service and goods are naturally bundled and interrelated with each and hence falls under composite supply. The Company has to provide both labour service and material without which the construction will not be completed and the entire work is to be provided by the Company only. Original work is defined para 2(zs) of the Notification 12/2017 Central Tax (Rate) as below:

The word 'railways' is not defined under GST Act however the same is defined as mentioned above in section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989 and also to be interpreted in its popular sense. "But while construing a word which occurs in a statute or statutory instrument in the absence of any definition in that very document it must be given the same meaning which people conversant with the subject matter understand it. It is hazardous to interpret a word in accordance with its definition in another statute or statutory instrument and more so when such statute is statutory instrument is not dealing with any cognate subject".

Therefore, unless a mention is specifically made to such dissimilar provisions, a reference to the CGST Act would also mean a reference to the same provision under the UPGST Act. Further for the purposes of this Advance Ruling, a reference to such a similar provision under the CGST Act/UPGST Act would be mentioned as being under the 'CGST Act'.

3.2 Simply put, a works contract is essentially a contract of service which may also involve supply of goods in the execution of the contract. It is basically a composite supply of both services and goods, with the service element being dominant in the contract between parties. In a general sense, a contract of works, may relate to both immovable and immovable property. E.g., if a sub-contractor, undertakes a sub-contract for the building work, it would be a works contract in relation to immovable property. Similarly, if a composite supply in relation to movable property such as fabrication/painting/annual maintenance contracts etc. is undertaken, the same would come within the ambit of the broad definition of a works contract.

Position under GST: Under GST laws, the definition of "Works Contract" has been restricted to any work undertaken for an "Immovable Property" unlike the existing VAT and Service Tax provisions where works contracts for movable properties were also considered.

The Works Contracts has been defined in Section 2(119) of the CGST Act, 2017 as "works contract" means a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of such contract."

The Railways Act, 1989, distinguishes between, but covers, Government Railway under section 2(20) and Non-Government Railway under section 2(25) of the Act. It, therefore, includes scope for railways under both Government and private administrations.

5. It is evident from the above discussion that the scope of work, as outlined in the Applicant's agreement with DVC, is that of works contract, as defined under section 2(119) of the GST Act, fit to be called an 'original work' within the meaning ascribed to the term in para 2(zs) of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) dated 28/06/2017, and pertains to 'railways', provided it is meant for public carriage of passengers or goods.

6. Whether the phrase "public carriage of passenger or goods" prevents a private siding from being included in the definition of 'railways' has repeatedly come up for judicial scrutiny. The courts generally held that the phrase 'public carriage of passengers or goods' cannot be construed in such manner as to exclude from the ambit of 'railways' the sidings built and owned by organizations other than the government.

[Cases relied upon: DMRC v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi [2008] 103 DRJ 369 (Delhi); CCE v. Anand Construction [2017] 51 STR 435 (CESTAT - New Delhi); SMS Infrastructure Ltd. v. CCE [2017] 47 STR 17 (CESTAT - Mumbai)]

7. Art 366(20) of the Constitution excludes from the ambit of 'railway' only (a) a tramway wholly within a municipal area and (b) any line of communication wholly situate in one State and declared by Parliament by law not to be a railway. The Parliament excludes by law, apart from the tramways, the lines of rails mentioned under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989, being rails built solely for the purpose of recreation. The term 'public carriage', therefore, cannot be given any meaning that may add more exclusion than specifically provided under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989.

DVC – a public sector undertaking - is the owner of the railway siding being built. It is meant for carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS. The purpose of the carriage of goods is, therefore, not recreation, but producing public goods like electricity. It is, therefore, not excluded under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989.

The construction of the private siding that the Applicant refers to, therefore, pertains to 'railways'.

In view of the foregoing, we rule as under

RULING

Construction of a private railway siding for carriage of coal and oil fuel to Raghunathpur TPS, as described in the agreement between the Applicant and DVC, is a composite supply of works contract taxable @ 12% under Serial No. 3(v)(a) of Notification no 11/2017-CT(Rate) dated 28.06.2017.

This Ruling is valid subject to the provisions under Section 103(2) until and unless declared void under Section 104(1) of the GST Act.

Provided further that the appropriate assessing authority shall determine the turnover taxable as applicable as per the rates of tax specified in the Schedules from the total taxable turnover ascertained after allowing deductions on account of labour charges and other like charges, on the basis of the records available before him and making such verifications as may be necessary in this behalf:

Provided also that the appropriate assesssing authortiy shall record in writing the reasons of determination of taxable quantum and applicable tax rate on such taxable quantum.]

(2) Where the dealer proves to the satisfaction of the prescribed authority that tax on the turnover of goods supplied by him in the course of execution of works contract, has been paid by his sub-contractor, the dealer shall not be liable to pay tax again on the turnover of such goods.

(3) Where a sub-contractor proves to the satisfaction of the prescribed authority that the tax leviable under sub-section (1) has, actually been paid by the dealer (his principal contractor) on the turnover of goods supplied to him by the dealer in the course of execution of works contract, the sub- contractor shall not be liable to pay tax again on the turnover of such goods.

(4) A dealer shall pay for each year, a tax under this Act on his taxable turnover in respect of the right to use any goods (whether or not for a specified period) at the rates specified in the Schedules under section 12 for the same goods had they been sold otherwise than by the transfer of the right to use them:

Provided further if the transfer of the right to use any goods is made by a dealer on more than one occasion in a year to the same or different party, the tax shall be leviable on each such occasion.

Explanation I: For the purposes of this section, the transfer of property in goods or transfer of right to use any goods for any purpose (whether or not for a specified period) shall be deemed to have taken place in Sikkim if the goods transferred are within the State at the time of their transfer or use application or appropriation for the execution of works contract, irrespective of the place where the agreement for the works contract is made and whether the consent of the other party, prior or subsequent to such use, application or appropriation has been obtained or not.

1. Our company has executed works contract for Central Rail Side Warehousing Corporation Ltd. (CRWC) at Ranchi (Jharkhand). We understand that Railways is exempted from service tax. The definition of railways as given in the Railways Act includes its warehouses. So, our company should not be liable to service tax on such works contract of construction, erection and installation of warehouses. Use of the warehouses is not exempted but construction of railway warehouses is exempted.

Constitution of CRWC is as follows: Indian Railways have entered into a MOU with the Central Warehousing Corporation (CWC) as its strategic partner for development of integrated railside warehouse complexes. CWC has created a SPV as its subsidiary, named as CRWC with the sole purpose of developing railside warehousing complexes (not other complexes). The Indian Railways has provided land near various railway terminals and the CRWC has constructed and erected railway warehousing complexes on the land by contracting with our company. Indian Railway will get its share of profit by way of profit sharing from CRWC.

Kindly enlighten us whether the stand of the company is correct that construction of railside warehousing by Indian Railways in partnership with CRWC should not be taxable.

Railway is defined in section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989; the same is reproduced below -

"railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods, and includes-

"(a)

all lands within the fences or other boundary marks indicating the limits of the land appurtenant to a railway;

(b)

all lines of rails, sidings, or yards, or branches used for the purposes of, or in connection with, a railway;

(c)

all electric traction equipments, power supply and distribution installations used for the purposes of, or in connection with, a railway;

(d)

all rolling stock, stations, officers warehouses, wharves, workshops, factories, fixed plant and machinery, roads and streets, running rooms, rest houses, institutes, hospitals, water works and water supply installations, staff dwellings and any other works constructed for the purpose of, or in connection with, railway;

(e)

all vehicles which are used on any road for the purposes of traffic of a railway and owned, hired or worked by a railway; and

(f)

all ferries, ships, boats and rafts which are used on any canal, river, lake or other navigable inland waters for the purposes of the traffic of a railway and owned, hired or worked by a railway administration,

but does not include-

(i)

a tramway wholly within a municipal area; and

(ii)

lines of rails built in any exhibition ground, fair, park or any other place solely for the purpose of recreation.

The relevant taxable services, viz., Commercial construction services and works contract services exclude services/works contracts in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams.

The query can be answer solely on basis of clause (d) of the definition, as it lists various places to be considered as 'railways'.

Services provided by railway include transport of passengers and goods and, constructions necessary therefor are covered by the term 'railways'. The words "officers warehouses"... "rest houses"... "any other works" … "for the purpose of railways" or "in connection with railways" are wide enough to cover warehouses meant for storage of goods transported by the railways.

If that is the case, the services will be considered as having been provided in respect of construction of warehouse for use of the railways.

However, construction of warehouses meant for commercial use by railways and not for use of railways will not be covered under 'railways' and services provided would be not considered as 'in respect of' railways.

Please note that the services must be provided "in respect of" railways and not merely "to" railways.

Hence, it appears that the services provided by your client would be liable to service tax.

As per section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989, "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. It doesn't include a tramway wholly within a Municipal area.

As per clause (20) of section 2 the aforesaid Act :

(20) "Government railway" means a railway owned by the Central Government;

As per the meaning given to it "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. Thus, railways may be Government owned or private owned. Even private-owned railways is railways within the meaning of the Act. However, a 'tramway' is excluded.

Further, present section 66D(o) provides that service of transportation of passengers, with or without accompanied belongings, by-

(i)

a stage carriage;

railways in a class other than-

(A)

first class; or

(B)

an air-conditioned coach;

metro, monorail or tramway;...

shall be in the negative list.

Thus, the present law conceives of 'railways' differently from 'metro or monorail or tramway'.

As per Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, a tram-train is a light-rail public transport system where trams run through from an urban tramway network to main-line railway lines which are shared with conventional trains. This combines the tram's flexibility and accessibility with a train's greater speed, and bridges the distance between a main railway station and a city centre. There is also a train-tram, which is a train modified to run also on tramlines. Generally, the tram-train and train-tram are interchangeable, although a train-tram is based on a train design modified to also run as a tram and a tram-train is based on a tram design modified also to run on a train line.

Hence, it appears that Delhi Metro is a 'tramway' and not a 'railway'. The services may not be eligible for exemption.

INTEREST ON CREDIT CARD OUTSTANDINGS NOT LIABLE TO SERVICE TAX

5. I am a user of credit cards. I use the same for payment of my utility bills, purchases, etc. Often, on account of one reason or the another, I delay in payment of the credit card outstandings and interest is charged for such delay (generally, no interest is charged when payment is made within due date, but some ancillary charges are debited). While going through my credit card bills, I find that the bank has charged service tax even on the interest amount. I understand that credit card management services may be liable to service tax, but, there can't be any charge of service tax on interest amount. Please clarify.

Interest on loans is excluded from charge of service tax by virtue of negative list entry under section 66D(n) of the Finance Act, 1994. As per section 65B(30), interest means interest payable in any manner in respect of any moneys borrowed or debt incurred (including a deposit, claim or other similar right or obligation).

Interest for delayed payment of consideration of services is excluded from value by virtue of Rule 6(2) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006.

In this regard, the Guidance Note, dated 20-6-2012 has clarified that charges for late payment of dues on credit card outstandings are not excludible from taxable value for the following reasons :

(i)

No exclusion under Rule 6(2) of Valuation Rules : Interest for delayed payment of any consideration for the sale of goods or provision of service has been specifically excluded from value by Rule 6 of the Valuation Rules. However, in the case of credit cards the credit extended is not for the delayed payment of consideration for the provision of services. The services in the case of the credit card are by way of levy of issuing charges or the commission charged from merchants, etc. The interest is not for the consideration for the use of the card. Thus, exclusion under valuation rules will not be available.

(ii)

No exclusion under the negative list : Such credit extended will also not amount to loans or advances. Loans and advances are meant to signify amounts contractually negotiated as such (loan or advance) and not merely a failure to pay an amount at the due date. The exorbitant charges have also no relationship with the prevailing interest rate for the same class of creditworthiness and are in the nature of consideration for the services rendered for using the convenience of using the services by way of a credit card and, hence, are taxable.

In a prima facie view expressed by the Tribunal in Canara Bank v. CCE&C (LTU), [2013] 29 taxmann.com 157 (Bang. - CESTAT), it was held that interest on credit card dues partakes character of 'interest on loan' and, therefore, it shall not form part of value of credit card related services.

The said prima facie view appears to be correct view, as 'interest' will fall under section 66D(n), even if rate is exorbitant. The view of the Department appears to be more based on economic sense rather than legal interpretation. The same doesn't appear to be correct.

Accordingly, as far as charge of interest by bank is concerned, you may bring this to the notice of the bank. If the bank refuses to accept this view (which is likely, so as to avoid any conflict and further, because burden is transferred to clients), you may seek action against the Bank or file a claim for refund of service tax paid by you under section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

Effective Rate of Tax As per the draft list of rates released by the GST council after its meeting on 18.05.2017, rate of GST applicable on construction sector is 12%, where the value of land is included in the purchase consideration. There is no further abatement/composition on this rate. Further, person cannot claim refund of Input Tax Credit (ITC) accumulated on account of higher tax rates on inputs/input services than on the rate of output. In other words, in case of accumulation of ITC because of the fact that tax rates on some inputs or input services will be 18% or even 28%, its refund will not be allowed to the assessee.

Further, if the value of land is not included, then the rate of tax applicable would be 18% (under service of Works Contract).

In addition, all special services provided by builders like preferential location charges (PLC), power backup charges (PBC), club service, administrative charges, cheque return, booking transfer charges etc. would be chargeable at the rate of 18%.

However, one issue for consideration is the treatment of car parking charges that are recovered separately from a flat buyer. Some people might argue that buying flat is a pre-requisite for buying such car parking space and hence supply of flat and car parking space are naturally bundled in course of business and will thus fall under the category of composite supply and accordingly rate of 12% will be applicable on the car parking charges also. It would a close call on the part of developers and would definitely invite litigation from the GST department. Thus, to be safer side the builder might charge 18% rate on car parking charges.

Larger Bench of Supreme Court has recently upheld the decision given by the Apex Court in K. Raheja Development Corpn. v. In this article the intricacies underlying Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka [2013] 38 taxmann.com 98 (SC) and K. Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) have been brought out.

Statutory provisions

2. Clause (h) of section 66E specifies service portion in execution of works contract as a 'Declared Service'. Clause (h) of section 66E reads as follow:

"(h) service portion in the execution of a works contract,"

'Works contract' is defined in section 65B(54), which reads as follows:

'(54) "works contract" means a contract wherein transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods and such contract is for the purpose of carrying out construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance renovation, alteration of any movable or immovable property or for carrying out any other similar activity or a part thereof in relation to such property'.

Facts of the case Larsen and Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka

3. Assessee (L&T) entered into a development agreement with the owner of the land for construction of a multi-storey apartment complex. A power of attorney was executed by the owner of the land in favour of L&T to enable it to negotiate and book orders from the prospective purchasers for allotment of built-up area.

Accordingly, L&T entered into agreements of sale with intended purchasers. The agreements provided that on completion of the construction, the apartments would be handed over to the purchasers who would get an undivided interest in the land also. Sale deeds, thus, were executed in favour of the intended purchasers by L&T and the owner.

State VAT Department argued that impugned 'development agreement' amounted to a works contract and was liable to VAT as per judgment in K. Raheja Development Corpn. (supra).

3.1 Arguments by assessee - Appellant argued that K.Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) did not lay down correct law. He submitted that insertion of clause 29-A (b) in article 366 following the 61st Law Commission Report was intended to separate the goods component from the labour and services component of a composite works contract. The amendment did not in any manner undo decision in State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. [1959] SCR 379, insofar as that decision defined what a works contract was. It was argued by him that in K. Raheja Development Corpn. (supra), it was incorrectly assumed that the definition of works contract was wide, although the definition of works contract in KST Act and Madras General Sales Tax Act under consideration in Gannon Dunkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. (supra) was identical.

3.2 Arguments on behalf of VAT Departments of States of Karnataka and Maharashtra - The statement of law in K. Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) that when a completed building is sold, there is no works contract and, therefore, no liability to tax, might not be correct statement of law. If the building was intended for sale and was, in fact, sold, tax was attracted to the deemed sale. Even in such cases, goods used in the construction are deemed to have been sold by the builder (dealer) to the purchaser.

It also stated that doubts on K. Raheja Development Corpn. case (supra) that a better view was possible was not good enough to reconsider the decision. While recommending reconsideration of an earlier decision, the Bench must first come to the conclusion that the earlier decision was clearly wrong for the reasons stated. Besides, K. Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) in May, 2005 almost all States had modified their laws in line with K. Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) and the need for change in a settled practice was not made out.

. Since the amount involved in the project is very high, we are little bit confused. Please clarify.

Since no outside services have been engaged while constructing the complex, no service tax is payable. It should be noted here that the tax is on service rendered for construction of complex and it is not a tax on buying and selling of complexes. If the builder himself builds a residential complex by using the services of his own staff and no outside service provider is involved, then no service tax is leviable. 6. We are a construction company and we have entered into a contract for construction of a big temple in Rajasthan and the cost of construction is around Rs. 100.00 crore and as per the agreement, the taxes including service tax are to be borne by the contractor, i.e., our company.

First of all I must inform you that the services provided by you with respect to the construction of a temple are not liable to service tax because under this head, only commercial and industrial constructions are liable to service tax. Hence, construction of temple is not liable to service tax and you need not charge or pay any service tax in this respect.

For this purpose, you can also refer to the CBEC Circular No. 80/2004-ST, dated 17-9-2004.

Though the services provided for construction of a temple are not liable to service tax, we are providing below the method of issuing bills in case of composite price or composite price contract for any service for the benefit of readers because the compulsion of showing service tax separately in the bill does not restrict the respective parties to enter into composite price (Inclusive of service tax) contract:—

In such cases, by applying the following formula, the amount of service tax can be calculated:—

ST = Composite price * Rate of Tax/Rate of Tax + 100.

To understand it with the help of an example, we assume that the composite price is Rs.100.00 and rate of tax is 10.2% including education cess. The amount of service tax will be:—

100 * 10.2/110.2 = Rs. 9.25

Denoting Rs. 9.25 as service tax, the service provider can raise the bill by showing Rs. 90.75 as the amount charged for service and Rs. 9.25 can be added as service tax to make the composite price at Rs. 100.00.

A contractor is constructing railway station for Metro Rail Project. Another contractor is installing telecommunication system for the Metro Rail Project. Are these contractors required to pay service tax?

No, these activities would not attract service tax liability. One can rely upon decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Shahdara (Delhi) Saharanpur Light Rly. Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Saharanpur AIR 1967 SC 1747 wherein it was held that definition of ‘railway’ is very wide and would include every structure or mechanical/communication/electrical system set up for the Metro Rail Project through the contractors for this rail transit system and it is not restricted to the railway tracks.

The same meaning should apply to the word ‘railways’ figuring in section 65(105)( zzzza) of the Finance Act, 1994. When the definition of ‘taxable services’ itself states that works contract in respect of ‘railways’ would not come within its scope, it would mean that each and every activity mentioned in the definition which is for a railway system, is outside its scope. Accordingly, construction of station building or setting up of telecommunication system for use in the Metro Rail Project is not subject to service tax under the category of ‘execution of works contract’.

The municipal corporation of a metro city is constructing a multi-storied building. It is to use 50 per cent of the space in the building for civic purposes and would rent the balance 50 per cent to various offices for commercial use. Whether the contractor is required to pay service tax on the construction of his building?

No, this activity would not fall under the category of ‘execution of works contract service’. One can rely upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of State of Orissa v. Joginder Patjoshi AIR 2004 SC 1039 wherein it was held that the expression ‘primary’ is used in contradiction with ‘secondary’. The main objective is referred to primary and a subsidiary objective as secondary. The thing which comes first is primary. For example, the primary education is followed by secondary education.

The municipal corporation will use civic centre primarily for its activities in the role of a civic body. It is only when there is space left after the purpose of municipal corporation is satisfied that it will give such surplus space on rent for use as office. Even, in such a case, it would not give more than 50 per cent of the space in the building on rent. If more than 50 per cent of the space is not given on rent, then it cannot be said that the building is used primarily for renting of space for commercial use. Hence, the building being constructed by the contractor would not be used ‘primarily’ for commerce or industry. Therefore, construction of the building of the municipal corporation is not taxable under the category of ‘Execution of works contract service’.

Whether a contractor who started executing the contract prior to June 1, 2007, is required to pay service tax on the amount received subsequent to this date?

Service tax on execution of works contract has been introduced from June 1, 2007. The value on which service tax is to be paid for a works contract has been prescribed in law. Rule 2A of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, prescribes the value which gets transferred in the execution of the contract to the customer, and VAT or sales tax on such transfer are to be deducted from the gross amount charged for the works contract. Thus, the whole of the works contract has been treated as a single transaction, the value of which is the starting point for computation of taxable value. There is no scope for considering the gross amount charged for the works contract to be less than the lump sum price. Therefore, computation of service tax based on a fraction of a contract price is not envisaged in law. For a contract, where execution started before June 1, 2007, it is not permissible to bifurcate the contract to pay service tax on the basis of quantum of activities performed on or after June 1, 2007, while considering the part performed prior to this date as not taxable.

Taxation on works contract has always been a source of litigation. An attempt is made to compile judgments on the issue and look at the direction where taxation on works contract is heading towards in general and its impact on service tax in particular.

Era before 46th Amendment

1. Prior to 46th amendment, composite contracts such as works contract, hire purchase contracts and catering contracts were not assessable as contracts for sale of goods.

In State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. AIR 1958 SC 560, the Supreme Court held that sale of goods in entry 48 of List II of 7th Schedule did not cover sale sought to be taxed by the State Government. In a building contract which is one, entire and indivisible, there is no sale of goods and it is not within the competence of the State Legislature to impose a tax on the supply of the materials used in such a contract treating it as a sale.

This decision led to 46th amendment to the Constitution amending article 366(29A) for the expression ‘tax on the sale or purchase of goods’.

Some relevant judgments

2. These are as under :

2.1 Builders Association of India v. UOI AIR 1989 SC 1371

u The Supreme Court held that after 46th amendment, works contract which was indivisible one, by a legal fiction is altered into a contract which is divisible into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services.

u Thus, it is possible for States to levy sales tax on transfer of property in goods involved in execution of a works contract. However, it does not enable the States to tax the entire works contract itself.

u Further when goods are used in a works contract, the property in them passes to the owner. The liability to tax arises as the goods are used and it is not necessary that to levy tax works contract should be completed.

2.2 Rainbow Colour lab v. State of MP AIR 2000 SC 808

u Supreme Court in this case held that it is now open for States to divide works contract into two separate contracts by legal fiction :

(i )Contract for sale of goods involved in the said works contract, and

(ii )Contract for supply of labour and service.

u However, the Court stated that division of contract can be made only if works contract involved a dominant intention to transfer the property in goods and no division in contracts where the transfer of property takes place as an incident of contract of service. (Dominant nature test)

u Thus, it is ruled that work done by a photographer is only in the nature of a service contract where the dominant nature is providing photography service and the contract does not involve any sale of goods.

2.3 Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. Comm. of Customs AIR 2001 SC 862

u The Supreme Court stated that conclusion arrived at in Rainbow Colour Lab runs counter to express provision contained in article 366(29A) and also to the decision of the Constitution Bench in Builders Association of India’s case (supra).

u It further held that even if dominant intention of the contract was to render service, after 46th amendment, States are empowered to levy sales tax only on materials used in such contract. (Disagreement with Rainbow Colour Lab’s case (supra)

2.4 C.K. Jidheesh v. UOI [2005] 2 STT 242 (SC)

u The issue involved taxation of amount received on developing and printing of colour photographic films.

u The Supreme Court held that contracts of the type entered into by persons like the petitioner are nothing else but service contracts, which are pure and simple and there is no element of sale of goods.

2.5 K. Raheja Development Corpn. v. State of Karnataka [2005] 2 STT 178 (SC)

u Applicants entered into development agreement with land owners and got plans sanctioned in the owners’ name and before construction of the comple, they entered into sale agreement with the intending purchasers.

u The Court held that if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, then there would be no works contract. But so long as the agreement is entered into before the construction is complete, it would be a works contract.

In an indivisible works contract, there was no sale of goods as there could be no agreement to sell materials as such and moreover, the property would not pass as movables. The material used therein became property of the other party on the theory of accretion and, as such, no sales tax could be levied on such material. 'Works Contract' was one of the ways of avoiding sales tax. Hence, Constitution was amended on 2nd February, 1983 (46th Amendment). Clause 29A was added to Article 366 to cover 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract'. Subsequently, most of the States have amended their sales tax laws to cover 'works contract', but Central Sales Tax Act was not amended till May, 2002. Thus, till 11-5-2002, CST was not leviable on indivisible works contracts.

Union of India [1989] 73 STC 370 (SC) - In this case Supreme Court observed that 'After the 46th Amendment, the works contract which was indivisible one, is by a legal fiction altered into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services. After 46th Amendment, it has become possible for States to levy tax on value of goods involved in a works contract in the same way in which the sales tax was leviable on the price of goods and materials supplied in a building contract which had been entered into two distinct and separate parts.'

4.8 Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs [2001] 124 STC 59 (SC) - In this case it was held that even if the dominant intention of the contract was rendering of service which would amount to a works contract, after Forty-Sixth Amendment to Constitution, the State would be empowered to levy sales tax on material used in such contract.

4.9 Builders Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 73 STC 370 (SC) - The background of this case is that after Amendment to Constitution in 1983, various State Governments imposed levy on works contract. The tax was levied by some State Governments on full value of contract which included the material cost and other costs like labour, supply of services, etc. However, in the judgment the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the power of States to levy tax on works contract was subject to limitation of Article 286, i.e., tax could not be levied by State on : (a) Outside the State, (b) during import/export, (c) Restrictions placed on 'declared goods' were applicable even while levying tax on works contract. Further, tax could not be imposed on full value of contract. The tax was on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract could be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

4.10 Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan [1993] 66 Taxman 229 (SC) - In this case it was held that taxable event is the transfer of property in the goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The said transfer of property takes place when goods are incorporated in the works. Hence, value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are not taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, Legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract. It is permissible to have a uniform rate for works contract. This rate may be different from the rates applicable to individual goods.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka [1993] 88 STC 248 (SC).

Case Study

4. The following case study has been analysed :

4.1 Case - M/s. GE, engaged in the business of generation of electricity, intends to set-up a power plant in India. Total project is split up into following two contracts -

one with M/s. CN for supply of equipment and another with M/s. SO for erection and commissioning services ;

The authorities opine that the total work is a turnkey project and, hence, is covered under works contract service, thereby making the assessee liable to pay service tax on works contract service under reverse charge basis on payment made to M/s. CN.

4.2 Solution - This case may be resolved as follows -

Contract speaks about total scope of work, i.e., from designing upto commissioning of plant and equipment. The total project is subsequently split up into two agreements. It fits into definition of works contract service.

The services provided by M/s. CN are works contract services and the assessee is liable to pay Service tax on payments made to CN on reverse charge basis.

Conclusion

5. While as works contracts are usually in the nature of contracts for the construction of immovable property such as buildings, power plants, etc., there are several kinds of contracts concerned with movable property that also fall within the scope of works contracts, including annual maintenance contracts, as they involve the transfer of property in goods coupled with the provision of works or services. In the case of work contracts, a sales tax is leviable on that portion of the contract which relates to the sale of goods. Most of the States in India provide for the payment of tax on works contracts separately to the value of the goods and materials sold at the rates specified under the respective State legislations.

However, some States provide for the payment of tax under a composition scheme at a fixed percentage. In a composition scheme the work contractor is required to pay the tax on the entire value of the contract without splitting up the value of the goods and materials supplied and the value of the services provided.

Facts in the case of Harekrishna Developers, In re [2008] 14 STT 175 (AAR - New Delhi) 3.2 The applicant-firm intends to develop on its own plot of land a residential complex having more than twelve residential units with a club house and other common facilities. It will sell plots of land inside the complex to prospective buyers who will enter into a works contract with the applicant for the construction of residential units. The applicant itself will execute a part of the works contract [‘activity No. 3’] and for remaining part, the applicant will further enter into a works contract with other contractors [‘activity No. 4’]. However, goods for construction will be purchased/acquired by the applicant and the property in those goods will be transferred to buyers of the housing units and such transfer would be exigible to tax as sale of goods. The applicant sought advance ruling of the Authority on questions of its liability in these two types of activities, and also on question of rate of tax in case of activity No. 3.

The applicant contends that since the works contract in activities 3 and 4 involves construction of a new building-such an activity can only be covered under(ii)( b) in the Explanation to section 65(105)(zzzza). Since the new building proposed to be constructed in the course of the execution of the works contract is a residential one, and is not for the purpose of commerce or industry, such a works contract will not fall under (b) and therefore, will not attract service tax. The applicant further states that a works contract for construction of a new building for residential purposes is also not covered under any of the remaining classifications in (ii) of the Explanation to clause (zzzza). The classification (c) which covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’ is not applicable in applicant’s case as the works contract is for construction of an individual residential unit and not for construction of a residential complex.

Decision in the case of Harekrishna Developers (supra )

3.3 Authority for Advance Ruling held:

1. To attract service tax under sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105), a works contract has to meet the two conditions: (i) and (ii) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). The facts narrated by the applicant indicated that condition (i) is met in the instant case as the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract is exigible to tax as sale of goods under the local Sales Tax Act. To meet condition (ii), the activity involved in the works contract in activity Nos. 3 and 4 has to be covered by at least one of the classifications (a ) to (e) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). Proceeding serially, one finds that building of a residential house on a sub-plot in a residential complex is clearly not covered in (a). As pointed out by the applicant itself, it is also not covered by (b) which covers construction of a new building intended primarily for commerce and industry and does not cover construction of a new building. Item (c) of sub-clause (zzzza) of clause (105) covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’.

2. As per the draft of the works contract submitted, it is clear that such contracts will be for construction of individual houses on sub-plots located within the plot owned by the applicant on which the applicant proposes to develop a residential housing project. As per the applicant’s own narration, the residential project to be constructed on this plot would have at least 12 residential units, a club house and other common facilities and the layout of the project would be approved by the prescribed authority under the relevant law in force. Such a project constructed as per activity Nos. 3 and 4 squarely conforms to the definition of a ‘residential complex’ given in clause (91a) of section 65, and the individual houses constructed get covered under the definition of a ‘residential unit’ contained therein. Execution of the works contract, thus, involves construction of a part of a new ‘residential complex’ and is covered by (c).

It is important to note that by the Finance Act, 2007, service tax is also levied on works contracts [section 65(105)( zzzza)]. It may be noted that under this service only the works contracts wherein transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract is exigible to VAT/sales tax, are covered, excluding works contract in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams. For the purpose of this sub-clause, "works contract" means a contract wherein,—

(i) transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods, and

(ii) such contract is for the purpose of carrying out,—

(a) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise, installation of electrical and electronic devices, plumbing, drain laying or other installations for transport of fluids, heating, ventilation or air-conditioning including related pipe work, duct work and sheet metal work, thermal insulation, sound insulation, fire proofing or water proofing, lift and escalator, fire escape staircases or elevators; or

(b) construction of a new building or a civil structure or a part thereof, or of a pipeline or conduit, primarily for the purpose of commerce or industry; or

(c) construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(d) completion and finishing services, repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services, in relation to (b) and (c); or

(e) turnkey projects including engineering, procurement and construction or commissioning (EPC) projects;

Thus, works contract in respect of specified infrastructure projects, namely, roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams are specifically excluded from the scope of the levy. Taxable value under this service is that part of the value of the works contract which is relatable to services provided in the execution of a works contract. Such value is to be determined on actual basis based on the records maintained by the assessee. However, an option is given to an assessee for a composition scheme. Under the composition scheme, the assessee was required to pay 2% of the total value of the works contract as service tax (now 4% w.e.f 1-3-2008). Assessee opting for the composition scheme is not entitled to avail CENVAT credit on inputs but can claim CENVAT credit on capital goods and input services required for use in the works contract.

State of Karnataka [2005] 2 STT 178 (SC) (Two Judge Bench) and lays a few essential laws as under :-

(a)

Any agreement entered into by the builder / promoter before the completion of construction tantamounts to works contract and, hence, is liable to Value Added Tax (VAT)/ sales tax.

(b)

When an agreement is entered into between the promoter/developer and the flat purchaser to construct a flat and eventually sell the flat with the fraction of land, it is obvious that such transaction involves the activity of construction inasmuch as it is only when the flat is constructed then it can be conveyed. The said activity will be covered by the term "works contract". The term "works contract" is nothing but a contract in which one of the parties is obliged to undertake or to execute works. Such activity of construction has all the characteristics or elements of a works contract.

(c)

In tripartite agreement between the owner of the land, the developer and the flat purchaser, there is nothing wrong if the transaction is treated as a composite contract comprising of both a works contract and a transfer of immovable property and levy sales tax on the value of the material involved in execution of the works contract.

Composition scheme

7. Service tax on services provided in relation to execution of a works contract will certainly trigger lot of controversies. The valuation of services in this respect will also pose some of the practical problems. Conclusion

5. Thus, keeping in mind all the latest amendments and judgments of the various Courts, it can be concluded that works contract will be taxed as follows :

u First, the VAT or sales tax is to be paid on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract. u Then, the service tax is to be paid on the gross amount charged for the works contract service, which will not include the paid VAT or sales tax. This value is the value based on the actuals of the works contract service, in a composite contract.

u If the service provider opts for the Composite Scheme, then he has to pay 4 per cent of the gross amount.

u In case of an indivisible works contract, the tax will be levied on the approximate gross amount of the service, minus the amount for transfer of property.

Service tax is widening every year, and will only contribute a fair amount to the Government exchequer and Gross Domestic Product of the country. The increase from 2 per cent to 4 per cent for the amount of service tax payable under composite schemes will hurt the service providers initially, but will prove to be essential in future, as it still is lesser than the amount to be paid under the normal service tax regime.

V.S. DATEY

A three member large bench of Supreme Court has delivered a very important judgment in respect of works contract, in case of Larsen & ToubroLtd. v. State of Karnataka [2013] 41 STT 113/38 taxmann.com 98 (SC 3 member bench).

Basically, this judgment has upheld validity of Vat on construction of residential flats and commercial premises. Though the judgment is in relation to Vat, it has significant impact on service tax aspects also.

BACKGROUND OF THE CASE

1. In K Raheja Development Corpn. v. State of Karnataka [2005] 2 STT 178 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some work on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

It was held that the developer would be liable to pay tax on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN DEVELOPER MODEL AND BUILDER MODEL OF CONTRACTS

2. In 'builder model' of building contracts, agreement to sale is executed with the intending purchasers. Conveyance is executed by builder only after building is complete and possession is handed over. The conveyance is in respect of land as well as construction.

In 'developer model', developer enters into contract with prospective buyers (allottees). After construction, possession is handed over. The owner of land directly transfers the entire land to society or owners of apartment, who become owners of undivided share of land. Separate agreement is not executed with developer (This is to save stamp duty).

The decision in case of K Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) was in respect of developer model. It was thought the decision of Supreme Court would not apply to builder model of contracts.

DECISION IN CASE OF K RAHEJA DEVELOPMENT CORPN. (SUPRA) DOUBTED

3. Decision of Supreme Court in case of K Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) was doubted in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka [2008] 16 STT 286. It was observed that if ratio of K Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) is accepted, there would be no difference between works contract and a contract for sale of chattel as a chattel. With these observations, the matter has been referred to a larger bench.

These observations supported a view that Vat will not apply in case of builder model of contracts.

DECISION IN CASE OF K RAHEJA DEVELOPMENT CORPN. (SUPRA) AFFIRMED BY LARGE BENCH OF SUPREME COURT

4. The large bench of SC, in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. (supra) has affirmed the decision in case of K Raheja.

In effect, it has been held that Vat applies to all types of construction agreements – whether builder model or developer model.

The summary of main issues decided is as follows–

Indivisible contracts can be segregated into (i) contract for sale of goods involved in works contract and (ii) for supply of labour and service [paras 63 and 101(viii)].

A contract may involve both a contract for work and labour and a contract for sale. In such composite contract, the distinction between contract for sale of goods and contract for work (or service) is virtually diminished [para 101(v)]

Lead Taxation - Sterlite Grid Ltd.

Introduction

1. Works contract is an indivisible contract. It is indivisible in the sense that value of goods to be incorporated in any form in the works and value of labour & other services to be rendered in execution cannot be segregated. It is also known as deemed sales.

In construction industries where entire work is assigned on completion basis, it always becomes matter of dispute as to what should be tax structure, as both the taxes - VAT/CST and service tax are applicable on such transaction. It is complex in nature due to non-synchronization in tax mechanism of the Central & State tax authorities. VAT is imposed by the State Government and on the other hand, the service tax is imposed by the Central Government. Calculation mechanism at both the stages is also different which results in unnecessary litigation & dispute burden on assessee.

Legal frameworks

2. Works contract in simple terms is a contract for carrying out certain works on any movable or immovable property of others. Sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A) of the Indian Constitution deals with the imposition of tax on transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of works contract.

Definition of works contract has been inserted in CST Act vide the Finance Act, 2005. Section 2(ja) of the Central Sales Tax Act defines works contract as follows—"Works contract means a contract for carrying out any work which includes assembling, construction, building, altering, manufacturing, processing, fabricating, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property."

All the State VAT Acts have defined works contract in a different manner but the meaning of works contract is similar in nature. After reading all definitions, the term "works contract" is nothing but a contract in which one of the parties is obliged to undertake or to execute works and property is transferred to other party, either as goods or in some other form.

3. Levy of tax on works contract

3.1 Provisions under State VAT Act - No VAT/CST is applicable on pure labour jobs where no material of his own is used/added by the job worker (vendor).

VAT/CST is applicable on Material Value (Deemed Sale) of the Works Contract.

Since segregation of material involved in works contract & services involved in works contract is difficult to arrive at the Material Value in the Contract, three methods are adopted under the State VAT Acts, namely:

(i)

Actual Non-material (Labour) Deduction Method

(ii)

Standard (Labour) Deduction Method

(iii)

Composition Tax/Compounding Tax (WCT) Method

If the Contractor dispatches his own materials from one State to another directly to the customer under the Indivisible WC, then it is a deemed inter-State sale of material subject to levy of CST by the State of dispatch.

Accordingly, the expression "tax on the sale or purchase of goods" in Entry 54, List II, Schedule VII, read with the definition clause (29A) includes the transfer of property in goods whether as goods or in the form other than goods involved in the execution of works contract. The taxable event, thus, is a deemed sale.17 3.3 Dominant Intention Test: The courts, in both the above-stated cases, have also laid down that it is not necessary to ascertain the dominant intention of the contract. Even if it is not to transfer property in goods and rather, is rendering of service or the ultimate transaction is transfer of immovable property, then also it is open to the States to levy sales tax on the material used in such contract if it otherwise has elements of works contract. Thus, the Supreme Court has completely ruled out that dominant intention of any contract has relevance if the contract has element of works contract18.

3.4 Conditions for sustaining levy of tax on goods sold in execution of works contract: Having discussed the scope and ambit of a works contract, the Court went on to broadly frame three conditions for sustaining the levy of tax on the goods sold in the execution of works contract, as under:

(i)

there must be a works contract;

(ii)

the goods should have been involved in the execution of works contract; and

(iii)

the property in those goods must be transferred to a third party either as goods or in some other form.19

GST & Works Contract

4. Having understood the conceptual bases surrounding the concept of works contracts, it finds itself at a juncture where the intersection between the peculiar taxation principles of works contracts with the proposed GST regime can be identified and evaluated.

The taxability of works contracts continues to be a contentious issue. We are yet to observe a mammoth reform in the form of Goods and Services Tax. The 100th Constitutional Amendment Bill has retained the concept of 'deemed sale'. However, the concept of 'sale' is to be done away with under the GST regime. It is known that works contract is taxable on sale and provision of services under the current regime. However, under the GST regime all the taxable events will be merged and there will only be one taxable event, being supply of good/service. If we look at the real estate sector, where works contracts find prevalence, compliances with multiple taxes constitutes a heavy burden. The GST seeks to remove these multiple taxes and bring in uniformity wherein the taxes would, in all probability, be levied at one rate. Further, it is expected that the cascading effect of taxes would be eliminated, at least in part owing to the GST.

4.1 Associated problems: It is believed that the GST regime would bring an end to the debate on works contract altogether. The issues relating to works contracts, in isolation, have been discussed above. However, GST would bring with itself a fresh and unprecedented set of complications:

The segregation of the components of a works contract is an arbitrary and contentious issue per se. Further, there is no clarity as to whether GST is applicable on real estate sector? This creates a huge gap in the GST base, leading to potential revenue losses.

The taxable event under the GST regime is supply of goods/service. What constitutes the taxable portion of a works contract has already been a widely and deeply litigated matter under the current tax regime; a new taxable event would lead to further interpretational issues.

It is an assumption that the GST will have a simple structure and goods and services will be taxed at a uniform rate. However, if a careful analysis of the Indian tax regime is conducted, convolutions in the law are easily identifiable. Different States have different needs, and, thus, it can be expected that different States would have different rates of taxation. This could lead to a more complex tax structure in the future.

Multiplicity in the rates of taxation is bound to lead us to retread the path of works contracts which, in turn, may culminate in complex interpretational and implementational issues.

Conclusion

5. The future relating to the taxation of works contract is very ambiguous. It cannot be predicted unless the law is brought in force. However, certain changes and measures which could be adopted as interim measures are briefly addressed:

The burden of taxation should be singular. Further, a uniform rate of taxation should be adopted by the States.

Long-term contracts which are still in force should incorporate clauses dealing with the changes, in law, and taxes.

Further, all components of taxation such as sale, service, etc., can be provided in the existing contracts, so as to save the margin of a service provider.

Proper documentation relating to the contracts should be maintained to avail of exemption, if any, to be provided in the new GST regime.

The issue relating to the treatment of deemed sales transactions needs to be addressed to by the Legislature. A definition relating to works contract could be included in the Amendment Bill for the sake of clear elucidation of the law.

A comprehensive Code relating to works contract taxation be provided, comprising of the taxable event, definition of works contract, valuation mechanism, etc., as an alternative to unending litigation.
