The applicant submits that it does not issue any consignment note in the course of providing transport services to 'P'. This being the case, the applicant is of the view that it does not qualify as a 'Goods Transport Agency' and thus transportation services provided by it may not be liable to GST.

The applicant's main contention is based on the premise that various services undertaken by it including transportation services as per second contract for which applicant issues separate invoices and separate consideration as has been decided in the contract shall be considered as stand alone service and should be taxed accordingly.

In order to examine this view of the applicant, it is necessary to examine the terms of the contract executed between the applicant and 'P'.

From the conjoined and harmonious reading of various clauses of first contract and second contract, it can be safely concluded that the agreement for setting up Tower Package TWO5 for +800KV transmission Line Project is a single indivisible contract. As the contract consists of two or more taxable supplies of goods and services and their combination, it is a composite supply as defined under section 2(30). For the proposition of law that the first contract and the second contract is one single indivisible contract, one may find support from the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Indure Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer [2010] 3 taxmann.com 542.

The next issue to be decided is whether this composite supplies constitute 'works contract', which is defined under section 2(119) as follows:

'Works contract' means a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of such contract.

The contract executed between the parties is for complete execution of the Tower Package Tower Package Two5 for + 800RV/HVDC Raigarh - Pugalur Transmission Line Part-V' associated with HYDC Bipole link between Western region (Raigarh, Chhattisgarh) and Southern Region (Pugalur, Tamil Nadu) - North Trichur (Kerala).

As such the subject contracts are for commissioning of immovable property, wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of said contracts. The contracts thus are clearly covered by the definition of 'works contract' as per section 2(119). The composite supplies in the nature of works contract as defined under section 2(119) is declared as supply of services as per section 7 read with Entry No. 6(a) of Schedule II of the GST Act.

In view of above discussion, the impugned supply of transportation service is not supply of stand alone service but integral component of composite supply in the nature of works contract as defined under section 2(119) and the entire contract is a supply of services as per Entry No. 6(a) of Schedule II of the GST Act and liable to GST as per Entry at Sr. No. 3(ii) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 bearing Heading No. 9954. [Para 5]

Ruling

The GST is leviable on the transportation charges levied by the applicant on 'P'. [Para 6]

On transportation charges, GST would be leviable at 18 per cent as per Entry at Sr. No. 3(ii) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 6]

10.8-2 Deductions permissible while calculating 'value' for purpose of tax

Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 66 Taxman 229 = 1993 AIR SCW 2621 = (1993) 1 SCC 364 = (1993) 88 STC 204 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) is another important judgment on 'Works Contract'. Here, it was held that taxable event is the transfer of property in the goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The said transfer of property takes place when goods are incorporated in the works. Hence, value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. - - Profits relatable to supply of material can be included in value of goods and profits which are relatable to supply of labour and services are to be excluded.

In aforesaid judgment, it was held that value of goods involved in the execution of a works contract will have to be determined by taking into account the value of entire works contract and deducting therefrom the charges towards labour and services, which cover - (a) Labour charges for execution of the works (b) Amount paid to a sub-contractor for labour and services (c) Charges for planning, designing and architect's fees (d) Charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of works contract (e) Cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of works contract, the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract (f) Cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services (g) Other similar expenses relatable to supply of labour and services (h) Profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services.

The amounts deductible under these heads will have to be determined in the light of the facts of a particular case, on the basis of the material produced by the contractor.

Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST Act and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST Act. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract.

It is permissible to have a uniform rate for works contract. This rate may be different from the rates applicable to individual goods.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka (1993) 88 STC 248 = AIR 1993 SC 991 = (1993) 1 SCC 409 = 1993 AIR SCW 152 (SC - 5 member bench).

In Daelim Industrial Co. v. State of Assam (2003) 130 STC 53 (Gau HC), it was held that in case of works contract, tax is payable only of value of goods and not on cost of design and engineering.

The Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in selling of electricity to the consumers and are collecting consideration and electrical energy is considered as 'goods'. Hence the Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in the sale of goods or in general, supply of goods to the consumers for consideration. The Explanation clause inserted which provides that for the purposes of this item, the term 'business' shall not include any activity or transaction undertaken by the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority in which they are engaged as public authorities does not apply as they are not activities undertaken by the Central Government or State Government or a local authority.[Para 11.9]

DELHI METRO RAIL CORPORATION IS NOT 'RAILWAYS' 2. Our company has executed works contract for the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) by way of supply and erection of PEB structures for six elevated stations of DMRC in New Delhi during 1st April, 2008 to 31st March, 2010. The value of the contract is say of Rs. 1 crore. The service tax department is asking for payment of service tax on works executed for DMRC. The company is of the view that DMRC is railways, and the works executed for railway is exempted in service tax. But the service tax department says that DMRC is not included in railways, as it is a separate corporation from the Indian Railways. We understand that the definition of 'railways' as per the Railways Act is not restricted to the Indian railways. It says "Railways means a railway or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods." Thus, whether it is DMRC or Indian Railways, both are railways and works contract executed to any of them is exempted.

You may kindly enlighten us whether the stand of the company is right that the works contract of supply and erection of PEB structures for six elevated stations of DMRC is exempted.

As per section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989, "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. It doesn't include a tramway wholly within a Municipal area.

The relevant taxable services, viz., commercial construction services and works contract services exclude services/works contract in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams.

As per clause (20) of section 2 the aforesaid Act :

(20) "Government railway" means a railway owned by the Central Government;

As per clause (g) ibid :

(g) "railway administration", in relation to-

(a)

a Government railway, means the General Manager of a Zonal Railway; and

(b)

a non-Government railway person means the person who is the owner or lessee of the railway or the person working for the railway under an agreement;

As per the meaning given to it "railway" means a railway, or any portion of a railway, for the public carriage of passengers or goods. Thus, railways may be Government owned or private owned. Even private-owned railways is railways within the meaning of the Act. However, a 'tramway' is excluded.

Further, present section 66D(o) provides that service of transportation of passengers, with or without accompanied belongings, by-

(i)

a stage carriage;

(ii)

railways in a class other than-

(A)

first class; or

(B)

an air-conditioned coach;

(iii)

metro, monorail or tramway;...

shall be in the negative list.

Thus, the present law conceives of 'railways' differently from 'metro or monorail or tramway'.

As per Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia, a tram-train is a light-rail public transport system where trams run through from an urban tramway network to main-line railway lines which are shared with conventional trains. This combines the tram's flexibility and accessibility with a train's greater speed, and bridges the distance between a main railway station and a city centre. There is also a train-tram, which is a train modified to run also on tramlines. Generally, the tram-train and train-tram are interchangeable, although a train-tram is based on a train design modified to also run as a tram and a tram-train is based on a tram design modified also to run on a train line.

Hence, it appears that Delhi Metro is a 'tramway' and not a 'railway'. The services may not be eligible for exemption.

[A useful reference may also be made to : http://www.hindustantimes.com/India-news/Mumbai/Mumbai-Metro-Is-it-a-tramway-or-a-railway/Article1-763834.aspx]

However, in Bangalore Metro Rail Corpn. Ltd. v. Ministry of Finance [2013] 39 STT 107/31 taxmann.com 381 (Kar.), the Court has ruled that services provided in relation to execution of works contract for Metro Rail Corporation would not be liable to service tax, in view of provisions of section 65(105)(zzzza), excluding services provided in relation to railways.

CONSTRUCTION FOR RAILWAY COACH FACTORY - NOT TAXABLE :

Sl. No. 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is the relevant entry which prescribes GST rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST+6 per cent SGST) in respect of services provided to the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory, a local authority, a Government Authority or a Government Entity by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of civil structure or any other original works meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. Thus to attract rate of tax at 12 per cent under Sl. No. 3(vi)(a), the specified service should primarily be provided to the Central Government/State Government/Union Territory/local authority/Government Authority/Government Entity and must be used for other than commercial, industrial, or any other business or professional activity.

Now it is required to examine the question whether the contractee in the instant case, i.e., TSSPDCL falls under the specified categories of recipient viz. Central Government/State Government/Union Territory/local authority/Governmental Authority/Government Entity on not. The phrase 'Government Entity' is defined under the Explanation appended to Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. The same reads as:

'Government Entity' means an authority or a board or any other body including a society, trust, corporation.

(i)

Set up by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature; or

(ii)

Established by any Government,

with 90 per cent or more participation by way of equity or control, to carry out a function entrusted by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or a local authority.

It is apparent from the schedule concerning 'shareholding of promoter' of the annual accounts of TSSPDCL that 100 per cent shares of the company were held by the Governor of Telangana. This clear indicates that the Government of Telangana have 100 per cent control over TSSPDCL. Thus TSSPDCL is evidently covered under the definition of 'Government Entity'.

The next issue to be decided in this regard is whether the impugned services supplied by the applicant are for the works which are used for other than commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. As per the details furnished by the applicant, the works undertaken are for execution/implementation of various projects for (i) Capacitor Bank Works in Nalgonda etc., (ii) HVDS-High Voltage Distribution Systems in Suryapet used for agricultural feeders. The applicant further stated that the Government of Telangana is reimbursing the money to TSSPDCL on behalf of the customers for agricultural services rendered. Thus TSSPDCL is not rendering any non-commercial services inasmuch as it is getting reimbursed for its activity on behalf of its customers. Therefore, this activity cannot be termed as other than commercial/business purposes.

The impugned works undertaken are for business/commercial purposes. Therefore, the benefit of concessional rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST) is not applicable to the services supplied by the applicant. Further the services supplied by the applicant are subjected to 18 per cent (9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST) in terms of Sl. No. 3(xii) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

Ruling

The applicant is not entitled for the benefit of concessional rate of GST at 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST) in respect of the works quoted in application in terms of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 2-6-2017 or any other concessional rate.

Whether a particular person is a Governmental Authority or a Government Entity is to be decided in terms of the definition adduced under Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 by applying the facts of each case.

The impugned works are used for commercial/business activities in view of the facts and circumstances and accordingly the same are taxable under GST Act.

INTEREST ON CREDIT CARD OUTSTANDINGS NOT LIABLE TO SERVICE TAX

5. I am a user of credit cards. I use the same for payment of my utility bills, purchases, etc. Often, on account of one reason or the another, I delay in payment of the credit card outstandings and interest is charged for such delay (generally, no interest is charged when payment is made within due date, but some ancillary charges are debited). While going through my credit card bills, I find that the bank has charged service tax even on the interest amount. I understand that credit card management services may be liable to service tax, but, there can't be any charge of service tax on interest amount. Please clarify.

Interest on loans is excluded from charge of service tax by virtue of negative list entry under section 66D(n) of the Finance Act, 1994. As per section 65B(30), interest means interest payable in any manner in respect of any moneys borrowed or debt incurred (including a deposit, claim or other similar right or obligation).

Interest for delayed payment of consideration of services is excluded from value by virtue of Rule 6(2) of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006.

In this regard, the Guidance Note, dated 20-6-2012 has clarified that charges for late payment of dues on credit card outstandings are not excludible from taxable value for the following reasons :

(i)

No exclusion under Rule 6(2) of Valuation Rules : Interest for delayed payment of any consideration for the sale of goods or provision of service has been specifically excluded from value by Rule 6 of the Valuation Rules. However, in the case of credit cards the credit extended is not for the delayed payment of consideration for the provision of services. The services in the case of the credit card are by way of levy of issuing charges or the commission charged from merchants, etc. The interest is not for the consideration for the use of the card. Thus, exclusion under valuation rules will not be available.

(ii)

No exclusion under the negative list : Such credit extended will also not amount to loans or advances. Loans and advances are meant to signify amounts contractually negotiated as such (loan or advance) and not merely a failure to pay an amount at the due date. The exorbitant charges have also no relationship with the prevailing interest rate for the same class of creditworthiness and are in the nature of consideration for the services rendered for using the convenience of using the services by way of a credit card and, hence, are taxable.

In a prima facie view expressed by the Tribunal in Canara Bank v. CCE&C (LTU), [2013] 29 taxmann.com 157 (Bang. - CESTAT), it was held that interest on credit card dues partakes character of 'interest on loan' and, therefore, it shall not form part of value of credit card related services.

The said prima facie view appears to be correct view, as 'interest' will fall under section 66D(n), even if rate is exorbitant. The view of the Department appears to be more based on economic sense rather than legal interpretation. The same doesn't appear to be correct.

Accordingly, as far as charge of interest by bank is concerned, you may bring this to the notice of the bank. If the bank refuses to accept this view (which is likely, so as to avoid any conflict and further, because burden is transferred to clients), you may seek action against the Bank or file a claim for refund of service tax paid by you under section 83 of the Finance Act, 1994, read with section 11B of the Central Excise Act, 1944.

UOI (2006) 3 SCC 1 = 152 Taxman 135 = 3 STT 245 = 3 VST 95 = 145 STC 91 = 282 ITR 273 = AIR 2006 SC 1383 = 2 STR 161 (SC 3 member bench), it has been clearly held that value of service cannot be included in price of goods. Conclusion (E) of the judgment (para 92 of SCC and STC and para 81 of STT) reads as follows, 'The aspect theory would not apply to enable the value of service to be included in the sale of goods or the price of goods in the value of service'.

Though tax is only on goods involved in works contract, it is difficult to find correct value in case of indivisible contract. Hence, composition scheme is permissible on optional basis. 10.8-1 Tax can be only on value of material

Builders Association of India v. UOI (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) is a landmark judgment of Supreme Court on 'works contract'. The background of this case is that after amendment to Constitution in 1983, various State Governments imposed levy on works contract. The tax was levied by some State Governments on full value of contract which included the material cost and other costs like labour, supply of services etc.

However, in the judgment, Hon. Supreme Court held that the power of States to levy tax on works contract is subject to limitation of Article 286 i.e. tax cannot be levied by State on (a) outside the State (b) during import/export. (c) Restrictions placed on 'declared goods' are applicable even while levying tax on works contract. Further, tax cannot be imposed on full value of contract. The tax is on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract can be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

In State of Jharkhand v. Voltas Ltd. (2007) 7 STR 106 = 7 VST 317 (SC) also it was confirmed that sales tax can be levied only on value of goods. All charges/amounts are deductible from value of works contract except value of goods sold in execution of works contract, for computing taxable value.

In Imagic Creative Pvt. Ltd. v. CCT (2008) 2 SCC 614 = 12 STT 392 = 12 VST 371 = 9 STR 337 (SC), it has been held that service tax and Vat (sales tax) are mutually exclusive. In case of a composite contract, Vat cannot be imposed on portion relating to value of service.

Restrictions applicable to declared goods apply to declared goods used in works contract - Provisions relating to declared goods are applicable even if the declared goods are used in works contract. Thus, Vat rate cannot be more than that applicable to declared goods - Smt B Narasamma v. DCCT (2016) 96 VST 357 (SC).

CST Act imposes restrictions on State Government in levying tax on declared goods. These restrictions apply to goods involved in works contract also - Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. State of Assam (2007) 9 VST 195 (Gau HC).

Vat/sales tax is payable on iron and steel used in works contract at rate applicable to declared goods - URC Construction Ltd. v. DCCT (2008) 11 VST 896 (Karn HC) - view confirmed in Smt B Narasamma v. DCTO (2016) 57 GST 39 = 72 taxmann.com 349 = 96 VST 357 (SC).

Effective Rate of Tax As per the draft list of rates released by the GST council after its meeting on 18.05.2017, rate of GST applicable on construction sector is 12%, where the value of land is included in the purchase consideration. The assessee was engaged in executing civil works contacts and was registered both under the Karnataka Value Added Tax Act, 2003 (KVAT Act) and the Central Sales Tax Act. It purchased building materials like hardware, sand and bricks falling under the Third Schedule to the KVAT Act, declared goods under section 15 of the CST Act and other non-scheduled goods from within and outside the State and from unregistered dealers. It moved an application before the Authority for Advance Clarification and Ruling for guidance on the rate of tax applicable for the execution of civil works contracts under the KVAT Act.

The AAR held that since there was no specific entry providing for the rate of tax on works contracts up to 31-3-2006, tax on goods used in the execution of works contract should be levied in accordance with the rate of tax applicable to the sale of goods under the KVAT Act 2003.

Subsequently, an order was passed in revision by the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes (Karnataka), Bangalore, holding that the orders of AAR were erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of the revenue. It was reasoned that there is a deemed sale in the course of the execution of a works contract by incorporation of the goods into the work and both before and after the amendment of section 4(1)(c) with effect from 1-4-2006, tax is levied on the taxable turnover of goods involved in the execution of a works contract.

A sales tax appeal was preferred against this order before the High Court of Karnataka which by the impugned order, allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Commissioner. 6. We are a construction company and we have entered into a contract for construction of a big temple in Rajasthan and the cost of construction is around Rs. 100.00 crore and as per the agreement, the taxes including service tax are to be borne by the contractor, i.e., our company.

First of all I must inform you that the services provided by you with respect to the construction of a temple are not liable to service tax because under this head, only commercial and industrial constructions are liable to service tax. Hence, construction of temple is not liable to service tax and you need not charge or pay any service tax in this respect.

For this purpose, you can also refer to the CBEC Circular No. 80/2004-ST, dated 17-9-2004.

Though the services provided for construction of a temple are not liable to service tax, we are providing below the method of issuing bills in case of composite price or composite price contract for any service for the benefit of readers because the compulsion of showing service tax separately in the bill does not restrict the respective parties to enter into composite price (Inclusive of service tax) contract:—

In such cases, by applying the following formula, the amount of service tax can be calculated:—

ST = Composite price * Rate of Tax/Rate of Tax + 100.

To understand it with the help of an example, we assume that the composite price is Rs.100.00 and rate of tax is 10.2% including education cess. The amount of service tax will be:—

100 * 10.2/110.2 = Rs. 9.25

Denoting Rs. 9.25 as service tax, the service provider can raise the bill by showing Rs. 90.75 as the amount charged for service and Rs. 9.25 can be added as service tax to make the composite price at Rs. 100.00.

16.2-1 Exemption to sub-contractor providing works contract service to other contractor

Following service is exempt - Sub-contractor providing services by way of works contract to another contractor providing works contract services which are exempt - clause 29(h) Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Thus, if main works contract is exempt, sub-contractor providing works contract service to main contractor will be exempt from service tax. This exemption is only when the sub-contractor provides works contract service and not in other cases.

16.2-2 Sub-contractor liable even if main contractor pays service tax

CBE&C vide circular No. 999.03/23.8.07 has clarified that a sub-contractor is also a taxable service provider. His services are taxable even if these are used by main provider for completion of his work. The sub-contractor is liable even if the service is input service of the main contractor.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor is exempt from service tax - CBE&C circular No. 138/7/2011-ST dated 6-5-2011.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor has paid service tax - Engineers India Technical Services v. CCE (2014) 73 VST 206 (CESTAT).

In Sew Construction Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 120 = 12 taxmann.com 12 (CESTAT), it has been held that sub-contractor was liable even prior to 23-8-2007.

However, if sub-contractor is providing a service which is exempt, then he will not be liable e.g. if a contractor is providing works contract service which is exempt and if he entrusts that work to sub-contractor, then the sub-contractor will be providing the works contract service (which is exempt) and hence he will also not be liable to pay service tax. However, if the sub-contractor provides some other service like consultancy, cargo handling, clearing and forwarding which is taxable, then the sub-contractor will be liable to service tax even if the main contractor is exempt - CBE&C circular No. 147/16/2011-ST dated 21-10-2011 (The circular is with reference to works contract service but is applicable to all services provided by sub-contractors).

23.1-8 Redevelopment is subject to GST

Generally in re-development project, land is owned by a society, comprising members of the society with each member entitled to his share by way of an apartment. When it becomes necessary after the lapse of a certain period, society or its flat owners may engage a promoter (builder/developer) for undertaking re-construction. Society/individual apartment owners give 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) or permission to the promoter (builder/developer), for re-construction. The promoter (builder/developer) constructs apartments with same or different carpet area for original owners of apartment and additionally may also be involved in one or more of the following: (i) construct some additional apartments for sale to others (ii) arrange for rental accommodation or rent payments for society members/original owners for stay during the period of re-construction (iii) pay an additional amount to the original owners of flats in the society.

Under this model, the promoter (builder/developer) receives consideration for the construction service provided by him, from two categories of service receivers. First category is the society/members of the society, who transfer development rights over the land (including the permission for additional number of apartments), to the promoter (builder/developer). The second category of service receivers consist of buyers of apartments other than the society/members. Generally, they pay by cash.

In both the cases, GST is payable as in first case, the promoter receives consideration in form of TDR and in other cases, by cash.

23.1-9 GST on Slum Rehabilitation Programmes

In Slum Rehabilitation programmes, Government transfers TDR/FSI to promoter. The promoter supplies apartments to slum dwellers without monetary consideration. The apartments constructed in addition to apartments given free to the slum dwellers are sold.

In both the cases, GST is payable - FAQ (Part II) Nos. 8 and 9 issued by CBI&C vide circular F No. 354/32/2019-TRU dated 14-5-2019.

10.8-5 Value of Material supplied by buyer to be added to 'sale price'

In Hardeo Singh v. State of Bihar (2004) 137 STC 497 (Jhar HC FB), material supplied by buyer was incorporated by buyer was used by seller (contractor) in execution of works contract. It was held that value of such material is required to be added in 'sale price' and contractor is liable to pay sales tax on that value. The reason is that if material supplied by buyer is incorporated by contractor in works contract, there is deemed transfer of property in goods involved in such works contract and sales tax can be levied on value of such goods at the hands of contractor.

However, in ACST v. Hindustan Construction Co. Ltd. (2010) 36 VST 163 (Bom HC DB), the contractee (Bombay Municipal Corporation) agreed to bear cost of water and sewage and accordingly deducted a fixed amount from the contractor's Bill. It was held that this amount is not part of bid price and not includible under composition scheme.

10.8-6 Royalty payable cannot be included for purpose of works contract tax

Royalty paid by holder of mining lease to lessor is not the price for removal of minerals. Royalty is not a tax. Royalty is a payment reserved by the grantor of a patent, lease of a mine or similar right, and payable proportionately to the use made of the right by grantee Mining lease is an interest in immovable property. It does not attract purchase tax - State of Himachal Pradesh v. Gujarat Ambuja Cement Ltd. (2005) 6 SCC 499 = 142 STC 1 (SC 3 member bench).

Earlier, in Cooch Bihar Contractors Association v. State of West Bengal (1996) 103 STC 477 (SC) [followed in Mysore Minerals v. KAT, Bangalore (2001) 124 STC 413 (Karn HC DB)], it was held that royalty payable to Government and recovered from customer is part of sale price of goods and is includible. This decision now stands overruled.

In ACTO v. R K Constructions (2001) 124 STC 701 (Raj HC), it was held that if material is supplied by Government to contractor for use in Government contract, there is no 'transfer of property in goods' to contractor and no sales tax is leviable, even if Government had collected royalty.

22.3-1 Works Contract is supply of service for rate of tax under GST

Works contract as defined in section 2(119) of CGST Act is a composite supply and shall be treated as 'supply of service' - Para 6(a) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

General rate of GST on composite supply of works contract services is 18%. This is irrespective of GST rate on individual goods used in execution of works contract.

Works Contract is deemed sale of goods as per Constitution - A tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract is deemed sale of goods under Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India. [Note that this Article in the Constitution of India is continuing even after Constitutional amendment].

Works contract is not limited to construction - The term 'works contract' is not limited to construction services. It covers all activities relating to plant, machinery or equipment which are immovable.

8. Section 7 CGST defines supply in an inclusive manner meaning it is a widened and broadened connotation. Essentially, a flat under construction and intended to be sold to a buyer is sale of immovable property, but when it is undergoing construction there is an element of service and consequently, it was necessary to treat construction of flats as a supply of service vide Section 7(1)(d) read with item no 5(b) of Schedule II. 9. Schedule of Goods and Service Tax rates for services approved by GST Council laying down fitment of rates of services states at entry 19 that "Construction of a complex, civil structure or part thereof intended for sale to a buyer wholly or partly" will bear GST at 12.5% with full input tax credit, but no refund of overflow of input tax credit. The entry also explains that the value of land is included in the amount charged from the service recipient. Simultaneously, rate of GST for composite works contract as defined in Section 2(119) vide entry 27 is 18% with full input tax credit. In substance and effect, though construction of flat is treated as a service yet it is akin to a works contract. Drawing such a cue implies that concession of 6% is given to factor in value of land thereby leading to a calculation of 33% of abatement on the total consideration. However, prescription of such a standard rate of abatement [assumed] does not take into realities of cheap, medium, semi-luxury, luxurious and elite segments where composition of land value would considerably vary. Moreover, in semi-rural developing towns, presumed rate of 33% in respect of land value may be on higher side leading to excess input credit over 12% output tax inasmuch as input supplies for builders mostly carry a rate of 18% to 28% which as per schedule of rates as seen above is not refundable. In cases, where input tax credit falls short of GST rate of 12% profits of builders will truncate or lead passing of burden on to consumers. In my opinion, this matters ought to have been formulated by the legislature in a flexible manner through a methodology by way of rules to reckon local factors.

10. Another daunting controversy that may arise is whether the overflow of input tax credit is to be worked per project or on a net basis for all projects put together. Section 16 of CGST provides that every person shall subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in Section 49 be entitled to the credit of any input tax in respect of any supply of goods and services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business and the amount shall be credited to the electronic ledger of such person. In my opinion, looking at the wording of Section 16 aforesaid read with Section 17 better view appears to be that an overall picture of all projects will have to be undertaken and not project wise. No guidance is found either in the Act or the relevant rules as what are the implications of GST in a case when a project undertaken by the builder where he has to give flats to the owner of land in discharge of consideration for obtaining development rights. Assuming in a particular case, the developers have to provide 100 flats to owners and there other 200 flats for free sale; in former case he will be a contractor levying GST at 18% with input tax credit, whereas in the latter case, the rate would be 12% with full input tax credit but no refund of overflow credit in a situation where flats are sold before they are fully developed. In the aforementioned example, there can controversy as to how the overflow of input tax credit to be computed being the difference between the rate of GST on input supplies and 18% GST rate more particularly, after considering common input supplies and capital goods employed for both types of flats. Moreover, disputes will arise as to what is time of supply of the 100 units to be allotted to owners more specifically, if land is not parted physically at one go, but in stages. Can we say the supply of flats is complete when possession of land is given despite the fact that flats are yet to be constructed? If the free sale flats are sold in stages question will emanate as to whether input tax credit is to be accumulated or can be claimed while construction is progressing without any sale? It would be best to issue clarifications on these and other potential roadblocks that may lead to avoidable litigation.

10.11-4 Taxability of BOT projects

Government gives many contracts on BOT (Build Operate and Transfer) basis to private parties. The private party makes its own investment in the project and then gets exclusive rights to collect toll or other amounts for prescribed period (in many cases, 20 years). After the prescribed period, the ownership is transferred to Government. In case of projects awarded by National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), the agreement is termed as 'concession agreement; and the contractee is termed as 'concessionaire' and not 'contractor'.

Really this is a grant of right to enjoy fruits of the immovable property for specified period. It is 'profit a prendre' i.e. grant of benefit arising out land. It is not 'works contract'.

This is not a construction contract given by Government. The 'concessionaire' (by whatever name called) is constructing the roads etc. for himself and not for Government.

This should not be taxable either under Vat or service tax.

10.11-5 Income Tax provisions

As per section 194C of Income Tax Act, tax is required to be deducted at source if assessee makes any payment to contractor for carrying out any work (including supply of labour for carrying out such work) in pursuance of a contract. CBDT, vide its circular No 891 dated 8-3-1991 has clarified that where contractor undertakes to supply any article or thing fabricated according to the specifications given by customer and the property in such article or thing passes to the customer only after such article or thing is delivered, the contract will be a contract for sale and as such outside the purview of section 194C. - - This is fully in line with general understanding of distinction between contract for sale and a works contract.

TDS only if it is contract for work - CBDT, vide circular No. 13/2006 dated 13-12-2006 has clarified that TDS provisions under section 194C apply only when there is contract for work and not when there is contract for sale of goods.

10.11-6 Service tax on works contracts

Service tax has been imposed on service portion of almost all works contracts of movable and immovable property w.e.f. 1-7-2012. [Till 1-7-2012, service tax on works contract was only in relation to immovable property].

Thus, these will be liable both for sales tax on 'goods involved in works contract', and 'service tax' in respect of service portion of works contract.

If the transaction is 'deemed sale' and hence comes under Entry 54 of List II, the goods portion cannot be taxed by Union Government.

In CCE v. BSBK Pvt. Ltd. (2010) 26 STT 263 = 253 ELT 522 (CESTAT 3 member LB), it has been held that turnkey contract can be vivisected and discernible service elements involved therein can be segregated and classifiable as well as valued for levy of service tax under Finance Act, 1994, provide such services are taxable services as defined by that Act. The basic reason given is that Article 366(29A)(b) of Constitution of India provides for 'deemed sale of goods' which envisages and allows vivisection of indivisible contracts.

This decision will equally apply to all works contracts.

Other Case-Laws 4. In the case of Gannan Durnkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. v. State of Madras AIR 1954 Mad. 1130, the Hon’ble Madras High Court held that the building contracts were not contracts for the sale of goods as defined under the Sale of Goods Act, 1930 and, therefore, the assessees were not liable to pay sales tax on the amounts received from the person for whom they had constructed buildings. However, the High Courts of Kerala, Nagpur, Rajasthan and Mysore had taken a different view. The Supreme Court in State of Madras v. Gannon Durnkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. AIR 1958 SC 560 held that there was no sale of goods and it was not within the competence of the provincial Legislature under Entry 48 in List II in the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, 1935 (now Entry 54 of List II under the Constitution of India) to impose a tax on the supply of material used in such a contract by treating it as a sale.

Constitutional Amendment

5. In order to overcome the above decision of the Supreme Court, a new clause viz., clause (29A) was introduced in article 366 of the Constitution by the 46th Amendment, which reads as under—

"‘(29A) tax on the sale or purchase of goods’ includes—

(a )A tax on the transfer, otherwise than in pursuance of a contract, or property in any goods for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration;

(b )a tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract."

Effect of Constitutional Amendment : Case-Laws

6. In Builder’s Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 2 SCC 645, the Supreme Court considered the 46th amendment to the Constitution and came to the conclusion that the State Governments could levy sales tax on the value of the goods involved in an indivisible works contract by the legal fiction created by the 46th amendment.

(a)

Date of applicability of this Order. Whether it can substitute the relevant valuation mechanism with retrospective effect?

One of the astonishing aspect of the circular is that there is no specific date of applicability mentioned in the circular. In case of Ranbir Singh Ram Gopal v. St. of Hr. [CWP No. 11994, dated 11-12-1996], it was held that the there shall be no retrospective enhancement in tax-rates by notification / circular. Other issues still to be addressed and wanting the uber-attention of Law Makers and Law Administrators — No modus operandi has been identified in regard to WCT deduction by the customers, as they cannot be considered as structured as a 'normal contractee' to a normal works contract. Whether every customer is required to deduct WCT and seek registration under Haryana VAT Act?

There is major requirement to insert an exception to WCT deduction provisions to exclude flat buyers from WCT deduction liability. Ironically, a normal individual flat buyer today stand's on same footing as a well structured works contractee, though ground reality is exactly different. Note: - There is a discreet difference in Delhi VAT and Haryana VAT in regard to deduction of WCT. In Delhi, where the individual/HUF is the contractee, they are not burdened with WCT deduction liability (as per section 36A of DVAT Act), while as in Haryana the same is not the case, hence, even the individual / HUF shall be covered in the ambit of contractee and thereby liable to deduct WCT.

(e)

A Million Dollar Question - Can the burden of additional taxes be passed on to the customer or not? Will it affect the service tax liabilities ?

Another very interesting issue to arise here is that most developers enter into an agreement with prospective buyers according to which additional taxes are to be borne by the customers (as a part of space buyer's agreement).

But the governing section 9 of composition scheme mandates the contractor/developer not to issue any tax invoices. Hence, no tax can be collected on the strength of tax invoice.

10.3-8 Works contract if contract for construction is made with prospective buyer

In K Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka AIR 2005 SC 2350 = (2005) 5 SCC 162 = 2 STT 178 = 141 STC 298 = 3 STR 337 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

Section 2(1)(vi) of Karnataka Sales Tax Act stated that 'works contract' includes any agreement for carrying out for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, the building, construction, manufacture, processing, fabrication, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property.

Section 5B of the Act provided for tax on transfer of property in goods, whether as goods or in some other form, in the execution of works contract.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some wok on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

It was held that the developer would be liable to pay tax on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract.

Decision in case of K Raheja affirmed by large bench of Supreme Court - Decision of SC in case of Raheja Development Corporation was doubted in Larsen and Toubro v. State of Karnataka (2008) 16 STT 286 = 17 VST 460 (SC). It was observed that the main contract (development agreement) is not a works contract. In such case, question is whether it can be treated as works contract on basis of second agreement, which is a tripartite agreement. It was observed that if ratio of K Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka is accepted, there would be no difference between works contract and a contract for sale of chattel as a chattel. With these observations, the matter has been referred to a larger bench.

The large bench of SC, in Larsen and Toubro v. State of Karnataka (2014) 1 SCC 708 = 41 STT 113 = 38 taxmann.com 98 = 303 ELT 3 (SC 3 member bench), has affirmed the decision in case of K Raheja.

The summary of main issues decided is as follows —

Indivisible contracts can be segregated into (i) contract for sale of goods involved in works contract and (ii) for supply of labour and service [paras 63 and 101(viii)].

A contract may involve both a contract for work and labour and a contract for sale. In such composite contract, the distinction between contract for sale of goods and contract for work (or service) is virtually diminished [para 101(v)]

The term 'Works contract' is broad and includes all obligations and all types of contracts. Even if some obligations are imposed in addition to supply of goods and materials and performance of services, such contract is still a 'works contract'.

'Works contract' is a contract for undertaking or bringing into existence some 'works' [para 76]

16.2

Coverage of 'works contract' under service tax

For purpose of service tax, the term 'works contract' has been defined as follows—

'"Works contract" means a contract wherein transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods and such contract is for the purpose of carrying out construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration of any movable or immovable property or for carrying out any other similar activity or a part thereof in relation to such property - section 65B(54) of Finance Act, 1994 as introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012.'

Coverage of services under works contract service - Though the definition of works contract under service tax and CST/State Vat Acts are quite different, practically most of the works contracts taxable under State Vat laws will get covered under service tax also. This is because definition of 'works contract' under service tax covers wide range of activities relating to both movable and immovable property.

This view has also been expressed in para 6.8.6 of CBE&C's 'Taxation of Services : An Education Guide' published on 20-6-2012.

Thus, following will get covered under this definition :

(a)

Erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures

(b)

Construction of buildings and civil structures

(c)

turnkey projects

(d)

maintenance services relating to goods where goods and service both are involved as composite contract (e.g. Annual Maintenance Contracts)

(e)

Job work (which does not amount to manufacture) where job worker uses some of his own material (which may be even minor) [Job work will get covered under the term 'alteration']

Departmental clarification - Laying of pipeline or conduit, erection, commissioning of machinery, equipment and structures, painting of building, renovation of building, flooring, repairs of building would be covered under 'works contract' - Paras 5.8.2 to 5.8.6 of Annexure A of MF(DR) TRU DO F. No. 334/1/2012-TRU dated 16-3-2012.

The circular stated that works contract will not cover 'tailoring or development of photograph'. However, in view of revised definition of 'works contract' under service tax law w.e.f. 1-7-2012, even tailoring or development of photograph will come under 'works contract' service.

State Vat/CST should be payable - One basic requirement is that the activity should be subject to tax as sale of goods. (The activity may be relating to movable or immovable property)

Laying of pipeline is not erection and commissioning service - Pipeline is not a plant, machinery, equipment or structure. The activity is not taxable as erection, installation and commissioning service - CCE v. Surindra Engineering (2015) 79 VST 436 (CESTAT).

In Indian Hume Pipe Co. Ltd. v. CCE (2008) 16 STT 136 = 26 VST 63 (CESTAT), assessee was manufacturing and supplying pre-stressed concrete pipes for water supply. He also undertook contract for construction of pipeline by excavation, conveying and lowering pipes and joining material, laying to proper grade and alignment, refilling trenches, construction of air valves. It was held that this is not installation and commissioning service. In case of laying of pipeline, appellant were not undertaking activity of erection of pipeline. The appellant did not set up a pipeline but constructed one. Long distance pipeline is not a 'plant'. - followed in Lalit Constructions v. CCE (2012) 37 STT 687 = 27 taxmann.com 194 (CESTAT).

In Strategic Engineering v. ACCE (2012) 49 VST 381 (Mad HC), it was held that laying of pipes for transportation of fluid is not erection, commissioning service.

Vat is payable by builders in Karnataka and Rajasthan for which various scheme are available. Vat is payable in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal also.

Conclusion

8.The concept of outsourcing all activities, barring the core area of specialization is gradually evolving globally, including in India. To avoid litigation surrounding levy of applicable tax, it is of paramount importance to have clarity on as to when does the process qualify as 'manufacture'? There are even greater complexities regarding the process involving both supply of goods and rendition of service, as identifying the correct base for levy of service tax on the service element becomes a challenging task. The proposed Goods and Services Tax ('GST') scenario looks optimistic for the job work sector when all the taxes, i.e., excise duty, service tax and VAT will get subsumed under the 'grand tax', as we may call it, and there will be one base for levy of GST without any distinction between goods and services.

The general rate of GST on construction and works contract service was 18% (9% CGST plus 9% SGST) or 18% IGST. However, in case of construction of complex, the builder charges a amount which is inclusive of land or undivided share of land. In that case, the land value will be taken as one third (33.33%) of total amount (i.e. value including land value) and GST is payable on balance amount. Thus, effectively GST rate was 12% (6% CGST plus 6% SGST) or 12% IGST, upto 31-3-2019:

22.6 Distinction between construction service and works contract service

There is no doubt that construction contract is also a 'works contract'. However, under GST, distinction has been made between 'works contract service' and 'construction of complex'.

The distinction is that in case of works contract, a customer (recipient of supply of service) approaches the supplier of service (contractor) to undertake construction as per his requirements. In almost all the cases, the land is owned by or taken on lease by customer. The contractor enters into contract with customer and then undertakes construction with his own material. If the material is supplied by recipient himself (customer), then it is not works contract. It is simple contract for work.

In construction of complex, the builder or developer normally does not have any identified customer. Even if he has some identified customers before commencement of construction, he is undertaking construction activity on his own and not on basis of contract with customer. The land never belongs to the customer.

22.7 Concessional in case of certain infrastructure related works contracts

In respect of some works contract services provided in relation to infrastructural projects, the tax rate was 12% from date as specified upto 18-7-2022 — Notification No. 11/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 8/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017 as amended from time to time.

Now, in most of the work contracts, the normal rate of 18% with ITC will apply after 18-7-2022.

YOUR QUERIES ON SERVICE TAX

A contractor is constructing railway station for Metro Rail Project. Another contractor is installing telecommunication system for the Metro Rail Project. Are these contractors required to pay service tax?

No, these activities would not attract service tax liability. One can rely upon decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Shahdara (Delhi) Saharanpur Light Rly. Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Board, Saharanpur AIR 1967 SC 1747 wherein it was held that definition of ‘railway’ is very wide and would include every structure or mechanical/communication/electrical system set up for the Metro Rail Project through the contractors for this rail transit system and it is not restricted to the railway tracks.

The same meaning should apply to the word ‘railways’ figuring in section 65(105)( zzzza) of the Finance Act, 1994. When the definition of ‘taxable services’ itself states that works contract in respect of ‘railways’ would not come within its scope, it would mean that each and every activity mentioned in the definition which is for a railway system, is outside its scope. Accordingly, construction of station building or setting up of telecommunication system for use in the Metro Rail Project is not subject to service tax under the category of ‘execution of works contract’.

The municipal corporation of a metro city is constructing a multi-storied building. It is to use 50 per cent of the space in the building for civic purposes and would rent the balance 50 per cent to various offices for commercial use. Whether the contractor is required to pay service tax on the construction of his building?

No, this activity would not fall under the category of ‘execution of works contract service’. One can rely upon the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of State of Orissa v. Joginder Patjoshi AIR 2004 SC 1039 wherein it was held that the expression ‘primary’ is used in contradiction with ‘secondary’. The main objective is referred to primary and a subsidiary objective as secondary. The thing which comes first is primary. For example, the primary education is followed by secondary education.

The municipal corporation will use civic centre primarily for its activities in the role of a civic body. It is only when there is space left after the purpose of municipal corporation is satisfied that it will give such surplus space on rent for use as office. Even, in such a case, it would not give more than 50 per cent of the space in the building on rent. If more than 50 per cent of the space is not given on rent, then it cannot be said that the building is used primarily for renting of space for commercial use. Hence, the building being constructed by the contractor would not be used ‘primarily’ for commerce or industry. Therefore, construction of the building of the municipal corporation is not taxable under the category of ‘Execution of works contract service’.

Whether a contractor who started executing the contract prior to June 1, 2007, is required to pay service tax on the amount received subsequent to this date?

Service tax on execution of works contract has been introduced from June 1, 2007. The value on which service tax is to be paid for a works contract has been prescribed in law. Rule 2A of the Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, prescribes the value which gets transferred in the execution of the contract to the customer, and VAT or sales tax on such transfer are to be deducted from the gross amount charged for the works contract. Thus, the whole of the works contract has been treated as a single transaction, the value of which is the starting point for computation of taxable value. There is no scope for considering the gross amount charged for the works contract to be less than the lump sum price. Therefore, computation of service tax based on a fraction of a contract price is not envisaged in law. For a contract, where execution started before June 1, 2007, it is not permissible to bifurcate the contract to pay service tax on the basis of quantum of activities performed on or after June 1, 2007, while considering the part performed prior to this date as not taxable.

We are doing the turnkey projects in environmental engineering. Our scope of work includes design, supply, erection, and installation and commissioning. Our order is generally composite contract. Payments terms indicate release of payments on basis of completion like certain amount as advance against order, submission of design, drawing, against supply of material, against erection and installation, against commissioning and finally against successful trial run, etc.

QUESTIONS :

1.What basic precaution is required to be taken while submitting tender or accepting the order from client keeping in view the implication of service tax ?

2.If order is composite, is it required to mention in the order the value of the various activities like Supply, Design and Drawing, Erection, Installation and Commissioning, etc., to ascertain the service tax obligation ? Is there any way to save the service tax by doing proper presentation in the order and bills, etc. What is that ?

3.We are already registered with Excise Department, Service Tax Cell, for our Consulting Engineer, Installation and Commissioning and Repairs and Maintenance. In the said Registration billing address is from our Registered office, i.e., A-116, whereas we are doing project all over India and registered under Sales Tax Act in each State wherever we are doing the project. In such situation we are billing from each of such States directly to the client. So what is the alternative with regard to billing for service tax in such case ?

4.As the rate of service tax has been increased from 8 per cent to 10.2 per cent (including 2 per cent cess) in the Budget, at what rate we have to pay to the Government for the payment realized after that particular date and billing done before that particular date ?

5.If we received a sub-contract from contractor who is charging the service tax to the main contractor, in such case are we exempted for paying service tax on account of double taxation ? What is the exact procedure to get exemption ? What type of documents/letters are required from the employer and or main contractor ?

6.If we give sub-contract to other sub-contractor, can he be exempt from service tax by not charging service tax from us on account of double taxation? What type of document we have to given to that sub-contractor for not charging and ultimately not paying the service tax ?

ANSWERS :

1. While giving tender ensure that amount stated in the tender is either inclusive of all taxes or it should be clearly mentioned that taxes, if any, would be charged separately. While quoting a figure inclusive of taxes,a note should be stated indicating that any increase in indirect tax rates would be borne by the customer. Ensure proper calculation of taxes (also refer ans. 2) so as to avoid short-collection subsequently.

2. The Government has issued Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003 with effect from July 1, 2003 whereby general exemption has been given from service tax levy on so much of the value of all the taxable services, as is equal to the value of goods and materials sold by the service provider to the recipient of service subject to the condition that there is documentary proof specifically indicating the value of the said goods and materials.

It is further clarified that this exemption would be available only in cases where the sale of such goods is evidenced and the sale value is quantified and shown separately in the invoice.

So, as mentioned above, service tax is not leviable on supply of material, provided the sales value of the material is separately mentioned in the invoice.

In the case of composite contract, where value of material supplied cannot be determined separately, service tax is to be paid at the rate of 8 per cent on 33 per cent of the total composite value.

Let us consider an example :

Value of composite contract 100 (out of which 60 is labour and 40 is material) :

If the invoice shows only the consolidated amount, i.e., Rs. 100, then amount of service tax to be paid would be 8 per cent (100 x 33 per cent) = Rs. 2.64.

If material supply of Rs. 40 is shown separately in the invoice, then service tax to be paid works out to 60 x 8 per cent = Rs. 4.8.

Now let us consider another contract of value Rs. 100 (wherein labour = 20 material = 80) :

If the invoice shows only the consolidated amount, i.e., Rs. 100, then amount of service tax to be paid would be 8 per cent (100 × 33 per cent) = Rs. 2.64.

WORKS CONTRACT-SALES OR SERVICE ?

Taxation on works contract has always been a source of litigation. An attempt is made to compile judgments on the issue and look at the direction where taxation on works contract is heading towards in general and its impact on service tax in particular.

Era before 46th Amendment

1. Prior to 46th amendment, composite contracts such as works contract, hire purchase contracts and catering contracts were not assessable as contracts for sale of goods.

In State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley & Co. (Madras) Ltd. AIR 1958 SC 560, the Supreme Court held that sale of goods in entry 48 of List II of 7th Schedule did not cover sale sought to be taxed by the State Government. In a building contract which is one, entire and indivisible, there is no sale of goods and it is not within the competence of the State Legislature to impose a tax on the supply of the materials used in such a contract treating it as a sale.

This decision led to 46th amendment to the Constitution amending article 366(29A) for the expression ‘tax on the sale or purchase of goods’.

2.1 Builders Association of India v. UOI AIR 1989 SC 1371

u The Supreme Court held that after 46th amendment, works contract which was indivisible one, by a legal fiction is altered into a contract which is divisible into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services.

SERVICE PORTION OF WORKS CONTRACT

16.1

Background

Works contract is composite contract of goods and services. Sales tax (Vat) is on goods involved in works contract. Sales tax can be imposed on value of goods involved in works contract and service tax can be imposed on value of services.

'Service portion in the execution of a works contract' is 'declared service' - section 66E(h) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

A tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract is deemed sale of goods under Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India. [As inserted by 46th Amendment to Constitution in 1982]

Earlier, in State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley - (1958) 9 STC 353 (SC) = 1959 SCR 379 = AIR 1958 SC 560, it was held that tax cannot be levied on works contract. This was because the Constitution did not define 'sale' and hence the term 'sale' has the same meaning as given in Sale of Goods Act. To get over the difficulty created by this judgment, Constitution was amended in 1982 by 46th Amendment and concept of 'deemed sale' was introduced to cover transfer of property in goods involved in works contract.

In Builders' Association of India v. UOI - (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member constitution bench), it has been observed : 'After the 46th amendment, the works contract which was indivisible one, is by a legal fiction altered into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services. After 46th amendment, it has become possible for States to levy tax on value of goods involved in a works contract in the same way in which the sales tax was leviable on the price of goods and materials supplied in a building contract which had been entered into two distinct and separate parts.

Distinction between a divisible contract and an indivisible contract came to an end after forty sixth Amendment to Constitution - National Organic Chemicals Industries Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 54 VST 271 (Bom HC DB).

In State of Karnataka v. Transglobal Power Ltd. (2015) 77 VST 509 (Karn HC DB), it has been held that if contract is divisible, it cannot be a works contract.

In an indivisible works contract, there was no sale of goods as there could be no agreement to sell materials as such and moreover, the property would not pass as movables. 4.9 Builders Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 73 STC 370 (SC) - The background of this case is that after Amendment to Constitution in 1983, various State Governments imposed levy on works contract. The tax was levied by some State Governments on full value of contract which included the material cost and other costs like labour, supply of services, etc. However, in the judgment the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the power of States to levy tax on works contract was subject to limitation of Article 286, i.e., tax could not be levied by State on : (a) Outside the State, (b) during import/export, (c) Restrictions placed on 'declared goods' were applicable even while levying tax on works contract. Further, tax could not be imposed on full value of contract. The tax was on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract could be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

4.10 Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan [1993] 66 Taxman 229 (SC) - In this case it was held that taxable event is the transfer of property in the goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The said transfer of property takes place when goods are incorporated in the works. Hence, value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are not taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, Legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract. It is permissible to have a uniform rate for works contract. This rate may be different from the rates applicable to individual goods.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka [1993] 88 STC 248 (SC).

A builder entering into contract for sale of flat or a developer entering into contract for construction of an individual flat for personal residential use of client were not liable to pay service tax.

Activity done for self is not works contract.

BOT projects not taxable except when payment is made to Government or sub-contractor by concessionaire.

Valuation

Broadly, two options were available to service provider -

(a)

Calculate value of service as per rule 2A of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006 (in short 'Valuation Rules' and pay service tax at normal rate on such 'value'. In such case, assessee can avail Cenvat credit of input services, inputs and capital goods

(b)

Pay service tax under 'composition scheme' at 4.80% w.e.f. 1-4-2012 [Earlier it was 4.12% upto 1-4-2012] of 'gross amount charged for works contract' (inclusive of education cess and SAH education cess), under 'Works Contract (Composition Scheme for Payment of Service tax) Rules, 2007'. The assessee could avail Cenvat credit of input services and capital goods but not of input goods and capital goods.

In both the cases, Vat/sales tax will not be included in the 'value' for purpose of calculating service tax.

Value of material supplied free by the contractee, or sold directly to contractee to be added - Under the service tax provisions in respect of construction services, service tax is payable on 33% of gross value of contract vide Notification No. 1/2006-ST dated 1-3-2006, if assessee does not avail Cenvat credit. In such cases, value of material supplied by contractee (service receiver) is required to be added to the gross amount charged. The reason is that gross amount should include value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used.

Till 7-9-2009, there was no such provision of adding value of material supplied by contractee (service receiver or other person) in case of composition scheme under works contract service tax. Value of material supplied by customer was not required to be added.

Exemptions

Construction and works contract services relating to ports exempt, but no exemption to finishing or repairing services - Notification No. 25/2007-ST dated 22-5-2007.

Introduction

1. Goods and Services Tax (GST) may be Good and Simple for others, but not for the God. Dream of residence for the God is costlier now as GST is payable @ 18% on construction of a religious place. "Dharma" is one of the important pillars in Indian culture and has a capacity to save human from an evil within a human. And this may be the reason why we all respect religion by one way or another way. It can be seen in the history of Indian taxation that religious trusts are kept out of the tax net. However, this trend seems to be unsettled by introduction of GST in India.

Construction of Religious building In GST net

2. Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28th June, 2017 exempts various services. In fact very first entry of the said notification exempts services provided by an entity registered under Section 12AA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 by way of charitable activities and words 'charitable activities' are defined to include advancement of religion, spirituality or yoga. Thus, charitable services provided by such trust are out of GST.

However, services received by a trust are not covered under the above entry and a person providing services to such trust has to pay GST. Construction of a building is a service and construction of temple building is also subject to GST and no exemption from GST is granted for construction of religious place like a Temple, Church, Gurudwara, Mosque etc.

Religious places are being built by non-profit motive trusts and those are dependent on donations and have very limited resources. If GST is payable at 18%, practically 18% less temples will be built in India, due to GST.

In terms of Entry Number 3 to the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28th June, 2017, in case of construction services 9% CGST (and so 9% SGST, total 18%) is required to be paid. Further, if construction contract is a composite contract, effective rate would be 12% provided value of land is also included in the contract value. Generally, land is not included in the price paid to the contractor who is awarded contract for construction of a temple and hence rate of 12% will not be applicable in such case. Hence, practically, construction of any religious place attracts 18% GST.

Conclusion

3. Construction of a religious place was exempt from levy of service tax under entry number 13(c) of the Notification No. 25/2012-ST. Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28th June, 2017 is issued as mega exemption notification in GST and it doesn't include any entry which exempts construction of temple from levy of GST. Many entries in the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) are carried forwarded from existing Notification 25/2012-ST of service tax. However, for unknown reason, entry related to construction of religion place is not carried forwarded to new notification under GST. This may be intention of the Government or may be unintentionally taxed under GST. Whatever may be the reason, but today, the fact is that construction of any religious place, including Ram Mandir, will attract GST of 18%.

If intention of the Government is not to collect GST on construction of Ram Mandir, some exemption is required to be granted by the Government.

Director of Inspection, Customs & Central Excise 1985 taxmann.com 421, held that after the 46th Amendment to the Constitution, even if the dominant intention of the contract was the rendering of a service, it would still amount to a work contract and, in the execution of such a contract, if the property in the material used was passed on, then it would be deemed as a sale and a sales tax can be levied. By the amendment to the Constitution and through various judgments, the intention of the Legislature to levy sales taxes on the transfer of goods in a works contract has become manifest. It was only the modalities of working out the valuation of the goods for the purpose of charging a sales tax that needed resolution. The sales have arrived at their own formulae to fix the value of goods in such contracts. Where an assessee is not able to demonstrate the actual percentage of goods from his own records, recourse is taken to the formulae derived by the State for taxing of the goods.

Case Study

4. The following case study has been analysed :

4.1 Case - M/s. GE, engaged in the business of generation of electricity, intends to set-up a power plant in India. Total project is split up into following two contracts -

one with M/s. CN for supply of equipment and another with M/s. SO for erection and commissioning services ;

in respect of the first contract no Service tax is paid while as for the second contract M/s. SO pays service tax under the taxable service category of 'erection and commissioning services'.

The authorities opine that the total work is a turnkey project and, hence, is covered under works contract service, thereby making the assessee liable to pay service tax on works contract service under reverse charge basis on payment made to M/s. CN.

4.2 Solution - This case may be resolved as follows -

Contract speaks about total scope of work, i.e., from designing upto commissioning of plant and equipment. The total project is subsequently split up into two agreements. It fits into definition of works contract service.

The services provided by M/s. CN are works contract services and the assessee is liable to pay Service tax on payments made to CN on reverse charge basis.

Conclusion

5. While as works contracts are usually in the nature of contracts for the construction of immovable property such as buildings, power plants, etc., there are several kinds of contracts concerned with movable property that also fall within the scope of works contracts, including annual maintenance contracts, as they involve the transfer of property in goods coupled with the provision of works or services. In the case of work contracts, a sales tax is leviable on that portion of the contract which relates to the sale of goods. Most of the States in India provide for the payment of tax on works contracts separately to the value of the goods and materials sold at the rates specified under the respective State legislations.

However, some States provide for the payment of tax under a composition scheme at a fixed percentage. In a composition scheme the work contractor is required to pay the tax on the entire value of the contract without splitting up the value of the goods and materials supplied and the value of the services provided.
