23.1-1 Statutory provisions in respect of construction of complex

Following is 'supply of service' as per para 5(b) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

Construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly, except where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier.

Explanation.- For the purposes of this clause- (1) the expression "competent authority" means the Government or any authority authorized to issue completion certificate under any law for the time being in force and in case of non-requirement of such certificate from such authority, from any of the following, namely - (i) an architect registered with the Council of Architecture constituted under the Architects Act, 1972; or (ii) a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers (India); or (iii) a licensed surveyor of the respective local body of the city or town or village or development or planning authority.

(2) the expression "construction" includes additions, alterations, replacements or remodeling of any existing civil structure.

Residential Complex - "Residential complex" means any complex comprising of a building or buildings, having more than one single residential unit - para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Single Residential Unit - "Single residential unit" means a self-contained residential unit which is designed for use, wholly or principally, for residential purposes for one family - para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Occupancy certificate granted in is equal to completion certificate - In Mumbai i.e. Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), occupancy certificate is granted. Sale after such occupancy certificate (even before completion certificate) will be sale of immovable property and outside service tax net - PIB (Press Information Bureau), Ministry of Finance dated 26-10-2015.

Same view has been held in Bindu Ventures, In re [2018] 100 taxmann.com 207 (AAR - Karnataka) in respect of occupancy certificate issued by Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike.

Facts in the case of Harekrishna Developers, In re [2008] 14 STT 175 (AAR - New Delhi) 3.2 The applicant-firm intends to develop on its own plot of land a residential complex having more than twelve residential units with a club house and other common facilities. It will sell plots of land inside the complex to prospective buyers who will enter into a works contract with the applicant for the construction of residential units. The applicant itself will execute a part of the works contract [‘activity No. 3’] and for remaining part, the applicant will further enter into a works contract with other contractors [‘activity No. 4’]. However, goods for construction will be purchased/acquired by the applicant and the property in those goods will be transferred to buyers of the housing units and such transfer would be exigible to tax as sale of goods. The applicant sought advance ruling of the Authority on questions of its liability in these two types of activities, and also on question of rate of tax in case of activity No. 3.

The applicant contends that since the works contract in activities 3 and 4 involves construction of a new building-such an activity can only be covered under(ii)( b) in the Explanation to section 65(105)(zzzza). Since the new building proposed to be constructed in the course of the execution of the works contract is a residential one, and is not for the purpose of commerce or industry, such a works contract will not fall under (b) and therefore, will not attract service tax. The applicant further states that a works contract for construction of a new building for residential purposes is also not covered under any of the remaining classifications in (ii) of the Explanation to clause (zzzza). The classification (c) which covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’ is not applicable in applicant’s case as the works contract is for construction of an individual residential unit and not for construction of a residential complex.

Decision in the case of Harekrishna Developers (supra )

3.3 Authority for Advance Ruling held:

1. To attract service tax under sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105), a works contract has to meet the two conditions: (i) and (ii) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). The facts narrated by the applicant indicated that condition (i) is met in the instant case as the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract is exigible to tax as sale of goods under the local Sales Tax Act. To meet condition (ii), the activity involved in the works contract in activity Nos. 3 and 4 has to be covered by at least one of the classifications (a ) to (e) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). Proceeding serially, one finds that building of a residential house on a sub-plot in a residential complex is clearly not covered in (a). As pointed out by the applicant itself, it is also not covered by (b) which covers construction of a new building intended primarily for commerce and industry and does not cover construction of a new building. Item (c) of sub-clause (zzzza) of clause (105) covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’.

2. As per the draft of the works contract submitted, it is clear that such contracts will be for construction of individual houses on sub-plots located within the plot owned by the applicant on which the applicant proposes to develop a residential housing project. As per the applicant’s own narration, the residential project to be constructed on this plot would have at least 12 residential units, a club house and other common facilities and the layout of the project would be approved by the prescribed authority under the relevant law in force. Such a project constructed as per activity Nos. 3 and 4 squarely conforms to the definition of a ‘residential complex’ given in clause (91a) of section 65, and the individual houses constructed get covered under the definition of a ‘residential unit’ contained therein. Execution of the works contract, thus, involves construction of a part of a new ‘residential complex’ and is covered by (c).

CCE [2007] 7 STT 68 (Bang. - CESTAT), the assessee entered into contracts with his customers for supplying plant, machinery or equipment and for commissioning or installation of the said plant, machinery or equipment. The revenue demanded service tax from the assessee on erection, installation, commissioning of machinery or equipment and labour component of the contract. The demand was confirmed by the Commissioner. But the Tribunal following the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Larsen & Toubro case (supra), upheld the assessee’s contention that service tax could not be levied on works contract and set aside the demands. Similar decision was given in case of L&T Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 9 STT 356 (Ahd. - CESTAT). The Tribunal held that turnkey contracts entered into for execution, would not get covered under consulting engineering services. Another aspect which was considered by the Tribunal was that the Finance Bill, 2007, had included works contract services as taxable in sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105). Since the service tax liability on works contract is brought into the net from 2007, it can be argued that these services were not to be taxed earlier. Thus, the Tribunal allowed the assessee’s application for waiver of pre-deposit of amounts.

It is important to note that by the Finance Act, 2007, service tax is also levied on works contracts [section 65(105)( zzzza)]. It may be noted that under this service only the works contracts wherein transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract is exigible to VAT/sales tax, are covered, excluding works contract in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams. For the purpose of this sub-clause, "works contract" means a contract wherein,—

(i) transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods, and

(ii) such contract is for the purpose of carrying out,—

(a) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise, installation of electrical and electronic devices, plumbing, drain laying or other installations for transport of fluids, heating, ventilation or air-conditioning including related pipe work, duct work and sheet metal work, thermal insulation, sound insulation, fire proofing or water proofing, lift and escalator, fire escape staircases or elevators; or

(b) construction of a new building or a civil structure or a part thereof, or of a pipeline or conduit, primarily for the purpose of commerce or industry; or

(c) construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(d) completion and finishing services, repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services, in relation to (b) and (c); or

(e) turnkey projects including engineering, procurement and construction or commissioning (EPC) projects;

Thus, works contract in respect of specified infrastructure projects, namely, roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams are specifically excluded from the scope of the levy. Taxable value under this service is that part of the value of the works contract which is relatable to services provided in the execution of a works contract. Such value is to be determined on actual basis based on the records maintained by the assessee. However, an option is given to an assessee for a composition scheme. Under the composition scheme, the assessee was required to pay 2% of the total value of the works contract as service tax (now 4% w.e.f 1-3-2008). Assessee opting for the composition scheme is not entitled to avail CENVAT credit on inputs but can claim CENVAT credit on capital goods and input services required for use in the works contract.

(a)

Any agreement entered into by the builder / promoter before the completion of construction tantamounts to works contract and, hence, is liable to Value Added Tax (VAT)/ sales tax.

(b)

When an agreement is entered into between the promoter/developer and the flat purchaser to construct a flat and eventually sell the flat with the fraction of land, it is obvious that such transaction involves the activity of construction inasmuch as it is only when the flat is constructed then it can be conveyed. Such activity of construction has all the characteristics or elements of a works contract.

In tripartite agreement between the owner of the land, the developer and the flat purchaser, there is nothing wrong if the transaction is treated as a composite contract comprising of both a works contract and a transfer of immovable property and levy sales tax on the value of the material involved in execution of the works contract.

Conclusion

5. Thus, keeping in mind all the latest amendments and judgments of the various Courts, it can be concluded that works contract will be taxed as follows :

u First, the VAT or sales tax is to be paid on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract. u Then, the service tax is to be paid on the gross amount charged for the works contract service, which will not include the paid VAT or sales tax. This value is the value based on the actuals of the works contract service, in a composite contract.

u If the service provider opts for the Composite Scheme, then he has to pay 4 per cent of the gross amount.

u In case of an indivisible works contract, the tax will be levied on the approximate gross amount of the service, minus the amount for transfer of property.

Service tax is widening every year, and will only contribute a fair amount to the Government exchequer and Gross Domestic Product of the country. V.S. DATEY

A three member large bench of Supreme Court has delivered a very important judgment in respect of works contract, in case of Larsen & ToubroLtd. v. State of Karnataka [2013] 41 STT 113/38 taxmann.com 98 (SC 3 member bench).

Basically, this judgment has upheld validity of Vat on construction of residential flats and commercial premises. Though the judgment is in relation to Vat, it has significant impact on service tax aspects also.

BACKGROUND OF THE CASE

1. In K Raheja Development Corpn. v. State of Karnataka [2005] 2 STT 178 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some work on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

It was held that the developer would be liable to pay tax on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN DEVELOPER MODEL AND BUILDER MODEL OF CONTRACTS

2. In 'builder model' of building contracts, agreement to sale is executed with the intending purchasers. Conveyance is executed by builder only after building is complete and possession is handed over. The conveyance is in respect of land as well as construction.

In 'developer model', developer enters into contract with prospective buyers (allottees). After construction, possession is handed over. The owner of land directly transfers the entire land to society or owners of apartment, who become owners of undivided share of land. Separate agreement is not executed with developer (This is to save stamp duty).

The decision in case of K Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) was in respect of developer model. It was thought the decision of Supreme Court would not apply to builder model of contracts.

DECISION IN CASE OF K RAHEJA DEVELOPMENT CORPN. (SUPRA) DOUBTED

3. Decision of Supreme Court in case of K Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) was doubted in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka [2008] 16 STT 286. It was observed that if ratio of K Raheja Development Corpn. (supra) is accepted, there would be no difference between works contract and a contract for sale of chattel as a chattel. With these observations, the matter has been referred to a larger bench.

These observations supported a view that Vat will not apply in case of builder model of contracts.

DECISION IN CASE OF K RAHEJA DEVELOPMENT CORPN. (SUPRA) AFFIRMED BY LARGE BENCH OF SUPREME COURT

4. The large bench of SC, in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. (supra) has affirmed the decision in case of K Raheja.

In effect, it has been held that Vat applies to all types of construction agreements – whether builder model or developer model.

Introduction

1. Works contract is an indivisible contract. It is indivisible in the sense that value of goods to be incorporated in any form in the works and value of labour & other services to be rendered in execution cannot be segregated. It is also known as deemed sales.

In construction industries where entire work is assigned on completion basis, it always becomes matter of dispute as to what should be tax structure, as both the taxes - VAT/CST and service tax are applicable on such transaction. It is complex in nature due to non-synchronization in tax mechanism of the Central & State tax authorities. VAT is imposed by the State Government and on the other hand, the service tax is imposed by the Central Government. Calculation mechanism at both the stages is also different which results in unnecessary litigation & dispute burden on assessee.

Legal frameworks

2. Works contract in simple terms is a contract for carrying out certain works on any movable or immovable property of others. Sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A) of the Indian Constitution deals with the imposition of tax on transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of works contract.

Definition of works contract has been inserted in CST Act vide the Finance Act, 2005. Section 2(ja) of the Central Sales Tax Act defines works contract as follows—"Works contract means a contract for carrying out any work which includes assembling, construction, building, altering, manufacturing, processing, fabricating, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property."

All the State VAT Acts have defined works contract in a different manner but the meaning of works contract is similar in nature. After reading all definitions, the term "works contract" is nothing but a contract in which one of the parties is obliged to undertake or to execute works and property is transferred to other party, either as goods or in some other form.

GST & Works Contract

4. Having understood the conceptual bases surrounding the concept of works contracts, it finds itself at a juncture where the intersection between the peculiar taxation principles of works contracts with the proposed GST regime can be identified and evaluated.

The taxability of works contracts continues to be a contentious issue. We are yet to observe a mammoth reform in the form of Goods and Services Tax. The 100th Constitutional Amendment Bill has retained the concept of 'deemed sale'. However, the concept of 'sale' is to be done away with under the GST regime. It is known that works contract is taxable on sale and provision of services under the current regime. However, under the GST regime all the taxable events will be merged and there will only be one taxable event, being supply of good/service. If we look at the real estate sector, where works contracts find prevalence, compliances with multiple taxes constitutes a heavy burden. The GST seeks to remove these multiple taxes and bring in uniformity wherein the taxes would, in all probability, be levied at one rate. Further, it is expected that the cascading effect of taxes would be eliminated, at least in part owing to the GST.

4.1 Associated problems: It is believed that the GST regime would bring an end to the debate on works contract altogether. The issues relating to works contracts, in isolation, have been discussed above. However, GST would bring with itself a fresh and unprecedented set of complications:

The segregation of the components of a works contract is an arbitrary and contentious issue per se. Further, there is no clarity as to whether GST is applicable on real estate sector? This creates a huge gap in the GST base, leading to potential revenue losses.

The taxable event under the GST regime is supply of goods/service. What constitutes the taxable portion of a works contract has already been a widely and deeply litigated matter under the current tax regime; a new taxable event would lead to further interpretational issues.

It is an assumption that the GST will have a simple structure and goods and services will be taxed at a uniform rate. However, if a careful analysis of the Indian tax regime is conducted, convolutions in the law are easily identifiable. Different States have different needs, and, thus, it can be expected that different States would have different rates of taxation. This could lead to a more complex tax structure in the future.

Multiplicity in the rates of taxation is bound to lead us to retread the path of works contracts which, in turn, may culminate in complex interpretational and implementational issues.

Conclusion

5. The future relating to the taxation of works contract is very ambiguous. It cannot be predicted unless the law is brought in force. However, certain changes and measures which could be adopted as interim measures are briefly addressed:

The burden of taxation should be singular. Further, a uniform rate of taxation should be adopted by the States.

Long-term contracts which are still in force should incorporate clauses dealing with the changes, in law, and taxes.

Further, all components of taxation such as sale, service, etc., can be provided in the existing contracts, so as to save the margin of a service provider.

Proper documentation relating to the contracts should be maintained to avail of exemption, if any, to be provided in the new GST regime.

The issue relating to the treatment of deemed sales transactions needs to be addressed to by the Legislature. A definition relating to works contract could be included in the Amendment Bill for the sake of clear elucidation of the law.

A comprehensive Code relating to works contract taxation be provided, comprising of the taxable event, definition of works contract, valuation mechanism, etc., as an alternative to unending litigation.

Decision of Tribunal in the case of CCE v. BSBK (P.) Ltd. [2009] 18 STT 1 (NEW DELHI - CESTAT) 1.2 The assessee was engaged in business of execution of turnkey contracts for engineering works. On scrutiny of the records, the officials found that during the period from 7-7-1997 to 31-3-2002, it had received from its clients amounts for different services, including those falling under ‘consulting engineer service’, but had failed to pay service tax on it. On adjudication, demand was confirmed on design and engineering work done by it along with interest and penalties. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) who set aside that order. The assessee contended that in a case of turnkey works contract, service tax was not payable as the contract could not be vivisected and the services relating to ‘design and engineering’ formed a minor portion of the total work. In its support the assessee relied on decision of Tribunal in Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 184. The case of the revenue on the other hand was that the contract could be divided into sale contract and service contract in accord with the 46th amendment of the Constitution of India.

The Tribunal observed that in Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) it was held that a work contract cannot be vivisected and part of it subjected to tax. Prima facie, the decision in Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) was not in accordance with the decision of the Supreme Court in Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd.’s case (supra) (BSNL). After referring to different sub-clauses of clause (29A) inserted in article 366 by the 46th Amendment, a three-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court in said decision held that the amendment especially allows specific composite contracts, viz., works contracts [sub-clause (b)]; hire purchase contracts [sub-clause (c)]; catering contracts [sub-clause (e)] by legal fiction to be divisible contracts where the sale element could be isolated and be subjected to sales tax. The Court further held that: If there is an instrument of contract which may be composite in form in any case other than the exceptions in article 366(29A), unless the transaction in truth represents two distinct and separate contracts and is discernible as such, then the State would not have the power to seperate the agreement to sell from the agreement to render service and impose tax on sale. The text, therefore, for composite, contracts other than those mentioned in article 366(29A) continues to be: Did the parties have in mind or intended separate rights arising out of the sale of goods? If there was no such intention, there would be no sale even if the contract could be disintegrated. The test for deciding whether a contract falls into one category or the other is to as what is ‘the substance of the contract’. It would, thus, follow that the dominant nature of test cannot be applied in the case of a works contract falling under sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A), and, therefore, it could not be pressed into service for treating turnkey works contract on different a footing. If ‘works contract’ can be split up into sale contract and service contract, a different treatment may not be given to the so-called turnkey contract, simply because the contract has been on a turnkey basis - although basically it is a works contract. According to Tribunal, prima facie, Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) was not correctly decided and the finding that the turnkey works contract cannot be vivisected required reconsideration.

The Tribunal further held that there was no dispute in that, theoretically, service tax can be levied on service part and, at the same time, sales tax can be levied on the sale part of the contract. No doubt, service tax can be levied only if the service is a ‘taxable service’, within the meaning of Act. In the case of a ‘turnkey contract’ if they are not split up only on the ground that the contract is on turnkey project basis, a question may arise as to whether the entire contract would be a sale contract. The answer apparently would be in the negative. Only that part of the contract which falls under sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A) - amounting to ‘deemed sale’ will constitute sale contract on which sales tax can be levied. What will happen to the rest of the contract? Whether it will go out of the net of the service tax? Answer again would be in the negative. No doubt, as observed above, and it went without saying, that the ‘service’ will have to qualify as a taxable service.

In a Post Budget Conference, R. Sekar, joint secretary, Ministry of Finance, has clarified that while accommodation in hotels has been excluded, commercial renting in hotels will attract service tax. Therefore, hotels leasing out shops and business centres will have to pay service tax. In real sense, this is the only service which can be called as a new service brought under service tax net. However, the proposal to include this one new service under the taxable services chargeable to service tax has not found favour with either the industry, real estate sector in particular, or the general public. The inclusion of this service in tax net could not have been proposed at a worse time. Last year, the prices for commercial property increased due to high demand and inadequate supply. Adding to the woes, the sealing drive undertaken by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi led to further escalation of rentals in and around the capital.

There are some issues involved with this service. Firstly, it can be argued that since the land and building are State subjects chargeable to State taxes (under Entry 49 of the Constitution, only States have the right to levy tax on land), it would be constitutionally incorrect to levy service tax, a Union tax, on such subjects. Secondly, the move will affect traders, retailers and export-oriented offices like BPOs the most. Since, they do not have any other service tax liabilities, it would not be possible for them to offset the service tax that will be levied on the rent. Retailers will increase prices as they have no option but to pass on this additional tax to the customer thereby fuelling the already high inflation. Thus, ultimately, the already costly services will end up getting costlier; digging a deeper hole in the customers’ pockets.

Finally, the most important issue is whether any service element is present in the renting of the property. However, Dr. Parthsarathy Shome, advisor to the Finance Minister, does not seem to buy this argument as he has said in a post budget interactive session that property rental whether horizontal or vertical are essentially services in nature and, therefore, have been brought into service tax net.

Service involved in the execution of a works contract

3. In a works contract, sales tax/VAT is levied on the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such works contract. Now, the Finance Bill, 2007 has proposed to levy service tax on the service element involved in the execution of a works contract. The proposed definition of works contract is an exhaustive one which covers only the following works contracts wherein transfer of property in goods involved in execution of such works contract is leviable to VAT/sales tax :—

(i)works contract for carrying out erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures

(ii)works contract for commercial or industrial construction

(iii)works contract for construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof

(iv)works contract for completion and finishing services, repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services, in relation to (ii) and (iii)

(v)works contract for turnkey projects including engineering, procurement and construction or commissioning (EPC) projects.

It is to be noted that works contracts in relation to specified infrastructure projects, viz., roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams have been excluded from the definition of works contract, thereby excluding these types of works contract from the scope of the service tax levy.

The Finance Minister, P. Chidambaram, in his Budget speech has announced a composition scheme for the service providers involved in the execution of a works contact. The scheme would give an option to the assessee to pay 2 per cent of the total value of the works contract as service tax. The assessees opting for the composition scheme would not be entitled to avail CENVAT credit of capital goods, inputs and input services required for use in the works contract. The assessees who do not opt for this scheme would pay service tax on the taxable value of the works contract which is relatable to services provided in the execution of a works contract. Such value would be determined on actual basis based on the records maintained by the assessee. Separate rules for valuing works contracts will be notified later.

Mining service

4. Geological, geophysical or other prospecting, surface or sub-surface surveying or map-making services relating to location or exploration of deposits of mineral, oil or gas are subjected to service tax under ‘survey and exploration of mineral service’. Other services in relation to mining such as ‘site formation and clearance, excavation and earth moving’, drilling wells for production/exploitation of hydrocarbons (development drilling), etc., are also individually classified under the appropriate taxable services.

Now the Finance Bill, 2007 has proposed to bring services provided in relation to mining of mineral, oil and gas under a separate service. Thus, now services provided in relation to both exploration and exploitation of mineral, oil or gas would be covered under the service tax net.

It may be noted that unlike all other services where appropriate definitions have been provided in the Finance Act, the term ‘mining’ has not been defined. To ensure clarity and avoid ambiguity, it would be better if the term is defined appropriately.

Construction of cleaning and grading yards Question - We are establishing cleaning and grading yards at various places. These are to provide facility of cleaning and grading of farm produce to traders and farmers. After harvesting, the farmers or traders can bring the farm produce at these places. The cleaning and grading machinery installed at these places can be used by farmers. This will improve quality of the farm produce and fetch better price in market.

The construction work is done by contractors with their material. Is the service of construction of these cleaning and grading yards liable to service tax?

Answer - The work done by the contractors is 'works contract'.

As per Sr. No. 14(e) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012, services by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to mechanised food grain handling system, machinery or equipment for units processing agricultural produce as food stuff excluding alcoholic beverages are exempt from service tax.

Original works means - (i) all new constructions (ii) all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable (iii) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise - Explanation I(a) to Rule 2A of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006 - same definition adopted for exemption notifications as per definition clause 2(y) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Thus, construction service pertaining to machinery or equipment for units processing agricultural produce as food stuff is exempt from service tax.

Meaning of process - In CIT v. Tara Agencies [2007] 162 Taxman 337 (SC), Mamta Surgical Cotton Industries v. Assistant Commissioner (Anti Evasion) [2014] 44 GST 397/43 taxmann.com 237 (SC), following definitions were quoted with approval - process - A continuous and regular action or succession of actions taking place or carried on in a definite manner and leading to the accomplishment of some result - Oxford dictionary. A process is series of things which are carried out in order to achieve a particular result - Collins English Dictionary

Based on aforesaid judgments, it can be safely concluded that cleaning and grading is a 'process'.

Foodstuff - Foodstuff - any substance suitable as food - Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Food - a nutritious substance, esp. solid in form, that can be taken into an animal or a plant to maintain life and growth - - Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Foodstuff need not necessarily mean only the final food product which is consumed. It also include raw food articles which may after processing be used as food by human beings. - K Janadhan Pillai v. Union of India AIR 1981 SC 1485.

Thus, farm produce like wheat, rice etc. is 'foodstuff'.

Rule of purposive construction - This rule states that any statutory provision is to be interpreted considering the purpose behind the provision.

Based on aforesaid case law, it can be safely concluded that clearing and grading of farm produce by use of machinery is a 'process'. Further, it is one of the processes for preparation of foodstuff. Hence, service tax should be exempt.

If we apply the principle of purposive construction, the answer will be same i.e. exemption from service tax is available to the construction service, as that interpretation achieves the purpose of exemption.

Hence, in my view, the exemption from service tax is available to the service of construction of cleaning and grading yard in terms of Sr No. 14(e) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012.

The constitutionality of the circular was successfully challenged on the ground that the tax can only be levied on the gross turnover and not on the value of land. The judgment shows that the Courts across the country intended to follow the ruling of L&T judgment in its literal sense in order to achieve a uniform result relating to the issue of taxability in the case of works contract. In the case of The Indian Hume Pipe Co. Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan 19 the same line of L&T judgment was followed and the prayer for exemption of levying of tax on the value of pipe was rejected. The Apex Court held that the sale of pipes involved was in the execution of works contract and hence was taxable under the sales tax. The case of NIIT Limited Hyderabad v. Deputy Commissioner, Hyderabad 20 gave a new direction to the concept of works contract. In this case the petitioner-company was engaged in the business of Computer Education and Training and also providing Technology solution. The parties signed a contract with the State for imparting computer education along with leasing of hardware software and other connected accessories on Build Own Operate Transfer (BOOT) basis. The contract was said to form part of works contract and, hence, liable to be taxed. The leasing of accessories on BOOT basis was considered as transfer of property, as they were getting fees in return. It was held that the dominant nature test has no application so it should not be applied in any case; therefore, the levy of tax was allowed.

The plethora of cases after L&T showed a positive sign about the uniform development of taxation regime in the area of works contract in the country. This case to some extent tried to define the ambit of works contract and laid down the conditions that were needed to be followed while determining a contract to be having nature of works contract. Firstly, it was made clear that the tax will be deducted from the time after the parties entered into the agreement and not before that. Secondly, it was clarified that in the case of construction business, the value of land shall be excluded from the total cost that shall be taxed.21

Conclusion

5. The issue of taxability of works contract moved through several phases and it was always difficult for the Courts to reach to a definite conclusion regarding this issue. Even after series of cases and reasoning by the Courts, they were unable to categorically define the term 'works contract'. But it can be said that these cases helped a lot in forming some concrete concept regarding the works contract. The analysis of situation makes us realize that L&T's judgments contributed to a great extent to establish the status of taxability of works contract in India. But various principles and conditions laid down in the case resulted in conflicts.

The dominant nature test was ruled out in L&T judgment but the application of the same led to conflicts, which can be demonstrated with the help of two cases, i.e., International Hospital case and Pro Ltd. case. In the case of International Hospital v. State of U.P. 22the petitioner was the owner of superspecialty hospital where the implants were used during the course of surgical procedures. It was not considered as sale and, hence, not to be taxed. It was held that the patients visited the hospital for the surgical process; any implantation was an intrinsic and integral part of such process. Tax could not be imposed on such implantation, as the essential nature of transaction was the performance of medical procedure which in essence was outside the ambit of sale.23 But, in the case of State of Karnataka v. Pro Ltd. 24the challenge was made to the constitutional validity of the power of the State to levy tax on the processing and supply of photographs, photo prints and photo negatives. It was held by the Apex Court that after 46th Amendment that the State was given the power to levy taxes on works contracts by fictionally dividing it into sale and supply part but there will be no application of dominant intention rule. The photographic service was considered as sale and hence taxable. Therefore, there was inconsistency in the application of the said rule.

Under these circumstances, it may be expected that the GST regime (expected to be implemented in India by April, 2016) will contribute positively to the taxation of works contracts. The basis of the expectation lies in the uniform applicability of GST regime across the States which will help to avoid conflicts. Having said that it would be curious to see how the new regime will shape the taxation of works contracts in India.

Concept of the Works Contract

3. The determination of composite transactions as works contracts has been one of the most litigated topics under the indirect tax regime, proving to be a cumbersome ordeal for businesses over the years. From being not taxed at all, to the levy of tax on sale portion, and finally levy on service portion, works contracts disputes have come a long way. However, the journey of the works contracts seems to be far from concluded, particularly given the fundamental changes that the GST regime is bound to being in.

The establishment of a nexus between the sphere of works contracts with the proposed GST necessitates an overview of the developments that shaped the principles associated with the taxability of works contracts. Prior to the 46th Amendment to the Constitution of India, on perusal of various authorities12, it becomes apparent that works contracts could not have been liable to be taxed under the State tax laws; State Legislatures did not have competence to charge sales tax under Entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution on an indivisible contract of sale of goods had components of labour and service and was not within the domain of the Assessing Officer to dissect an indivisible contract to distinguish between the two constituent elements. Further, whether a particular contract was a works contract or a contract for sale of goods was dependent on the dominant intention, as reflected, inter alia, from the terms and conditions of the contract. There existed no strait-jacket formula to determine the nature of the contract, given its dependence on the facts and circumstances of each case.

Post 46th Amendment, with the insertion of sub-section (29A) under Article 366 of the Constitution, it became evident13 that the Courts started interpreting works contracts in a Constitutional backdrop. Cases which involved transfer of property along with an element of service in the context of work rendered, stood treated as works contracts.

It is pertinent to note that several principles of significance have been laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the judgments rendered in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka14 and Kone Elevator India Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Tamil Nadu15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in both these cases, has made a departure from the traditional understanding of the term "works contract" as had been laid down in preceding adjudications.

3.1 What Is A Works Contract ?: The term "works contract" as envisaged in Article 366(29A)(b), opined the Supreme Court, is amply wide and cannot be confined to a particular understanding of the term, or to a particular form. The term encompasses a wide range and many varieties of contracts. The Parliament had such wide meaning of "works contract" in its view at the time of 46th Amendment. For the purposes of determining the difference between a works contract and contract of sale, the Court has further discussed several cases and finally concluded that a contract may involve both, a contract of work and labour and a contract of sale of goods. The distinction between contract for sale of goods and contract for work (or service) has almost diminished in the matters of composite contract involving both, a contract of work/labour and a contract for the sale for the purposes of Article 366(29A)(b)16.

3.2 Taxable Event For Works Contract: It was observed by the Hon'ble Court in the Larsen & Toubro Ltd. case (supra) that following the 46th Amendment, a transfer of property in goods under clause (29A)(b) of Article 366 came to be deemed to be a sale of the goods involved in the execution of works contract by the person making the transfer and the purchase of those goods by the person to whom such transfer is made. By virtue of the 46th Amendment, States were conferred with the power to tax indivisible contract of works, by enlarging the scope of the expression "tax on the sale or purchase of goods", wherever it occurred in the Constitution. Accordingly, the expression "tax on the sale or purchase of goods" in Entry 54, List II, Schedule VII, read with the definition clause (29A) includes the transfer of property in goods whether as goods or in the form other than goods involved in the execution of works contract. The taxable event, thus, is a deemed sale.17

. Valuation of taxable service given in rule 2A of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006, has resulted in this. Accordingly, an assessee can pay service tax on the contract price after reducing the value of goods and the amount of sales tax/VAT paid on such goods. However, under this option, the assessee cannot avail CENVAT credit on such goods. There is no bar on taking CENVAT credit on capital goods or input services. Works contractors have been given another option of paying tax at the rate of 2 per cent on the contract price after reducing it by the amount of sales tax/VAT paid on the transfer of property in the goods involved in the contract. The assessee opting for this composition scheme is not entitled to take CENVAT credit on such goods. An assessee opting for this scheme has to exercise the option prior to payment of service tax on the works contract and the option cannot be changed midway during the contract. Some assessees have been paying service tax on construction services or erection, commissioning and installation services and availing abatement of 67 per cent for paying service tax and they would like to migrate to the composition scheme from June 1, 2007. But they are not clear whether it is permissible under the law as they have already paid tax for this contract. It should be noted that the contracts of such assessee which involve transfer of property in goods in the execution of the contracts can be taxable only as works contract service and not under other classifications under which they have been paying service tax. Therefore, they will be paying service tax for the first time under the works contract category. A composite contract cannot be subjected to taxation under two different classifications for different periods.

Even if an assessee wants to pay 2 per cent tax on contract remaining to be completed as on June 1, 2007, the computation of tax would not be easy. Whether, the option is to adopt valuation under rule 2A or to pay 2 per cent tax under the composition scheme, the starting point is ‘gross amount charged for the works contract’. The works contract is one and indivisible. Therefore, the ‘gross amount charged for works contract’ is towards the entire responsibility and not what is received on or after June 1, 2007 with respect to continuing contracts. Tax computed on this basis for the balance period from June 1, 2007 is unreasonable and iniquitous. If machinery for computation tax provided in the law fails, it can be argued that levy is not intended.

VAT applicability on works contract

4. Composite contracts came on the way of States levying sales tax on the goods transferred to the customers in the execution of works contract. By legal fiction, the 46th Constitutional amendment made such indivisible contracts divisible, so that the States can levy sales tax/VAT on the value of such goods. The Supreme Court, in Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. v. UOI [2006] 3 STT 245, has held that apart from the works contract, the composite price can be split only with respect to one more deemed sale introduced by the Constitution amendment, which is supply of food and beverages as part of the service in restaurants and hotels. In respect of the other four types of deemed sales, a composite contract cannot be split to tax the activities, which are subject-matter of such deemed sales. Even for pure sale transactions, courts have held that the add-on service would be treated as part of a sale transaction if it is incidental or ancillary to transfer of property in the goods.

10.9

Valuation rules to determine sale price of works contract

So far, no specific provision was made in CST and hence 'sale price' was required to be determined on basis of definition of 'sale price' as contained in section 2(h) of CST Act. As per this definition, freight or delivery or the cost of installation is not includible when separately charged.

This definition is not sufficient to determine 'sale price' when the contract is an indivisible contract which comprises of both goods and services. In sales tax laws or VAT laws of many States, there is provision of 'composition scheme' to pay sales tax on gross value of contract on some ad hoc basis. So far, there was no similar provision in CST Act.

Now, proviso to section 2(h) (inserted w.e.f. 13th May 2005) provides that in case of transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of works contract, the 'sale price' of such goods shall be determined in the prescribed manner by making such deductions from the total consideration for the works contract as may be prescribed and such price shall be deemed to be the sale price for the purposes of section 2(h).

Thus, now 'sale price' in case of sale of 'goods involved in works contract' will be determined on the basis of rules that may be made by Central Government.

Taxable Event For Works Contract

2.2 It was observed by the Hon'ble Court in the Larsen & Toubro Case that following the 46th Amendment, a transfer of property in goods under clause (29-A)(b) of Article 366 came to be deemed to be a sale of the goods involved in the execution of works contract by the person making the transfer and the purchase of those goods by the person to whom such transfer is made. The taxable event, thus, is a deemed sale.8

Dominant Intention Test

2.3 The courts, in both the above-stated cases, have also laid down that it is not necessary to ascertain the dominant intention of the contract. Even if it is not to transfer property in goods and rather, is rendering of service or the ultimate transaction is transfer of immovable property, then also it is open to the States to levy sales tax on the material used in such contract if it otherwise has elements of a works contract. Thus, the Supreme Court has completely ruled out that dominant intention of any contract has relevance if the contract has element of works contract9.

2.4 Conditions For Sustaining Levy Of Tax On Goods Sold In Execution Of Works Contract

Having discussed the scope and ambit of a works contract, the Court went on to broadly frame three conditions for sustaining the levy of tax on the goods sold in the execution of works contract, as under:

(i)

there must be a works contract;

(ii)

the goods should have been involved in the execution of works contract; and

(iii)

the property in those goods must be transferred to a third party either as goods or in some other form.10

Treatment of Works Contract under GST- The twist in the tale

3. The taxable event in the GST regime is the supply of goods or services. Thus, a transaction will come under the purview of the GST law if either it is a supply of goods or a supply of service. A bird's eye view of the provisions of the now applicable GST laws demonstrates that the levy of tax on works contract seems to be settled. As per Section 2(110) of the Central Goods and Services Act, 2017 ('CGST Act), works contract is defined as follows:

"(110) "works contract" means a contract wherein transfer of property in goods is involved in the execution of such contract and includes contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property."

Further, Schedule II of the CGST Act provides for certain supplies to be treated as supplies of goods or services. Entry 5 of the Schedule provides for certain transactions to be treated as supply of services. Consequently, it has been provided as:

(f) works contract including transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract;

Thus, works contract under GST would be treated as a supply of service and, thus, the rate of tax as provided under the tariff would be applicable on the same. Thus, the dispute as to determination of a contract as a pure sale or a pure service or a works contract has been settled as works contract has to be treated as a supply of service.

73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member constitution bench), States had argued that if any goods had been supplied by the person for whose benefit a building, factory or bridge was being constructed for the purpose of such construction, the value of those goods would not be included in the taxable turnover [This submission was noted but not commented upon by Constitution Bench]. Now, States seem to have changed their stand. In any case, 'sale' requires complete transfer of property to buyer. When there was no complete transfer of property, how there can be a 'sale'? If the material supplied by contractee (buyer) to contractor is 'sale', then the sale of these goods by contractor to contractee (buyer) should be 'second sale' and contractor will be entitled to get VAT credit of tax so paid.

As discussed above, the value of material supplied by buyer may be held as includible in value of goods involved in works contract while levying sales tax on the contractor.

Contrary views - In CST v. Executive Engineer (2006) 144 STC 183 (Uttaranchal HC), it was held that cost of cement supplied by Public Works Department for its own work is not a 'sale' - relying on UP Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Karyalaya v. CST (1990) 78 STC 417 (All HC).

10.11-2 'C' form can be supplied/received for purchases/sales for works contract

Many High Courts have held that 'C' form can be issued for purchase of goods which are used in works contract. The dealer is entitled to registration and he can receive sales tax forms in respect of his sales. See the discussions under 'C Form' in para 20.4-9. These judgments pertain to period prior to 11-5-2002.

After amendment of definition of 'sale' w.e.f. 11-5-2002, now C form can certainly be issued as 'works contract' has been specifically included in definition of 'sale'.

10.11-3 TDS on works contract

Provision of Tax Deduction at Source (TDS) on works contract is valid, as safeguards of adjudication, appeal and revision have been provided. - Steel Authority of India v. State of Orissa (1998) 110 STC 113 (Ori HC DB) * Arunodoi Construction v. State of Assam (2002) 127 STC 561 (Gau HC DB) * Mahabir Transport Agency v. Food Corporation of India (1998) 109 STC 99 (Gau HC) * B Seenaiah v. DCCT (1998) 110 STC 110 (Kar HC) {In this case, there was a provision for obtaining certificate from Assessing Officer that no deduction should be made}.

In Siemens Ltd. v. State of Kerala (2002) 128 STC 452 (Ker HC DB), TDS was required to be deducted on all turnover including turnover covered by inter-state sales, sale in course of import, sale outside the State etc. The provision was held invalid, as State has no powers to tax these transactions - same view in Jaiprakash Associates v. State of MP (2007) 6 VST 1 (MP HC FB) * Jaihind Projects Ltd. v. State of MP (2007) 8 VST 1 (MP HC DB). * Builders' Association of India v. State of West Bengal (2010) 35 VST 22 (WBTT 3 member bench).

In VTP Constructions v. State of Chhattisgarh (2006) 145 STC 185 (Chhattisgarh HC DB), the State Sales Tax Act provided for TDS on works contract @ 2%. There was no provision for ascertainment of value and nature of goods supplied during execution of works contract, nor for determination of value of goods supplied in the course of inter state sale. The provision was held invalid - view confirmed in State of Chhattisgarh v. VTP Constructions (2008) 2 SCC 578 = 12 VST 14 (SC).

Works Contract - Divisible

Works contract can be divided into two separate contracts by legal fiction as provided in sub-clause (b) of clause (29A) of article 366 of the Constitution; (i) contract for the sale of goods involved in the said works contract, and (ii) for supply of labour and service. This division of contract can be made only if the works contract involved a dominant intention to transfer the property in goods and not in contracts where the transfer in property takes place as an incident of the contract of service. What is pertinent to ascertain what was the intention of the contract. [see Rainbow Colour Lab v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2000) 2 SCC 385]. The Supreme Court in Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CC (2001) 4 SCC 593 doubted this saying :

"The conclusion arrived at in Rainbow Colour Lab v. State of MP (2000) 2 SCC 385, in our opinion, runs counter to the express provision contained in article 366(29A) as also of the Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Builders Association of India v. Union of India (1989) 2 SCC 645".

The Supreme Court in BSNL v. Union of India [2006] 152 Taxman 135 agreed. However, the Supreme Court in C. K. Jideesh v. Union of India (2005) 8 SCALE 784 had held that aforesaid observations in Associated Companies Ltd.’s case were merely obiter and that Rainbow Colour Lab’s case was still good law.

16.8

Valuation of works contract for Vat/sales tax

In Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. v. UOI (2006) 3 SCC 1 = 152 Taxman 135 = 3 STT 245 = 3 VST 95 = 145 STC 91 = 282 ITR 273 = AIR 2006 SC 1383 (SC 3 member bench), it has been clearly held that value of service cannot be included in price of goods. Conclusion (E) of the judgment (para 92 of SCC and STC and para 81 of STT ) reads as follows, 'The aspect theory would not apply to enable the value of service to be included in the sale of goods or the price of goods in the value of service'.

In Builders Association of India v. UOI (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member Constitution bench), it was held that sales tax cannot be imposed on full value of contract. The tax is on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract can be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

Service tax and Vat are mutually exclusive - In Imagic Creative Pvt. Ltd v. CCT (2008) 2 SCC 614 = 12 STT 392 = 12 VST 371 (SC), it has been held that service tax and Vat (sales tax) are mutually exclusive. In case of a composite contract, Vat cannot be imposed on portion relating to value of service.

Deductions permissible while calculating 'value' for purpose of sales tax/Vat - In Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 66 Taxman 229 = 1993 AIR SCW 2621 = (1993) 1 SCC 364 = 88 STC 204 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) it was held that value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. It was held that value of goods involved in the execution of a works contract will have to be determined by taking into account the value of entire works contract and deducting therefrom the charges towards labour and services, which cover—

(a)

Labour charges for execution of the works

(b)

Amount paid to a sub-contractor for labour and services

(c)

Charges for planning, designing and architect's fees

(d)

Charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of works contract

(e)

Cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of works contract, the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract

(f)

Cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services

(g)

Other similar expenses relatable to supply of labour and services and

(h)

Profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services.

The amounts deductible under these heads will have to be determined in the light of the facts of a particular case, on the basis of the material produced by the contractor. Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are not taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, Legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka (1993) 88 STC 248 = AIR 1993 SC 991 = (1993) 1 SCC 409 = 1993 AIR SCW 152 (SC - 5 member bench) * State of Jharkhand v. Voltas Ltd. (2007) 7 VST 317 (SC).

It can be easily seen that whatever has been excluded from 'value' for purpose of Vat/sales tax in Gannon Dunkerley' case (explained above), has been included in valuation for purpose of service tax in rule 2A(i)(b) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006.

Calculation of value of property in goods involved in works contract, transferred works contract - In Vat, the dealer can pay Vat (or sales tax) either on value of material on actual basis or under composition scheme. If Vat or sales tax has been paid or payable on actual value of material, that amount will be deductible from total value of works contract to calculate value of taxable service.

The actual words used in the rule as follows - Where value added tax (Vat) has been paid or payable on the actual value of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract, then, such value adopted for the purposes of payment of value added tax or sales tax, shall be taken as the value of transfer of property in goods transferred in the execution of the works contract for determining the value of works contract service under this clause [Rule 2A(i)(c) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006].

However, if the dealer has paid under composition scheme (i.e. at flat rate without separately calculating value of material), the value of material will have to be calculated on basis of actuals. Note that 'value' includes profit relating to goods also.

Vat or sales tax paid will not form part of value for service tax - Gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include value added tax or sales tax, as the case may be, paid, if any, on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

In Sobha Developers v. CCE (2010) 24 STT 425 (CESTAT), assessee was paying Vat on 70% of value of works contract as per Karnataka Vat Act and paid service tax on 30% of value as service tax. It was held that no differential service tax is payable, even if value of material is not shown separately in invoice. - departmental appeal against the decision has been admitted by SC for hearing - CCE v. Sobha Developers (2014) 47 GST 766 = 49 taxmann.com 595 (SC).

Splitting of contract permissible - In Essar Projects v. CCE (2014) 46 GST 582 = 47 taxmann.com 152 (CESTAT), assessee had entered into two different contracts - one for supply of material/equipment and other for erection/commissioning. There were a separate defect liability clauses for different contracts. Property in goods got transferred when equipment was supplied to customer. It was held that both cannot be treated as single contract for purpose of valuation under composition scheme of works contract.

16.3-2 Composition scheme for payment of service tax

Though service tax is legally payable only on value of service and Vat/sales tax is payable on value of goods, in a composite/indivisible contract, it is difficult to find value of goods and services. Hence, both under service tax and State Vat, a provision has been made for payment of tax under composition scheme.

In a composition scheme, tax can be paid on some ad hoc basis at the option of the tax payer.

In State of Kerala v. Builders Association of India 104 STC 134 = (1997) 2 SCC 183 = AIR 1997 SC 3640 = 1997 AIR SCW 977, the position was that a convenient, hassle-free and simple method, which was 'rough and ready method' was evolved by State Government for collection of sales tax on Works Contract. This was optional to assessee. It was held that Legislature can evolve such alternate, simplified and hassle-free methods of assessment, making it optional to assessee. - . - In the field of taxation, legislation must be allowed greater 'play in joints'. Allowance must be made for 'trial and error' by the legislature. - - Contractor who has opted to the alternate method of taxation cannot complain. Having voluntarily, and with the full knowledge of the alternate method of taxation, opted to be governed by it, a contractor cannot be heard to question the validity of relevant sub-sections or the rules - followed in Karnataka State Construction Corporation v. State of Karnataka (2004) 138 STC 75 (Kar HC DB) * Indian Oil Corp v. Prasanna Welding Industries (2007) 7 VST 101 (Gau HC).

In Mycon Construction v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 2156 = 127 STC 105 (SC), it was held that a simplified composition scheme instead of regular assessment, can be evolved, if it is on optional basis. Validity of such provision has been upheld.

Government can make a provision allowing contractors option to opt for composition by paying a sum based on total consideration of contract. - Mytcon Construction v. State of Karnataka (1998) 111 STC 322 (Karn HC).

16.3-4 Illustration

Question - The contract for industrial construction is for Rs. 8,00,000 which includes value of services plus material which is to be supplied by contractor. Value of material used by contractor is Rs. 5,00,000 and the value of service is Rs. 3,00,00 (Total Rs. 8,00,000). The customer has agreed to supply steel to contractor free of cost (FOC), the value of which is Rs. 1,80,000 and certain services free of cost. Value of such free services is Rs. 20,000. The value of steel and services supplied free were not considered in quotation given by contractor. The land belongs to customer. Its value is Rs. 4,00,000. Service tax paid on input services is Rs. 10,300 and excise duty paid on inputs used for construction is Rs. 41,200, Calculate service tax under composition scheme and also under normal scheme assuming service tax rate of 12.36%, if (a) the contract is covered under State works contract tax and (b) the contract is not covered under works contract service.

Answer - Under composition scheme, value of material supplied by customer free of cost is required to be added. In that case, total value of contract (including material and services supplied free by customer, but excluding value of land) is Rs. 10,00,000. The contractor can opt to pay duty @ 40% on total value i.e. on Rs. 4,00,000, if he is covered under State Works contract tax. Service tax payable will be 12.36% of Rs. 4,00,000 i.e. Rs. 49,440.

The contractor can avail Cenvat credit of Rs. 10,000.

If value of land is not shown separately, then service tax will be payable @ 40% of gross amount which will include value of land plus value of material and services supplied free by customer.

If the contract is covered under State Works Contract Tax, the service tax payable is 4.944% of Rs. 10,00,000 i.e. Rs. 49,440. He can avail Cenvat credit of Rs. 10,320. Thus, net tax payable is Rs. 39,120.

Supply of Ballast to the Railways—Whether it amounts to "sale" or "works contract"?

Their Lordships of the Andhra Pradesh High Court after perusing the material filed by the parties held that the contract in question were only for sale of ballast and not for work and labour and that the contractors were rightly assessed on the turnover of supply of ballast. [Anumolu Seshagri Rao & Co. v. State of Andhra Pradesh, (1973) 32 STC 51 (A.P.)]

it was held that a contract has to be characterized according to dominant nature (i.e. whether sale or service). The whole contract must be treated as a sale where the dominant intention of the contract is a sale even if some incidental or ancillary services were provided and vice versa. However, dominant nature test would be irrelevant in case of deemed sale of goods under works contract [Though dominant nature is not relevant, the fact remains that contract has to be a works contract i.e. contract for work]. In Vanguard Rolling Shutters v. CST - (1977) 39 STC 372 (SC) = AIR 1977 SC 1505, it was observed that it is difficult to lay down any rule of universal application to decide whether a contract is a works contract or contract for sale of goods. If the contract is primarily for supply of materials at prices agreed and the work or service is incidental to the execution of contract, it will be contract for sale. On the other hand, where contract is primarily a contract of work and labour and materials are supplied in execution of such contract, it is a works contract.

In Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. State of Orissa 55 STC 327 (SC) = (1984) 1 SCC 706 = AIR 1984 SC 744 (SC 3 members), HAL imported materials and components on behalf of Government of India and manufactured aircrafts on behalf of Government of India. The goods belonged to Government of India but were entrusted to HAL for manufacture of aircraft to be delivered to Air Force. It was held that it is a works contract. It was observed that in contract for work, person producing has no 'property' in the thing produced as a whole, even if part or even whole of material used by him may have been his property. In contract of sale, the thing produced as a whole has individual existence as sole property of the party who produces it sometime before delivery and the property therein passes only under the contract relating thereto to the other party for a price.

A plain reading of Sr. No. 3, clause (v) reveals that 'composite supply of WCS supplied by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to, railways attracts a tax rate of 6 per cent each of CGST and SGST. The applicant has submitted that they have been sub-contracted by the main contractor to supply WCS and in turn the main contractor is supplying WCS to the railways. From the submissions made by the applicant it appears that the WCS provided by them is the same or a part of the main contract entered into between the main contractor and the railways. It also appears that works contract service is civil works performed by the sub-contractor for the railways and the property in goods (materials used in the supply of Works Contract Service) also gets transferred to the railways directly. In such a case as per the abovementioned clause (v) of Notification No. 20/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) dated 22-10-2017, the works contract service provided by the sub-contractor to the main contractor would be supply of works contract pertaining to railways and, therefore, chargeable to tax at the rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent of CGST and SGST each). However, the benefit of 12 per cent tax rate would be available to the applicant only if the Works Contract services provided by them are Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, supplied by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to railways. The word 'pertain' is synonymous with the word 'relate', see Corpus Juris Secundum, Volume 17, page 693.

48. The expression 'in relation to' (so also 'pertaining to') is a very broad expression which pre-supposes another subject matter. These are words of comprehensiveness which might both have a direct significance as well as an indirect significance depending on the context, see State Wakf Board v. Abdul Aziz (A.I.R.1933 All.649) and 76 Corpus Juris Secundum 621. Assuming that the investments in shares and in lands do not form part of the undertakings but are different subject matters, even then these would be brought within the purview of the vesting by reason of the above expressions. In this connection reference may be made to 76 Corpus Juris Secundum at pages 620 and 621 where it is stated that the term 'relate' is also defined as meaning to bring into association or connection with. It has been clearly mentioned that 'relating to' has been held to be equivalent to or synonymous with as to 'concerning with' and 'pertaining to'. The expression 'pertaining to' is an expression of expansion and not of contraction."

(i) Works Contract

The Works Contracts has been defined in Section 2(119) of the CGST Act. 2017 as "works contract" means a contract (or building, construction, fabrication. completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of such contract."

The service to be provided as per the agreement and clearly falls under works contract as per above definition which is a contract for Construction of railway station, platform, buildings, parking etc on the land allotted by NRANSCCL in Sector 22 Atal Nagar Nava Raipur.

(ii) Composite Supply:

As per Sec. 2(30) of CGST Act of 2017, 'Composite Supply' is a kind of supply made by a taxable person to a recipient that includes two or more taxable supplies of goods or services or both, or their combination, that are naturally bundled and supplied in conjunction to each other in the ordinary course of business out of which one constitutes to be a Principal Supply.

That, in their case, the supply is a composite that includes taxable services of construction service (labour) and taxable goods (construction material) for execution of the works. Both the taxable service and goods are naturally bundled and interrelated with each and hence falls under composite supply. The Company has to provide both labour service and material without which the construction will not be completed and the entire work is to be provided by the Company only. Hence the works contract service provided is a composite supply.

(iii) Original Works

Original work is defined para 2(zs) of the Notification 12/2017 Central Tax (Rate) as below:

(zs) "original works" means- all new constructions;

(i) all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable;

(ii) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise;

It is clearly evident by the tender and agreement that the construction of the railway station is a new project and new construction and hence the condition of original works is satisfied for the service to be under Sr no 3(v) of Notification no 11/2017 dated 28 June 2017.

(iv) Pertains to railways:

Meaning of pertains to;

In addition, original works pertain to railways and that the meaning of "pertains to' which means 'relates to' or 'connected to'. The purpose behind interpretation is to clarify the meaning of the words used in the statutes which might not be that clear. The true meaning 'pertains to railways' should be taken into consideration which is all works related to railways and hence will include all the structures like railway platform, station, offices, buildings, stay areas, parking, roads etc.

3.4 Meaning of railways:

The word 'railways' is not defined under GST Act however the same is defined as mentioned above in section 2(31) of the Railways Act, 1989 and also to be interpreted in its popular sense. In this regard, The Apex Court in the case of MSCO (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India 1984 taxmann.com 491/AIR 1985 SC 76/19 ELT 15 held.

"But while construing a word which occurs in a statute or statutory instrument in the absence of any definition in that very document it must be given the same meaning which people conversant with the subject matter understand it.
