Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 66 Taxman 229 = 1993 AIR SCW 2621 = (1993) 1 SCC 364 = (1993) 88 STC 204 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) is another important judgment on 'Works Contract'. Here, it was held that taxable event is the transfer of property in the goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The said transfer of property takes place when goods are incorporated in the works. Hence, value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. - - Profits relatable to supply of material can be included in value of goods and profits which are relatable to supply of labour and services are to be excluded.

In aforesaid judgment, it was held that value of goods involved in the execution of a works contract will have to be determined by taking into account the value of entire works contract and deducting therefrom the charges towards labour and services, which cover - (a) Labour charges for execution of the works (b) Amount paid to a sub-contractor for labour and services (c) Charges for planning, designing and architect's fees (d) Charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of works contract (e) Cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of works contract, the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract (f) Cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services (g) Other similar expenses relatable to supply of labour and services (h) Profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services.

The amounts deductible under these heads will have to be determined in the light of the facts of a particular case, on the basis of the material produced by the contractor.

Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST Act and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST Act. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract.

It is permissible to have a uniform rate for works contract. This rate may be different from the rates applicable to individual goods.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka (1993) 88 STC 248 = AIR 1993 SC 991 = (1993) 1 SCC 409 = 1993 AIR SCW 152 (SC - 5 member bench).

In Daelim Industrial Co. v. State of Assam (2003) 130 STC 53 (Gau HC), it was held that in case of works contract, tax is payable only of value of goods and not on cost of design and engineering.

No. 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is the relevant entry which prescribes GST rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST+6 per cent SGST) in respect of services provided to the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory, a local authority, a Government Authority or a Government Entity by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of civil structure or any other original works meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. Thus to attract rate of tax at 12 per cent under Sl. No. 3(vi)(a), the specified service should primarily be provided to the Central Government/State Government/Union Territory/local authority/Government Authority/Government Entity and must be used for other than commercial, industrial, or any other business or professional activity.

Now it is required to examine the question whether the contractee in the instant case, i.e., TSSPDCL falls under the specified categories of recipient viz. Central Government/State Government/Union Territory/local authority/Governmental Authority/Government Entity on not. The phrase 'Government Entity' is defined under the Explanation appended to Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. The same reads as:

'Government Entity' means an authority or a board or any other body including a society, trust, corporation.

(i)

Set up by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature; or

(ii)

Established by any Government,

with 90 per cent or more participation by way of equity or control, to carry out a function entrusted by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or a local authority.

It is apparent from the schedule concerning 'shareholding of promoter' of the annual accounts of TSSPDCL that 100 per cent shares of the company were held by the Governor of Telangana. This clear indicates that the Government of Telangana have 100 per cent control over TSSPDCL. Thus TSSPDCL is evidently covered under the definition of 'Government Entity'.

The next issue to be decided in this regard is whether the impugned services supplied by the applicant are for the works which are used for other than commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. As per the details furnished by the applicant, the works undertaken are for execution/implementation of various projects for (i) Capacitor Bank Works in Nalgonda etc., (ii) HVDS-High Voltage Distribution Systems in Suryapet used for agricultural feeders. The applicant further stated that the Government of Telangana is reimbursing the money to TSSPDCL on behalf of the customers for agricultural services rendered. Thus TSSPDCL is not rendering any non-commercial services inasmuch as it is getting reimbursed for its activity on behalf of its customers. Therefore, this activity cannot be termed as other than commercial/business purposes.

The impugned works undertaken are for business/commercial purposes. Therefore, the benefit of concessional rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST) is not applicable to the services supplied by the applicant. Further the services supplied by the applicant are subjected to 18 per cent (9 per cent CGST + 9 per cent SGST) in terms of Sl. No. 3(xii) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

Whether a particular person is a Governmental Authority or a Government Entity is to be decided in terms of the definition adduced under Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 by applying the facts of each case.

The impugned works are used for commercial/business activities in view of the facts and circumstances and accordingly the same are taxable under GST Act.

Notings in the Government files are not relevant for interpretation of the statutes and the statute has to be interpreted by the wordings explicitly used therein and if there is no ambiguity in the language used therein, there is no need to refer to the notings in the Government file. On that ground also, the observation of the adjudicating authority has no bearing to the facts on hand and has to be rejected. [Para 5.2]

The adjudicating authority has relied on the definition of section 66D(o) in the context of transportation of passengers by various modes such as monorail, tramways, metro rails etc. This definition came into force only with effect from 1-7-2012 but the demands in the impugned order pertain to the period prior to 1-7-2012 and, therefore, this definition has no bearing whatsoever and not applicable for interpreting the law as it stood at the relevant time. Delhi Metro Rail is Government Railway as defined in the Indian Railway Act. If that be so, the question of levy of Service Tax under 'Commercial or Industrial Construction Service' would not arise at all as such constructions in respect of Railways stands excluded from the scope of the levy. [Para 5.4]

Indian Railway itself is an organization, which is meant to run on commercial basis. Recognizing these facts, there is a provision for a separate Railway-Budget to be presented before the Parliament and whenever there is a surplus, the Railways declared a dividend and pass it on to the Consolidated Fund of India. Therefore, the argument that only DMRC is run on commercial basis and not Indian Railway, is not an acceptable proposition. In view of the specific exclusion of 'railways' from commercial and industrial construction service, the question of imposing any Service Tax on the railways run by the DMRC does not arise at all. [Para 7]

Notification No. 12/2012-S.T., (and 25/2012-ST, Entry 14(a)) provides for exemption from Service Tax in respect of the services provided by way of construction, erection, commissioning and installation of original works pertaining to Railways, including monorail or metro. This exemption was provided when all services were brought under tax net except those specified in the negative list with effect from 1-7-2012. This exemption also clearly indicates the legislative intent of not taxing construction work pertaining to Railways. [Para 8]

Hence, demand of Service Tax on construction undertaken for Delhi Metro Rail is clearly unsustainable in law. [Para 9]

The courts generally held that the phrase 'public carriage of passengers or goods' cannot be construed in such manner as to exclude from the ambit of 'railways' the sidings built and owned by organizations other than the government. [Para 6] Article 366(20) of the Constitution excludes from the ambit of 'railway' only (a) a tramway wholly within a municipal area and (b) any line of communication wholly situate in one State and declared by Parliament by law not to be a railway. The Parliament excludes by law, apart from the tramways, the lines of rails mentioned under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989, being rails built solely for the purpose of recreation. The term 'public carriage', therefore, cannot be given any meaning that may add more exclusion than specifically provided under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. DVC - a public sector undertaking - is the owner of the railway siding being built. It is meant for carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS. The purpose of the carriage of goods is, therefore, not recreation, but producing public goods like electricity. It is, therefore, not excluded under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. The construction of the private siding that the applicant refers to, therefore, pertains to 'railways'. In view of the foregoing, it was to be ruled that construction of a private railway siding for carriage of coal and oil fuel to RTPS, as described in the agreement between the applicant and DVC, is a composite supply of works contract taxable at the rate of 12 per cent under Serial No 3(v)(a) of Notification no 11/2017-CT(Rate) dated 28-06-2017. 16.1-7 Mere supply of labour or job work without material not works contract

Taxable event is transfer of property in goods. In case of contract for supply of labour, there is no transfer of property in goods and hence there is no tax liability - Ashok Kumar Garg v. UOI (2002) 128 STC 442 (P&H HC DB) * Rajiv Gumber v. Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd.. (2002) 128 STC 494 (P&H HC DB).

Thus, simple job work will not be taxable, if there are no goods involved in the job work - K V Nagarajan v. DCTO (2007) 5 STR 325 = 208 ELT 165 (Mad HC DB) - same view in K C Nagarajan v. DCTO (2007) 7 VST 585 = 11 STT 411 (Mad HC).

In contract of labour job of repairs and replacement of faulty cables etc. there is no transfer of property and hence TDS provisions do not apply - Jarnail Singh v. Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. (2009) 1 GST 61 (P&H HC DB).

Mere labour contract is not works contract - Geogy George v. State of Kerala (2014) 50 taxmann.com 391 = 71 VST 510 (Ker HC DB).

Pure service contract to carry out seismic survey without transfer of any goods is not a works contract - Asian Oilfield Services v. State of Tripura (2015) 81 VST 536 (Tripura HC DB).

16.1-8 Works contract if contract for construction is made with prospective buyer

In K Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka AIR 2005 SC 2350 = (2005) 5 SCC 162 = 2 STT 178 = 141 STC 298 = 3 STR 337 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

Section 2(1)(v-i) of Karnataka Sales Tax Act stated that 'works contract' includes any agreement for carrying out for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, the building, construction, manufacture, processing, fabrication, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property.

Section 5B of the Act provided for tax on transfer of property in goods, whether as goods or in some other form, in the execution of works contract.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some work on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

It was held that the developer would be liable to pay tax on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract.

that no tax could be levied on works contract, as tax could be levied only on 'sale of goods' defined in Sale of Goods Act. In an indivisible works contract, there was no sale of goods as there could be no agreement to sell materials as such and moreover, the property would not pass as movables. The material used therein became property of the other party on the theory of accretion and, as such, no sales tax could be levied on such material. 'Works Contract' was one of the ways of avoiding sales tax. Hence, Constitution was amended on 2nd February, 1983 (46th Amendment). Clause 29A was added to Article 366 to cover 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract'. Subsequently, most of the States have amended their sales tax laws to cover 'works contract', but Central Sales Tax Act was not amended till May, 2002. Thus, till 11-5-2002, CST was not leviable on indivisible works contracts.

4.7 Builders' Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 73 STC 370 (SC) - In this case Supreme Court observed that 'After the 46th Amendment, the works contract which was indivisible one, is by a legal fiction altered into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services. After 46th Amendment, it has become possible for States to levy tax on value of goods involved in a works contract in the same way in which the sales tax was leviable on the price of goods and materials supplied in a building contract which had been entered into two distinct and separate parts.'

4.8 Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs [2001] 124 STC 59 (SC) - In this case it was held that even if the dominant intention of the contract was rendering of service which would amount to a works contract, after Forty-Sixth Amendment to Constitution, the State would be empowered to levy sales tax on material used in such contract.

4.9 Builders Association of India v. Union of India [1989] 73 STC 370 (SC) - The background of this case is that after Amendment to Constitution in 1983, various State Governments imposed levy on works contract. The tax was levied by some State Governments on full value of contract which included the material cost and other costs like labour, supply of services, etc. However, in the judgment the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the power of States to levy tax on works contract was subject to limitation of Article 286, i.e., tax could not be levied by State on : (a) Outside the State, (b) during import/export, (c) Restrictions placed on 'declared goods' were applicable even while levying tax on works contract. Further, tax could not be imposed on full value of contract. The tax was on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract could be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

4.10 Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan [1993] 66 Taxman 229 (SC) - In this case it was held that taxable event is the transfer of property in the goods involved in the execution of a works contract. The said transfer of property takes place when goods are incorporated in the works. Hence, value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are not taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, Legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract. It is permissible to have a uniform rate for works contract. This rate may be different from the rates applicable to individual goods.

The judgment in this case was subsequently followed in Builders' Association of India v. State of Karnataka [1993] 88 STC 248 (SC).

4.11 Daelim Industrial Co. v. State of Assam [2003] 130 STC 53 (Gau.) - It was held that in case of works contract tax is payable only of value of goods and not on cost of designing and engineering.

Deductions permissible while calculating 'value' for purpose of sales tax/Vat - In Gannon Dunkerley & Co. v. State of Rajasthan (1993) 66 Taxman 229 = 1993 AIR SCW 2621 = (1993) 1 SCC 364 = 88 STC 204 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) it was held that value of goods at the time of incorporation in the works can constitute measure for levy of tax. However, cost of incorporation of the goods in works contract cannot be made part of measure for the levy of tax. It was held that value of goods involved in works contract would have to be considered for taxation on works contract. Charges for labour and services have to be deducted from total value of works contract. It was held that value of goods involved in the execution of a works contract will have to be determined by taking into account the value of entire works contract and deducting therefrom the charges towards labour and services, which cover—

(a)

Labour charges for execution of the works

(b)

Amount paid to a sub-contractor for labour and services

(c)

Charges for planning, designing and architect's fees

(d)

Charges for obtaining on hire or otherwise machinery and tools used for the execution of works contract

(e)

Cost of consumables such as water, electricity, fuel etc., used in the execution of works contract, the property in which is not transferred in the course of execution of a works contract

(f)

Cost of establishment of the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services

(g)

Other similar expenses relatable to supply of labour and services and

(h)

Profit earned by the contractor to the extent it is relatable to supply of labour and services.

The amounts deductible under these heads will have to be determined in the light of the facts of a particular case, on the basis of the material produced by the contractor. Moreover, tax cannot be levied on goods which are not taxable under sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST and goods covered under sections 14 and 15 of CST. If contractor is not able to give detailed break up, Legislature can prescribe scales for deductions permissible on account of cost of labour and services for various types of works contract.

The Parliament excludes by law, apart from the tramways, the lines of rails mentioned under section 2(31) (ii) of the Railways Act, 1989, being rails built solely for the purpose of recreation. The term 'public carriage', therefore, cannot be given any meaning that may add more exclusion than specifically provided under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. The intended civil work is for Construction of rail infrastructure for providing Railways siding at SECL Kusmunda Project, District Korba, Chhattisgarh for dispatch of washed and raw coal. The purpose of the carriage of coal is, therefore, not recreation, but producing public goods like electricity. It is, therefore, not excluded under section 2(31)(ii) of the Railways Act, 1989. RITES Ltd available in public domain online, it is seen that Rail India Technical and Economical Services limited (RITES Ltd.) is a Public Sector Undertaking wherein ownership of the Government of lndia (72.02% in equity shares) and is an engineering consultancy company, specializing in the field of transport infrastructure. Established in 1974 by the Government of India, the company's initial charter was to provide consultancy services in rail transport management to operators in India and abroad. RITES has since diversified into planning and consulting services for either infrastructure, including airports, ports, highways and urban planning.

As the proposed work is in connection with construction of rail infrastructure for providing Railways siding at SECL Kusmunda Project, District Korba, Chhattisgarh for dispatch of washed and raw coal, the same can reasonably be held to be pertaining to Railways. The term "pertaining to Railways", as appearing at Sl.No. 3(v)(a) of Notification No. 11/2017 Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended, vide Notification 01/2018 Central Tax (Rate), dated 25-1-2018 is more expansive and includes other establishments other than Indian Railways. Needless to mention here that there is no stipulation in the said entry claimed for exemption supra, that this work must be executed to the Railways but it is sufficient that it must be "pertaining to Railways", meaning therein that the supplier and the recipient is immaterial. Thus, we are of the considered opinion that the work intended to be undertaken by the applicant for RITES Limited pertains to railways and accordingly this prerequisite stands fulfilled.

Conclusion

8.The concept of outsourcing all activities, barring the core area of specialization is gradually evolving globally, including in India. To avoid litigation surrounding levy of applicable tax, it is of paramount importance to have clarity on as to when does the process qualify as 'manufacture'? There are even greater complexities regarding the process involving both supply of goods and rendition of service, as identifying the correct base for levy of service tax on the service element becomes a challenging task. The proposed Goods and Services Tax ('GST') scenario looks optimistic for the job work sector when all the taxes, i.e., excise duty, service tax and VAT will get subsumed under the 'grand tax', as we may call it, and there will be one base for levy of GST without any distinction between goods and services.

In K Raheja Development Corporation v. State of Karnataka AIR 2005 SC 2350 = (2005) 5 SCC 162 = 2 STT 178 = 141 STC 298 = 3 STR 337 (SC), appellants were carrying on business of real estate development and allied contracts. They enter into development agreements with owners of land. Thereafter, they will get the plans for construction of residential apartments or commercial complexes approved. They used to enter into 'agreement of sale' before construction was complete. The agreements by 'developer' with 'prospective purchaser' would provide that on completion of construction, the residential apartment or commercial complex would be handed over to prospective purchasers, who would get undivided interest on the land also.

In this case, the builder had entered into agreement of sale with intended purchasers of flats. Cost of land and building was shown separately in the agreement (probably to save stamp duty). After construction, the purchaser of flat would get undivided interest in the land also. The agreement provided for payment of instalments at various stages of construction of flat. The Karnataka Sales Tax Act specifically stated that works contract will cover any agreement relating to construction.

Section 2(1)(vi) of Karnataka Sales Tax Act stated that 'works contract' includes any agreement for carrying out for cash, deferred payment or other valuable consideration, the building, construction, manufacture, processing, fabrication, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property.

Section 5B of the Act provided for tax on transfer of property in goods, whether as goods or in some other form, in the execution of works contract.

It was held that definition of 'works contract' in Karnataka Sales Tax Act is wide. It is not restricted to 'works contract' as commonly understood, i.e. a contract to do some wok on behalf of somebody else. The definition does not make a distinction based on who carries on the construction activity. A works contract, within the meaning of term, can be said to be construction of commercial units.

It was held that the developer would be liable to pay tax on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract.

Case Study

4. The following case study has been analysed :

4.1 Case - M/s. GE, engaged in the business of generation of electricity, intends to set-up a power plant in India. Total project is split up into following two contracts -

one with M/s. CN for supply of equipment and another with M/s. SO for erection and commissioning services ;

in respect of the first contract no Service tax is paid while as for the second contract M/s. SO pays service tax under the taxable service category of 'erection and commissioning services'.

The authorities opine that the total work is a turnkey project and, hence, is covered under works contract service, thereby making the assessee liable to pay service tax on works contract service under reverse charge basis on payment made to M/s. CN.

4.2 Solution - This case may be resolved as follows -

Contract speaks about total scope of work, i.e., from designing upto commissioning of plant and equipment. The total project is subsequently split up into two agreements. It fits into definition of works contract service.

The services provided by M/s. CN are works contract services and the assessee is liable to pay Service tax on payments made to CN on reverse charge basis.

Conclusion

5. While as works contracts are usually in the nature of contracts for the construction of immovable property such as buildings, power plants, etc., there are several kinds of contracts concerned with movable property that also fall within the scope of works contracts, including annual maintenance contracts, as they involve the transfer of property in goods coupled with the provision of works or services. In the case of work contracts, a sales tax is leviable on that portion of the contract which relates to the sale of goods. Most of the States in India provide for the payment of tax on works contracts separately to the value of the goods and materials sold at the rates specified under the respective State legislations.

However, some States provide for the payment of tax under a composition scheme at a fixed percentage. In a composition scheme the work contractor is required to pay the tax on the entire value of the contract without splitting up the value of the goods and materials supplied and the value of the services provided.

SERVICE PORTION OF WORKS CONTRACT

16.1

Background

Works contract is composite contract of goods and services. Sales tax (Vat) is on goods involved in works contract. Sales tax can be imposed on value of goods involved in works contract and service tax can be imposed on value of services.

'Service portion in the execution of a works contract' is 'declared service' - section 66E(h) of Finance Act, 1994 introduced w.e.f. 1-7-2012.

A tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract is deemed sale of goods under Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India. [As inserted by 46th Amendment to Constitution in 1982]

Earlier, in State of Madras v. Gannon Dunkerley - (1958) 9 STC 353 (SC) = 1959 SCR 379 = AIR 1958 SC 560, it was held that tax cannot be levied on works contract. This was because the Constitution did not define 'sale' and hence the term 'sale' has the same meaning as given in Sale of Goods Act. To get over the difficulty created by this judgment, Constitution was amended in 1982 by 46th Amendment and concept of 'deemed sale' was introduced to cover transfer of property in goods involved in works contract.

In Builders' Association of India v. UOI - (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member constitution bench), it has been observed : 'After the 46th amendment, the works contract which was indivisible one, is by a legal fiction altered into one for sale of goods and the other for supply of labour and services. After 46th amendment, it has become possible for States to levy tax on value of goods involved in a works contract in the same way in which the sales tax was leviable on the price of goods and materials supplied in a building contract which had been entered into two distinct and separate parts.

Distinction between a divisible contract and an indivisible contract came to an end after forty sixth Amendment to Constitution - National Organic Chemicals Industries Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra (2012) 54 VST 271 (Bom HC DB).

In State of Karnataka v. Transglobal Power Ltd. (2015) 77 VST 509 (Karn HC DB), it has been held that if contract is divisible, it cannot be a works contract.

) had been rejected by the Apex Court in the case of Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd. v. Commissioner [2004] 170 ELT A181 (SC). Similar issue had also been decided in the case of CCE&C v. Larsen & Toubro Ltd. [2006] 4 STT 12 (CESTAT - Mum.). The same position of law was reiterated in many of the other cases of Tribunals, which hardly need any reiteration. In the case of State of Uttar Pradesh v. UOI [2006] 4 STT 362 (SC), the Supreme Court has held that levy of service tax on a particular service is no bar to levy trade tax on it. Recently, in the case of Mahim Patram (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2007] 7 STT 136 (SC), the Supreme Court has held that in respect of transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract, provisions of Central Sales Tax Act would apply and so long as the Central Government does not make any rules, determination of value of goods involved in execution of works contract, in course of inter-state trade and commerce, may be carried out in terms of relevant State Rules. In the case of Blue Star Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 68 (Bang. - CESTAT), the assessee entered into contracts with his customers for supplying plant, machinery or equipment and for commissioning or installation of the said plant, machinery or equipment. The revenue demanded service tax from the assessee on erection, installation, commissioning of machinery or equipment and labour component of the contract. The demand was confirmed by the Commissioner. But the Tribunal following the decision of the Tribunal in the case of Larsen & Toubro case (supra), upheld the assessee’s contention that service tax could not be levied on works contract and set aside the demands. Similar decision was given in case of L&T Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 9 STT 356 (Ahd. - CESTAT). The Tribunal held that turnkey contracts entered into for execution, would not get covered under consulting engineering services. Another aspect which was considered by the Tribunal was that the Finance Bill, 2007, had included works contract services as taxable in sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105). Since the service tax liability on works contract is brought into the net from 2007, it can be argued that these services were not to be taxed earlier. Thus, the Tribunal allowed the assessee’s application for waiver of pre-deposit of amounts.

It is important to note that by the Finance Act, 2007, service tax is also levied on works contracts [section 65(105)( zzzza)]. It may be noted that under this service only the works contracts wherein transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract is exigible to VAT/sales tax, are covered, excluding works contract in respect of roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams. For the purpose of this sub-clause, "works contract" means a contract wherein,—

(i) transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract is leviable to tax as sale of goods, and

(ii) such contract is for the purpose of carrying out,—

(a) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise, installation of electrical and electronic devices, plumbing, drain laying or other installations for transport of fluids, heating, ventilation or air-conditioning including related pipe work, duct work and sheet metal work, thermal insulation, sound insulation, fire proofing or water proofing, lift and escalator, fire escape staircases or elevators; or

(b) construction of a new building or a civil structure or a part thereof, or of a pipeline or conduit, primarily for the purpose of commerce or industry; or

(c) construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof; or

(d) completion and finishing services, repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services, in relation to (b) and (c); or

(e) turnkey projects including engineering, procurement and construction or commissioning (EPC) projects;

Thus, works contract in respect of specified infrastructure projects, namely, roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams are specifically excluded from the scope of the levy. Taxable value under this service is that part of the value of the works contract which is relatable to services provided in the execution of a works contract. Such value is to be determined on actual basis based on the records maintained by the assessee. However, an option is given to an assessee for a composition scheme. Under the composition scheme, the assessee was required to pay 2% of the total value of the works contract as service tax (now 4% w.e.f 1-3-2008). Assessee opting for the composition scheme is not entitled to avail CENVAT credit on inputs but can claim CENVAT credit on capital goods and input services required for use in the works contract.

Introduction

1. Works contract is an indivisible contract. It is indivisible in the sense that value of goods to be incorporated in any form in the works and value of labour & other services to be rendered in execution cannot be segregated. It is also known as deemed sales.

In construction industries where entire work is assigned on completion basis, it always becomes matter of dispute as to what should be tax structure, as both the taxes - VAT/CST and service tax are applicable on such transaction. It is complex in nature due to non-synchronization in tax mechanism of the Central & State tax authorities. VAT is imposed by the State Government and on the other hand, the service tax is imposed by the Central Government. Calculation mechanism at both the stages is also different which results in unnecessary litigation & dispute burden on assessee.

Legal frameworks

2. Works contract in simple terms is a contract for carrying out certain works on any movable or immovable property of others. Sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A) of the Indian Constitution deals with the imposition of tax on transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of works contract.

Definition of works contract has been inserted in CST Act vide the Finance Act, 2005. Section 2(ja) of the Central Sales Tax Act defines works contract as follows—"Works contract means a contract for carrying out any work which includes assembling, construction, building, altering, manufacturing, processing, fabricating, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, repair or commissioning of any movable or immovable property."

All the State VAT Acts have defined works contract in a different manner but the meaning of works contract is similar in nature. After reading all definitions, the term "works contract" is nothing but a contract in which one of the parties is obliged to undertake or to execute works and property is transferred to other party, either as goods or in some other form.

3. Levy of tax on works contract

3.1 Provisions under State VAT Act - No VAT/CST is applicable on pure labour jobs where no material of his own is used/added by the job worker (vendor).

VAT/CST is applicable on Material Value (Deemed Sale) of the Works Contract.

Since segregation of material involved in works contract & services involved in works contract is difficult to arrive at the Material Value in the Contract, three methods are adopted under the State VAT Acts, namely:

(i)

Actual Non-material (Labour) Deduction Method

(ii)

Standard (Labour) Deduction Method

(iii)

Composition Tax/Compounding Tax (WCT) Method

If the Contractor dispatches his own materials from one State to another directly to the customer under the Indivisible WC, then it is a deemed inter-State sale of material subject to levy of CST by the State of dispatch.

8. Section 7 CGST defines supply in an inclusive manner meaning it is a widened and broadened connotation. Essentially, a flat under construction and intended to be sold to a buyer is sale of immovable property, but when it is undergoing construction there is an element of service and consequently, it was necessary to treat construction of flats as a supply of service vide Section 7(1)(d) read with item no 5(b) of Schedule II. 9. Schedule of Goods and Service Tax rates for services approved by GST Council laying down fitment of rates of services states at entry 19 that "Construction of a complex, civil structure or part thereof intended for sale to a buyer wholly or partly" will bear GST at 12.5% with full input tax credit, but no refund of overflow of input tax credit. The entry also explains that the value of land is included in the amount charged from the service recipient. Simultaneously, rate of GST for composite works contract as defined in Section 2(119) vide entry 27 is 18% with full input tax credit. In substance and effect, though construction of flat is treated as a service yet it is akin to a works contract. Drawing such a cue implies that concession of 6% is given to factor in value of land thereby leading to a calculation of 33% of abatement on the total consideration. However, prescription of such a standard rate of abatement [assumed] does not take into realities of cheap, medium, semi-luxury, luxurious and elite segments where composition of land value would considerably vary. Moreover, in semi-rural developing towns, presumed rate of 33% in respect of land value may be on higher side leading to excess input credit over 12% output tax inasmuch as input supplies for builders mostly carry a rate of 18% to 28% which as per schedule of rates as seen above is not refundable. In cases, where input tax credit falls short of GST rate of 12% profits of builders will truncate or lead passing of burden on to consumers. In my opinion, this matters ought to have been formulated by the legislature in a flexible manner through a methodology by way of rules to reckon local factors.

10. Another daunting controversy that may arise is whether the overflow of input tax credit is to be worked per project or on a net basis for all projects put together. Section 16 of CGST provides that every person shall subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed and in the manner specified in Section 49 be entitled to the credit of any input tax in respect of any supply of goods and services or both to him which are used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of his business and the amount shall be credited to the electronic ledger of such person. In my opinion, looking at the wording of Section 16 aforesaid read with Section 17 better view appears to be that an overall picture of all projects will have to be undertaken and not project wise. No guidance is found either in the Act or the relevant rules as what are the implications of GST in a case when a project undertaken by the builder where he has to give flats to the owner of land in discharge of consideration for obtaining development rights. Assuming in a particular case, the developers have to provide 100 flats to owners and there other 200 flats for free sale; in former case he will be a contractor levying GST at 18% with input tax credit, whereas in the latter case, the rate would be 12% with full input tax credit but no refund of overflow credit in a situation where flats are sold before they are fully developed. In the aforementioned example, there can controversy as to how the overflow of input tax credit to be computed being the difference between the rate of GST on input supplies and 18% GST rate more particularly, after considering common input supplies and capital goods employed for both types of flats. Moreover, disputes will arise as to what is time of supply of the 100 units to be allotted to owners more specifically, if land is not parted physically at one go, but in stages. Can we say the supply of flats is complete when possession of land is given despite the fact that flats are yet to be constructed? If the free sale flats are sold in stages question will emanate as to whether input tax credit is to be accumulated or can be claimed while construction is progressing without any sale? It would be best to issue clarifications on these and other potential roadblocks that may lead to avoidable litigation.

The constitutionality of the circular was successfully challenged on the ground that the tax can only be levied on the gross turnover and not on the value of land. The judgment shows that the Courts across the country intended to follow the ruling of L&T judgment in its literal sense in order to achieve a uniform result relating to the issue of taxability in the case of works contract. In the case of The Indian Hume Pipe Co. Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan 19 the same line of L&T judgment was followed and the prayer for exemption of levying of tax on the value of pipe was rejected. The Apex Court held that the sale of pipes involved was in the execution of works contract and hence was taxable under the sales tax. The case of NIIT Limited Hyderabad v. Deputy Commissioner, Hyderabad 20 gave a new direction to the concept of works contract. In this case the petitioner-company was engaged in the business of Computer Education and Training and also providing Technology solution. The parties signed a contract with the State for imparting computer education along with leasing of hardware software and other connected accessories on Build Own Operate Transfer (BOOT) basis. The contract was said to form part of works contract and, hence, liable to be taxed. The leasing of accessories on BOOT basis was considered as transfer of property, as they were getting fees in return. It was held that the dominant nature test has no application so it should not be applied in any case; therefore, the levy of tax was allowed.

The plethora of cases after L&T showed a positive sign about the uniform development of taxation regime in the area of works contract in the country. This case to some extent tried to define the ambit of works contract and laid down the conditions that were needed to be followed while determining a contract to be having nature of works contract. Firstly, it was made clear that the tax will be deducted from the time after the parties entered into the agreement and not before that. Secondly, it was clarified that in the case of construction business, the value of land shall be excluded from the total cost that shall be taxed.21

Conclusion

5. The issue of taxability of works contract moved through several phases and it was always difficult for the Courts to reach to a definite conclusion regarding this issue. Even after series of cases and reasoning by the Courts, they were unable to categorically define the term 'works contract'. But it can be said that these cases helped a lot in forming some concrete concept regarding the works contract. The analysis of situation makes us realize that L&T's judgments contributed to a great extent to establish the status of taxability of works contract in India. But various principles and conditions laid down in the case resulted in conflicts.

The dominant nature test was ruled out in L&T judgment but the application of the same led to conflicts, which can be demonstrated with the help of two cases, i.e., International Hospital case and Pro Ltd. case. In the case of International Hospital v. State of U.P. 22the petitioner was the owner of superspecialty hospital where the implants were used during the course of surgical procedures. It was not considered as sale and, hence, not to be taxed. It was held that the patients visited the hospital for the surgical process; any implantation was an intrinsic and integral part of such process. Tax could not be imposed on such implantation, as the essential nature of transaction was the performance of medical procedure which in essence was outside the ambit of sale.23 But, in the case of State of Karnataka v. Pro Ltd. 24the challenge was made to the constitutional validity of the power of the State to levy tax on the processing and supply of photographs, photo prints and photo negatives. It was held by the Apex Court that after 46th Amendment that the State was given the power to levy taxes on works contracts by fictionally dividing it into sale and supply part but there will be no application of dominant intention rule. The photographic service was considered as sale and hence taxable. Therefore, there was inconsistency in the application of the said rule.

Under these circumstances, it may be expected that the GST regime (expected to be implemented in India by April, 2016) will contribute positively to the taxation of works contracts. The basis of the expectation lies in the uniform applicability of GST regime across the States which will help to avoid conflicts. Having said that it would be curious to see how the new regime will shape the taxation of works contracts in India.

He charged development charges for common facilities (like compound wall, drainage, club house, street lighting etc.) under a separate agreement. It was held development charges are liable to sales tax.

Supply of computers plus training to students in schools - In NIIT Ltd. v. Deputy Commissioner (CT) (2014) 71 VST 481 (AP HC DB), the dealer had contract with State Government for leasing of computer equipment in schools plus training the students on Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) basis. Ownership of computers would be transferred to Government at end of contract period. It was held that it is works contract. Levy of tax on transfer of property in equipment is permissible.

Contract for manufacture, supply and erection of equipment - A composite contract for manufacture, supply and erection of equipment (for irrigation system in this case) with composite rates for skill, labour and material is an indivisible works contract - Sinha Engineering Construction v. WBSTT (1999) 116 STC 631 (WBTT).

A contract for supply, fabrication and installation of complete machinery and equipment of electrode plant, where composite price covers design, manufacture, fabrication and installation is a works contract. Property to customer is transferred only when plant is immovable - Heera Electronics v. CST (2006) 143 STC 290 (All KC).

Contract for supply and installation of electrical equipment is a works contract - State of Karnataka v. Birla GTM Entrepose (2006) 144 STC 16 (Karn HC DB).

Brick making from raw material supplied - If raw material is supplied to contractor who makes the bricks, the contractor at no stage owns the bricks. Hence, it is not a contract of sale - Ganpat Ram v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 105 STC 305 (Raj HC DB) * Verma Construction Co. v. State of Rajasthan (1997) 105 STC 266 (Raj HC DB).

Taking additional prints of a cinema film - Taking additional prints of film is a works contract - not sale, as contract is for use of skill and labour to bring desired results. - CST v. Radio Advertising Service (1997) 106 STC 50 (Bom HC DB).

Film Producer - Film producer engaged to shoot, direct, edit produce and complete film is engaged in 'work of art' and not for sale of goods, though for purchase of raw films, he may be liable to purchase tax.

Textile processing - In S Kumars Ltd. v. CCT (2013) 66 VST 468 (MP HC DB), it was held that processing of grey cloth on job work basis, involving processes of washing, cleaning, bleaching and dyeing, with use of chemicals and dyes is works contract.

In Teaktex Processing Complex v. State of Kerala (2004) 136 STC 435 (Ker HC DB), it was held that in case of works contract of dyeing of yarn and fabrics, dyes are seen as colour in end product and its property does pass to buyer. However, in case of consumables like water, fuel and chemicals, these get consumed and its property does not pass to the buyer, as these do not form identifiable part of works contract executed.

Dyeing of textile is sale of goods - State of Tamil Nadu v. Jansons Textile Processors (2014) 69 VST 443 (Mad HC DB).

Chemicals used in dyeing or bleaching of cloth are subject to sales tax, even if chemicals are washed away - State of Tamil Nadu v. S S M Processing Mills (2014) 69 VST 445 (Mad HC DB).

In a contrary decision, in CTT v. Bathwal Udyog (2014) 47 GST 347 = 48 taxmann.com 338 (All HC DB), it has been held that chemicals and dyes used in process of dyeing, colouring, printing etc., are not subject to sales tax as they get consumed during the process.

Builders Association of India v. UOI (1989) 2 SCR 320 = 73 STC 370 = (1989) 2 SCC 645 = AIR 1989 SC 1371 (SC 5 member Constitution bench) is a landmark judgment of Supreme Court on 'works contract'. The background of this case is that after amendment to Constitution in 1983, various State Governments imposed levy on works contract. The tax was levied by some State Governments on full value of contract which included the material cost and other costs like labour, supply of services etc.

However, in the judgment, Hon. Supreme Court held that the power of States to levy tax on works contract is subject to limitation of Article 286 i.e. tax cannot be levied by State on (a) outside the State (b) during import/export. (c) Restrictions placed on 'declared goods' are applicable even while levying tax on works contract. Further, tax cannot be imposed on full value of contract. The tax is on 'transfer of property in goods involved in execution of works contract.' Thus, tax on works contract can be levied only on 'value of goods involved' and not on whole value of works contract.

In State of Jharkhand v. Voltas Ltd. (2007) 7 STR 106 = 7 VST 317 (SC) also it was confirmed that sales tax can be levied only on value of goods. All charges/amounts are deductible from value of works contract except value of goods sold in execution of works contract, for computing taxable value.

In Imagic Creative Pvt. Ltd. v. CCT (2008) 2 SCC 614 = 12 STT 392 = 12 VST 371 = 9 STR 337 (SC), it has been held that service tax and Vat (sales tax) are mutually exclusive. In case of a composite contract, Vat cannot be imposed on portion relating to value of service.

Restrictions applicable to declared goods apply to declared goods used in works contract - Provisions relating to declared goods are applicable even if the declared goods are used in works contract. Thus, Vat rate cannot be more than that applicable to declared goods - Smt B Narasamma v. DCCT (2016) 96 VST 357 (SC).

CST Act imposes restrictions on State Government in levying tax on declared goods. These restrictions apply to goods involved in works contract also - Afcons Infrastructure Ltd. v. State of Assam (2007) 9 VST 195 (Gau HC).

Vat/sales tax is payable on iron and steel used in works contract at rate applicable to declared goods - URC Construction Ltd. v. DCCT (2008) 11 VST 896 (Karn HC) - view confirmed in Smt B Narasamma v. DCTO (2016) 57 GST 39 = 72 taxmann.com 349 = 96 VST 357 (SC).

6. We are a construction company and we have entered into a contract for construction of a big temple in Rajasthan and the cost of construction is around Rs. 100.00 crore and as per the agreement, the taxes including service tax are to be borne by the contractor, i.e., our company.

How do we raise the bill since as per the service tax rules, the service tax is required to be shown separately in the bill.

First of all I must inform you that the services provided by you with respect to the construction of a temple are not liable to service tax because under this head, only commercial and industrial constructions are liable to service tax. Hence, construction of temple is not liable to service tax and you need not charge or pay any service tax in this respect.

For this purpose, you can also refer to the CBEC Circular No. 80/2004-ST, dated 17-9-2004.

Though the services provided for construction of a temple are not liable to service tax, we are providing below the method of issuing bills in case of composite price or composite price contract for any service for the benefit of readers because the compulsion of showing service tax separately in the bill does not restrict the respective parties to enter into composite price (Inclusive of service tax) contract:—

In such cases, by applying the following formula, the amount of service tax can be calculated:—

ST = Composite price * Rate of Tax/Rate of Tax + 100.

To understand it with the help of an example, we assume that the composite price is Rs.100.00 and rate of tax is 10.2% including education cess. The amount of service tax will be:—

100 * 10.2/110.2 = Rs. 9.25

Denoting Rs. 9.25 as service tax, the service provider can raise the bill by showing Rs. 90.75 as the amount charged for service and Rs. 9.25 can be added as service tax to make the composite price at Rs. 100.00.

23.1-1 Statutory provisions in respect of construction of complex

Following is 'supply of service' as per para 5(b) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

Construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly, except where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier.

Explanation.- For the purposes of this clause- (1) the expression "competent authority" means the Government or any authority authorized to issue completion certificate under any law for the time being in force and in case of non-requirement of such certificate from such authority, from any of the following, namely - (i) an architect registered with the Council of Architecture constituted under the Architects Act, 1972; or (ii) a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers (India); or (iii) a licensed surveyor of the respective local body of the city or town or village or development or planning authority.

(2) the expression "construction" includes additions, alterations, replacements or remodeling of any existing civil structure.

Residential Complex - "Residential complex" means any complex comprising of a building or buildings, having more than one single residential unit - para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Single Residential Unit - "Single residential unit" means a self-contained residential unit which is designed for use, wholly or principally, for residential purposes for one family - para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Occupancy certificate granted in is equal to completion certificate - In Mumbai i.e. Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), occupancy certificate is granted. Sale after such occupancy certificate (even before completion certificate) will be sale of immovable property and outside service tax net - PIB (Press Information Bureau), Ministry of Finance dated 26-10-2015.

State of Kerala (2001) 122 STC 1 (Ker HC DB), the 'explanation' was read down (instead of declaring it as unconstitutional) to hold that the explanation will not apply if sale is as per sections 3, 4 and 5 of CST Act. It was held that if execution of works contract is inter-state, it cannot be intra-State merely on the basis of situs of goods at the time of transfer. This decision was followed in Siemens India Ltd. v. State of Kerala (2003) 132 STC 418 (Ker HC DB). In this case, dealer had two separate contracts - one for supply of goods and other for erection and commissioning of equipment. It was held that if goods were supplied inter-state under the contract for supply of goods, it will not be part of works contract within the State.

However, in J.D.P. Associates v. State of Tamil Nadu (2003) 131 STC 334 (TNTST), goods were purchased from out of State. These were used in the execution of works contract. It was held that the taxable event in the execution of works contract takes place when goods are incorporated in the work, which happened after receipt of goods in State. Hence, sales tax in Tamil Nadu will be payable on goods involved in works contract.

In State of Kerala v. Unitech Machines (2010) 3 GST 73 = 32 VST 80 (Ker HC DB), the dealer purchased goods from outside Kerala under C form and used them in works contract. It was held that works contract tax is payable on entire value including material purchased from outside the State.

10.10-4 Judgments that there can be Inter-State Works Contract

Though now CST can be levied on works contract, following decisions support the view that there can be inter-State works contract.

Central Sales Tax cannot be levied on works contract - Thomson Press (I) Ltd. v. State of Haryana - (1996) 100 STC 417 (P&H HC FB). - in this case, the dealer was printing lottery tickets for buyers outside the State. Printing of lottery tickets was held as 'works contract' and hence it was held that no Central Sales Tax can be levied on lottery tickets sold to buyers outside the State - same view in - DG of Agricultural Income Tax and Sales Tax v. Dy CST (2001) 123 STC 548 (MP HC). - Probably, decision could have been different if above judgments were cited] [Now CST can be levied on these transactions w.e.f. 11-5-2002].

In Elgi Tyres & Tread v. Dy CCT (2000) 120 STC 261 (Karn HC DB), the dealer entered into contract of getting old tyres from party in AP, retread tyres and send back to party in Andhra Pradesh. It was held that it is Inter-State sale in works contract and not liable to sales tax. - same view in Sundaram Industries v. CTO (2002) 128 STC 358 (Mad HC DB) [Now CST can be levied on these transactions w.e.f. 11-5-2002].

In Siemens Ltd. v. State of Kerala (2001) 122 STC 1 (Ker HC DB), it was held that if execution of works contract is inter-state, it cannot be intra-state merely on the basis of situs of goods at the time of transfer.

Case law in respect of TDS on Inter-State works contract - In Steel Authority of India v. State of Orissa (2000) 3 SCC 200 = 118 STC 297 (SC 3 member bench), it was held that since there is no CST on Inter-State sale, provisions of TDS (Tax Deduction at Source) cannot apply in respect of inter-state works contract. - followed in Nathpa Jhakri v. State of HP (2000) 3 SCC 319 = 118 STC 306 (SC) * Rapti Commission Agency v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2006) 147 STC 566 (SC). * Larsen & Toubro v. CST (2001) 124 STC 162 (Guj HC DB).

The applicant submits that it does not issue any consignment note in the course of providing transport services to 'P'. This being the case, the applicant is of the view that it does not qualify as a 'Goods Transport Agency' and thus transportation services provided by it may not be liable to GST.

The applicant's main contention is based on the premise that various services undertaken by it including transportation services as per second contract for which applicant issues separate invoices and separate consideration as has been decided in the contract shall be considered as stand alone service and should be taxed accordingly.

In order to examine this view of the applicant, it is necessary to examine the terms of the contract executed between the applicant and 'P'.

From the conjoined and harmonious reading of various clauses of first contract and second contract, it can be safely concluded that the agreement for setting up Tower Package TWO5 for +800KV transmission Line Project is a single indivisible contract. As the contract consists of two or more taxable supplies of goods and services and their combination, it is a composite supply as defined under section 2(30). For the proposition of law that the first contract and the second contract is one single indivisible contract, one may find support from the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Indure Ltd. v. Commercial Tax Officer [2010] 3 taxmann.com 542.

The next issue to be decided is whether this composite supplies constitute 'works contract', which is defined under section 2(119) as follows:

'Works contract' means a contract for building, construction, fabrication, completion, erection, installation, fitting out, improvement, modification, repair, maintenance, renovation, alteration or commissioning of any immovable property wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of such contract.

The contract executed between the parties is for complete execution of the Tower Package Tower Package Two5 for + 800RV/HVDC Raigarh - Pugalur Transmission Line Part-V' associated with HYDC Bipole link between Western region (Raigarh, Chhattisgarh) and Southern Region (Pugalur, Tamil Nadu) - North Trichur (Kerala).

As such the subject contracts are for commissioning of immovable property, wherein transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) is involved in the execution of said contracts. The contracts thus are clearly covered by the definition of 'works contract' as per section 2(119). The composite supplies in the nature of works contract as defined under section 2(119) is declared as supply of services as per section 7 read with Entry No. 6(a) of Schedule II of the GST Act.

In view of above discussion, the impugned supply of transportation service is not supply of stand alone service but integral component of composite supply in the nature of works contract as defined under section 2(119) and the entire contract is a supply of services as per Entry No. 6(a) of Schedule II of the GST Act and liable to GST as per Entry at Sr. No. 3(ii) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 bearing Heading No. 9954. [Para 5]

Ruling

The GST is leviable on the transportation charges levied by the applicant on 'P'. [Para 6]

On transportation charges, GST would be leviable at 18 per cent as per Entry at Sr. No. 3(ii) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 6]

Calculation of value of property in goods involved in works contract, transferred works contract - In Vat, the dealer can pay Vat (or sales tax) either on value of material on actual basis or under composition scheme. If Vat or sales tax has been paid or payable on actual value of material, that amount will be deductible from total value of works contract to calculate value of taxable service.

The actual words used in the rule as follows - Where value added tax (Vat) has been paid or payable on the actual value of transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract, then, such value adopted for the purposes of payment of value added tax or sales tax, shall be taken as the value of transfer of property in goods transferred in the execution of the works contract for determining the value of works contract service under this clause [Rule 2A(i)(c) of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006].

However, if the dealer has paid under composition scheme (i.e. at flat rate without separately calculating value of material), the value of material will have to be calculated on basis of actuals. Note that 'value' includes profit relating to goods also.

Vat or sales tax paid will not form part of value for service tax - Gross amount charged for the works contract shall not include value added tax or sales tax, as the case may be, paid, if any, on transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the said works contract.

In Sobha Developers v. CCE (2010) 24 STT 425 (CESTAT), assessee was paying Vat on 70% of value of works contract as per Karnataka Vat Act and paid service tax on 30% of value as service tax. It was held that no differential service tax is payable, even if value of material is not shown separately in invoice. - departmental appeal against the decision has been admitted by SC for hearing - CCE v. Sobha Developers (2014) 47 GST 766 = 49 taxmann.com 595 (SC).

Splitting of contract permissible - In Essar Projects v. CCE (2014) 46 GST 582 = 47 taxmann.com 152 (CESTAT), assessee had entered into two different contracts - one for supply of material/equipment and other for erection/commissioning. There were a separate defect liability clauses for different contracts. Property in goods got transferred when equipment was supplied to customer. It was held that both cannot be treated as single contract for purpose of valuation under composition scheme of works contract.

16.3-2 Composition scheme for payment of service tax

Though service tax is legally payable only on value of service and Vat/sales tax is payable on value of goods, in a composite/indivisible contract, it is difficult to find value of goods and services. Hence, both under service tax and State Vat, a provision has been made for payment of tax under composition scheme.

In a composition scheme, tax can be paid on some ad hoc basis at the option of the tax payer.

In State of Kerala v. Builders Association of India 104 STC 134 = (1997) 2 SCC 183 = AIR 1997 SC 3640 = 1997 AIR SCW 977, the position was that a convenient, hassle-free and simple method, which was 'rough and ready method' was evolved by State Government for collection of sales tax on Works Contract. This was optional to assessee. It was held that Legislature can evolve such alternate, simplified and hassle-free methods of assessment, making it optional to assessee. - . - In the field of taxation, legislation must be allowed greater 'play in joints'. Allowance must be made for 'trial and error' by the legislature. - - Contractor who has opted to the alternate method of taxation cannot complain. Having voluntarily, and with the full knowledge of the alternate method of taxation, opted to be governed by it, a contractor cannot be heard to question the validity of relevant sub-sections or the rules - followed in Karnataka State Construction Corporation v. State of Karnataka (2004) 138 STC 75 (Kar HC DB) * Indian Oil Corp v. Prasanna Welding Industries (2007) 7 VST 101 (Gau HC).

In Mycon Construction v. State of Karnataka 2002 AIR SCW 2156 = 127 STC 105 (SC), it was held that a simplified composition scheme instead of regular assessment, can be evolved, if it is on optional basis. Validity of such provision has been upheld.

Government can make a provision allowing contractors option to opt for composition by paying a sum based on total consideration of contract. - Mytcon Construction v. State of Karnataka (1998) 111 STC 322 (Karn HC).

Decision of Tribunal in the case of CCE v. BSBK (P.) Ltd. [2009] 18 STT 1 (NEW DELHI - CESTAT) 1.2 The assessee was engaged in business of execution of turnkey contracts for engineering works. On scrutiny of the records, the officials found that during the period from 7-7-1997 to 31-3-2002, it had received from its clients amounts for different services, including those falling under ‘consulting engineer service’, but had failed to pay service tax on it. On adjudication, demand was confirmed on design and engineering work done by it along with interest and penalties. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals) who set aside that order. The assessee contended that in a case of turnkey works contract, service tax was not payable as the contract could not be vivisected and the services relating to ‘design and engineering’ formed a minor portion of the total work. In its support the assessee relied on decision of Tribunal in Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 184. The case of the revenue on the other hand was that the contract could be divided into sale contract and service contract in accord with the 46th amendment of the Constitution of India.

The Tribunal observed that in Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) it was held that a work contract cannot be vivisected and part of it subjected to tax. Prima facie, the decision in Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) was not in accordance with the decision of the Supreme Court in Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd.’s case (supra) (BSNL). After referring to different sub-clauses of clause (29A) inserted in article 366 by the 46th Amendment, a three-Judge Bench of the Supreme Court in said decision held that the amendment especially allows specific composite contracts, viz., works contracts [sub-clause (b)]; hire purchase contracts [sub-clause (c)]; catering contracts [sub-clause (e)] by legal fiction to be divisible contracts where the sale element could be isolated and be subjected to sales tax. The Court further held that: If there is an instrument of contract which may be composite in form in any case other than the exceptions in article 366(29A), unless the transaction in truth represents two distinct and separate contracts and is discernible as such, then the State would not have the power to seperate the agreement to sell from the agreement to render service and impose tax on sale. The text, therefore, for composite, contracts other than those mentioned in article 366(29A) continues to be: Did the parties have in mind or intended separate rights arising out of the sale of goods? If there was no such intention, there would be no sale even if the contract could be disintegrated. The test for deciding whether a contract falls into one category or the other is to as what is ‘the substance of the contract’. It would, thus, follow that the dominant nature of test cannot be applied in the case of a works contract falling under sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A), and, therefore, it could not be pressed into service for treating turnkey works contract on different a footing. If ‘works contract’ can be split up into sale contract and service contract, a different treatment may not be given to the so-called turnkey contract, simply because the contract has been on a turnkey basis - although basically it is a works contract. According to Tribunal, prima facie, Daelim Industrial Co. Ltd.’s case (supra) was not correctly decided and the finding that the turnkey works contract cannot be vivisected required reconsideration.

The Tribunal further held that there was no dispute in that, theoretically, service tax can be levied on service part and, at the same time, sales tax can be levied on the sale part of the contract. No doubt, service tax can be levied only if the service is a ‘taxable service’, within the meaning of Act. In the case of a ‘turnkey contract’ if they are not split up only on the ground that the contract is on turnkey project basis, a question may arise as to whether the entire contract would be a sale contract. The answer apparently would be in the negative. Only that part of the contract which falls under sub-clause (b) of article 366(29A) - amounting to ‘deemed sale’ will constitute sale contract on which sales tax can be levied. What will happen to the rest of the contract? Whether it will go out of the net of the service tax? Answer again would be in the negative. No doubt, as observed above, and it went without saying, that the ‘service’ will have to qualify as a taxable service.

The whole contract must be treated as a sale where the dominant intention of the contract is a sale even if some incidental or ancillary services were provided and vice versa. On the other hand, where contract is primarily a contract of work and labour and materials are supplied in execution of such contract, it is a works contract.

In Hindustan Aeronautics Ltd. v. State of Orissa 55 STC 327 (SC) = (1984) 1 SCC 706 = AIR 1984 SC 744 (SC 3 members), HAL imported materials and components on behalf of Government of India and manufactured aircrafts on behalf of Government of India. In contract of sale, the thing produced as a whole has individual existence as sole property of the party who produces it sometime before delivery and the property therein passes only under the contract relating thereto to the other party for a price.

As I understand, there is 1% Vat in Maharashtra and 0.6% in Gujarat.

In AP VAT the builders have a special option of paying VAT @ 1.25% (Other options are also available).

Vat is payable by builders in Karnataka and Rajasthan for which various scheme are available. Vat is payable in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal also.

In MP, it seems, the transaction is treated as deemed sale of goods and taxed by excluding value of land. In Haryana, as I understand, builders are not liable to pay State Vat but they have to deduct tax (TDS) and pay to Government. Really, TDS does not mean that Vat is payable by the builder.

It seems in Delhi, department is of the view that Vat is payable but builders are not agreeing on basis of Raheja's case. In any case, they are liable to deduction tax at source on works contract. However, TDS does not mean they are paying State Vat on the works contract.

Thus, in States where the builders/developers are not liable to pay Vat, their service will have to be classified as 'construction' service and not 'works contract' service. The effect would be that they are not entitled to pay service tax under composition scheme of 40%/60%.

However, they can avail 25%/30% abatement scheme if the value includes value of land.

Builders can pay service tax on value of services - Even where builder finds that 25% scheme is not suitable, it does not mean that they have to pay service tax on entire value of works contract. Service tax would still be payable only on value of services. However, in many construction contracts, finding value of service is not easy. In my view, they can still follow the principles of composition scheme, though legally they are not entitled to that scheme.

Builders/Developers liable to pay Vat on construction of residential flats/commercial shops if State law provides - If State Vat Act provides, builders/developers will be liable to pay Vat on construction of residential flats/commercial shops. The issue is discussed in next chapter.

16.2-1 Exemption to sub-contractor providing works contract service to other contractor

Following service is exempt - Sub-contractor providing services by way of works contract to another contractor providing works contract services which are exempt - clause 29(h) Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Thus, if main works contract is exempt, sub-contractor providing works contract service to main contractor will be exempt from service tax. This exemption is only when the sub-contractor provides works contract service and not in other cases.

16.2-2 Sub-contractor liable even if main contractor pays service tax

CBE&C vide circular No. 999.03/23.8.07 has clarified that a sub-contractor is also a taxable service provider. His services are taxable even if these are used by main provider for completion of his work. The sub-contractor is liable even if the service is input service of the main contractor.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor is exempt from service tax - CBE&C circular No. 138/7/2011-ST dated 6-5-2011.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor has paid service tax - Engineers India Technical Services v. CCE (2014) 73 VST 206 (CESTAT).

In Sew Construction Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 120 = 12 taxmann.com 12 (CESTAT), it has been held that sub-contractor was liable even prior to 23-8-2007.

However, if sub-contractor is providing a service which is exempt, then he will not be liable e.g. if a contractor is providing works contract service which is exempt and if he entrusts that work to sub-contractor, then the sub-contractor will be providing the works contract service (which is exempt) and hence he will also not be liable to pay service tax. However, if the sub-contractor provides some other service like consultancy, cargo handling, clearing and forwarding which is taxable, then the sub-contractor will be liable to service tax even if the main contractor is exempt - CBE&C circular No. 147/16/2011-ST dated 21-10-2011 (The circular is with reference to works contract service but is applicable to all services provided by sub-contractors).

Contrary views - In CST v. Executive Engineer (2006) 144 STC 183 (Uttaranchal HC), it was held that cost of cement supplied by Public Works Department for its own work is not a 'sale' - relying on UP Avas Evam Vikas Parishad Karyalaya v. CST (1990) 78 STC 417 (All HC).

10.11-2 'C' form can be supplied/received for purchases/sales for works contract

Many High Courts have held that 'C' form can be issued for purchase of goods which are used in works contract. The dealer is entitled to registration and he can receive sales tax forms in respect of his sales. See the discussions under 'C Form' in para 20.4-9. These judgments pertain to period prior to 11-5-2002.

After amendment of definition of 'sale' w.e.f. 11-5-2002, now C form can certainly be issued as 'works contract' has been specifically included in definition of 'sale'.
