Other aspects relating to works contract are discussed below.

10.11-1 Supply of material to contractor can be a sale

In some contracts, the contractor charges only labour charges and material is supplied by Principal. In such cases, naturally, there is no 'sale'. However, in some cases, the contractor quotes for full value of goods (including material). However, the Principal (buyer) agrees to supply material to supplier at fixed price (Usually this is done to ensure quality or uninterrupted work). In such case, supply of material by buyer to the contractor may be held as 'sale' if absolute property in goods is transferred to contractor and price is adjusted against dues to contractor. In such case, sales tax will be payable. - Hindustan Steel v. 22.3-1 Works Contract is supply of service for rate of tax under GST

Works contract as defined in section 2(119) of CGST Act is a composite supply and shall be treated as 'supply of service' - Para 6(a) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

General rate of GST on composite supply of works contract services is 18%. This is irrespective of GST rate on individual goods used in execution of works contract.

Works Contract is deemed sale of goods as per Constitution - A tax on the transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of a works contract is deemed sale of goods under Article 366(29A) of Constitution of India. [Note that this Article in the Constitution of India is continuing even after Constitutional amendment].

Works contract is not limited to construction - The term 'works contract' is not limited to construction services. It covers all activities relating to plant, machinery or equipment which are immovable.

FACT: The applicant-company is primarily engaged in the construction business and provides works services to various customers including Government, public sector undertakings, Government entities and private sector entities.

The applicant entered into a contractual arrangement with GVSCCL, which is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 at the city level, in which the State and the urban local body (GVMC) are the promoters with 50:50 equity shareholding. The Government of India (GOI) initiated 'Smart City Mission', as a part of which Special Purpose Vehicles (SPV) are created. The SPVs will plan, appraise, approve, release funds, implement, manage, operate, monitor, and evaluate the Smart City development projects. Each Smart City will have a SPV which will be headed by a full time CEO and have nominees of Central Government, State Government and Urban Local Bodies (ULB) on its Board. GVSCCL is one of such Special Purpose Vehicles (SPV).

The applicant entered into an agreement with GVSCCL for beautification of streets including Streets cape Design, Landscaping and intersection Redesign in Visakhapatnam's Area Based development under smart Cities Mission. The agreement includes the supply of materials and provisions of services by the supplier to the applicant.

The applicant is seeking advance ruling on questions as to whether the services provided by the applicant is a composite supply of works contracts as per clauses (30) and (119) of section 2 and whether the services provided by the applicant are taxable at rate of 12 per cent as per the Sl. No. 3 (vi)(a) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

HELD: The applicant is providing the supplies to the GVSCCL of (a) construction of the project; (b) development of the project including plantation, landscaping, Street lighting etc., and (c) maintenance of the project.

The Composite supply of works contract as defined at section 2 is treated as supply of service in terms of Sl. No. 6, Schedule II of CGST Act, 2017 and APGST Act, 2017.

GVSCCL is a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) created by the Government of Andhra Pradesh. GVSCCL is a limited company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013 in which the Andhra Pradesh State Government and the Greater Visakhapatnam Municipal Corporation are the promoters having 50:50 equity shareholding, which substantiates more than 90 per cent of participation of the Government. With reference to the 'control' wielded by the shareholders, all the directors of the board are public authorities. Initially the board was constituted with the Principal Secretary for Municipal Administration and Urban Development, Govt. of A.P. (under promoter category) as chairman. The District Collector and Commissioner, GVMC (under Promoter Category) and other 11 members were nominated by the Authorities in the State Government, ULB and Central Government as per the said G.O. The SPV is owned by the Government of A.P. and GVMC on 50:50 ratio and is governed by a Board of Directors answerable to the Government of A.P., Government of India and GVMC. The Government of A.P. and GVMC are the shareholders in the GVSCCL.

Accordingly, the GVSCCL rightly fits into the definition of the 'Government Entity' as per Sl. No. 4(x) of Notification No. 31/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 13-10-2017. The functions carried out by the said GVSCCL are the functions which were entrusted by the Central Government, State Government and Local Authority i.e. of Municipal Administration.

Furthermore, the service provided by the applicant is composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2, provided to a Government Entity by way of construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion, fitting out, repair, maintenance, renovation, or alteration of a civil structure or any other original works meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. The same is classifiable under the Heading No. 9954 Entry at Sl. No. 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as amended from time to time and liable to tax at the rate of 12 per cent (6 per cent CGST + 6 per cent SGST).

Thus, the services provided by the applicant to a composite supply of works contract as per clauses (30) and (119) of section 2 and are taxable at rate of 12 per cent under Entry No. 3(vi)(a) of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. [Para 7]

QUESTIONS :

1.What basic precaution is required to be taken while submitting tender or accepting the order from client keeping in view the implication of service tax ?

2.If order is composite, is it required to mention in the order the value of the various activities like Supply, Design and Drawing, Erection, Installation and Commissioning, etc., to ascertain the service tax obligation ? 3.We are already registered with Excise Department, Service Tax Cell, for our Consulting Engineer, Installation and Commissioning and Repairs and Maintenance. In the said Registration billing address is from our Registered office, i.e., A-116, whereas we are doing project all over India and registered under Sales Tax Act in each State wherever we are doing the project. In such situation we are billing from each of such States directly to the client. So what is the alternative with regard to billing for service tax in such case ?

4.As the rate of service tax has been increased from 8 per cent to 10.2 per cent (including 2 per cent cess) in the Budget, at what rate we have to pay to the Government for the payment realized after that particular date and billing done before that particular date ?

5.If we received a sub-contract from contractor who is charging the service tax to the main contractor, in such case are we exempted for paying service tax on account of double taxation ? What is the exact procedure to get exemption ? What type of documents/letters are required from the employer and or main contractor ?

6.If we give sub-contract to other sub-contractor, can he be exempt from service tax by not charging service tax from us on account of double taxation? What type of document we have to given to that sub-contractor for not charging and ultimately not paying the service tax ?

ANSWERS :

1. While giving tender ensure that amount stated in the tender is either inclusive of all taxes or it should be clearly mentioned that taxes, if any, would be charged separately. While quoting a figure inclusive of taxes,a note should be stated indicating that any increase in indirect tax rates would be borne by the customer. Ensure proper calculation of taxes (also refer ans. 2) so as to avoid short-collection subsequently.

2. The Government has issued Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003 with effect from July 1, 2003 whereby general exemption has been given from service tax levy on so much of the value of all the taxable services, as is equal to the value of goods and materials sold by the service provider to the recipient of service subject to the condition that there is documentary proof specifically indicating the value of the said goods and materials.

It is further clarified that this exemption would be available only in cases where the sale of such goods is evidenced and the sale value is quantified and shown separately in the invoice.

So, as mentioned above, service tax is not leviable on supply of material, provided the sales value of the material is separately mentioned in the invoice.

In the case of composite contract, where value of material supplied cannot be determined separately, service tax is to be paid at the rate of 8 per cent on 33 per cent of the total composite value.

Let us consider an example :

Value of composite contract 100 (out of which 60 is labour and 40 is material) :

If the invoice shows only the consolidated amount, i.e., Rs. 100, then amount of service tax to be paid would be 8 per cent (100 x 33 per cent) = Rs. 2.64.

If material supply of Rs. 40 is shown separately in the invoice, then service tax to be paid works out to 60 x 8 per cent = Rs. 4.8.

Now let us consider another contract of value Rs. 100 (wherein labour = 20 material = 80) :

If the invoice shows only the consolidated amount, i.e., Rs. 100, then amount of service tax to be paid would be 8 per cent (100 × 33 per cent) = Rs. 2.64.

Facts in the case of Harekrishna Developers, In re [2008] 14 STT 175 (AAR - New Delhi) 3.2 The applicant-firm intends to develop on its own plot of land a residential complex having more than twelve residential units with a club house and other common facilities. It will sell plots of land inside the complex to prospective buyers who will enter into a works contract with the applicant for the construction of residential units. The applicant itself will execute a part of the works contract [‘activity No. 3’] and for remaining part, the applicant will further enter into a works contract with other contractors [‘activity No. 4’]. However, goods for construction will be purchased/acquired by the applicant and the property in those goods will be transferred to buyers of the housing units and such transfer would be exigible to tax as sale of goods. The applicant sought advance ruling of the Authority on questions of its liability in these two types of activities, and also on question of rate of tax in case of activity No. 3.

The applicant contends that since the works contract in activities 3 and 4 involves construction of a new building-such an activity can only be covered under(ii)( b) in the Explanation to section 65(105)(zzzza). Since the new building proposed to be constructed in the course of the execution of the works contract is a residential one, and is not for the purpose of commerce or industry, such a works contract will not fall under (b) and therefore, will not attract service tax. The applicant further states that a works contract for construction of a new building for residential purposes is also not covered under any of the remaining classifications in (ii) of the Explanation to clause (zzzza). The classification (c) which covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’ is not applicable in applicant’s case as the works contract is for construction of an individual residential unit and not for construction of a residential complex.

Decision in the case of Harekrishna Developers (supra )

3.3 Authority for Advance Ruling held:

1. To attract service tax under sub-clause (zzzza) of section 65(105), a works contract has to meet the two conditions: (i) and (ii) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). The facts narrated by the applicant indicated that condition (i) is met in the instant case as the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of the works contract is exigible to tax as sale of goods under the local Sales Tax Act. To meet condition (ii), the activity involved in the works contract in activity Nos. 3 and 4 has to be covered by at least one of the classifications (a ) to (e) in the Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). Proceeding serially, one finds that building of a residential house on a sub-plot in a residential complex is clearly not covered in (a). As pointed out by the applicant itself, it is also not covered by (b) which covers construction of a new building intended primarily for commerce and industry and does not cover construction of a new building. Item (c) of sub-clause (zzzza) of clause (105) covers ‘construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof’.

2. As per the draft of the works contract submitted, it is clear that such contracts will be for construction of individual houses on sub-plots located within the plot owned by the applicant on which the applicant proposes to develop a residential housing project. As per the applicant’s own narration, the residential project to be constructed on this plot would have at least 12 residential units, a club house and other common facilities and the layout of the project would be approved by the prescribed authority under the relevant law in force. Such a project constructed as per activity Nos. 3 and 4 squarely conforms to the definition of a ‘residential complex’ given in clause (91a) of section 65, and the individual houses constructed get covered under the definition of a ‘residential unit’ contained therein. Execution of the works contract, thus, involves construction of a part of a new ‘residential complex’ and is covered by (c).

Tailoring work - A contract to stitch suit as per cloth supplied by the customer is a contract for work and labour. However, if tailor promises to stitch and deliver a suit for price agreed upon, investing his own cloth and stitching material, it will be 'sale' even if customer might have chosen piece of cloth as per his own liking - Hindustan Shipyard Ltd. v. Supply and fixation of rolling shutters - Transaction of fabrication of a rolling shutter and its actual fitting at site is a continuous one, it is a composite contract for supply of material, labour and services. Accordingly, an assessee can pay service tax on the contract price after reducing the value of goods and the amount of sales tax/VAT paid on such goods. However, under this option, the assessee cannot avail CENVAT credit on such goods. There is no bar on taking CENVAT credit on capital goods or input services. Works contractors have been given another option of paying tax at the rate of 2 per cent on the contract price after reducing it by the amount of sales tax/VAT paid on the transfer of property in the goods involved in the contract. The assessee opting for this composition scheme is not entitled to take CENVAT credit on such goods. An assessee opting for this scheme has to exercise the option prior to payment of service tax on the works contract and the option cannot be changed midway during the contract. Some assessees have been paying service tax on construction services or erection, commissioning and installation services and availing abatement of 67 per cent for paying service tax and they would like to migrate to the composition scheme from June 1, 2007. But they are not clear whether it is permissible under the law as they have already paid tax for this contract. It should be noted that the contracts of such assessee which involve transfer of property in goods in the execution of the contracts can be taxable only as works contract service and not under other classifications under which they have been paying service tax. Therefore, they will be paying service tax for the first time under the works contract category. A composite contract cannot be subjected to taxation under two different classifications for different periods.

Even if an assessee wants to pay 2 per cent tax on contract remaining to be completed as on June 1, 2007, the computation of tax would not be easy. Whether, the option is to adopt valuation under rule 2A or to pay 2 per cent tax under the composition scheme, the starting point is ‘gross amount charged for the works contract’. The works contract is one and indivisible. Therefore, the ‘gross amount charged for works contract’ is towards the entire responsibility and not what is received on or after June 1, 2007 with respect to continuing contracts. Tax computed on this basis for the balance period from June 1, 2007 is unreasonable and iniquitous. If machinery for computation tax provided in the law fails, it can be argued that levy is not intended.

4. Composite contracts came on the way of States levying sales tax on the goods transferred to the customers in the execution of works contract. By legal fiction, the 46th Constitutional amendment made such indivisible contracts divisible, so that the States can levy sales tax/VAT on the value of such goods. The Supreme Court, in Bharat Sanchar Nigam Ltd. v. UOI [2006] 3 STT 245, has held that apart from the works contract, the composite price can be split only with respect to one more deemed sale introduced by the Constitution amendment, which is supply of food and beverages as part of the service in restaurants and hotels. In respect of the other four types of deemed sales, a composite contract cannot be split to tax the activities, which are subject-matter of such deemed sales. Even for pure sale transactions, courts have held that the add-on service would be treated as part of a sale transaction if it is incidental or ancillary to transfer of property in the goods.

16.3-4 Illustration

Question - The contract for industrial construction is for Rs. 8,00,000 which includes value of services plus material which is to be supplied by contractor. Value of material used by contractor is Rs. 5,00,000 and the value of service is Rs. 3,00,00 (Total Rs. 8,00,000). The customer has agreed to supply steel to contractor free of cost (FOC), the value of which is Rs. 1,80,000 and certain services free of cost. Value of such free services is Rs. 20,000. The value of steel and services supplied free were not considered in quotation given by contractor. The land belongs to customer. Its value is Rs. 4,00,000. Service tax paid on input services is Rs. 10,300 and excise duty paid on inputs used for construction is Rs. 41,200, Calculate service tax under composition scheme and also under normal scheme assuming service tax rate of 12.36%, if (a) the contract is covered under State works contract tax and (b) the contract is not covered under works contract service.

Answer - Under composition scheme, value of material supplied by customer free of cost is required to be added. In that case, total value of contract (including material and services supplied free by customer, but excluding value of land) is Rs. 10,00,000. The contractor can opt to pay duty @ 40% on total value i.e. on Rs. 4,00,000, if he is covered under State Works contract tax. Service tax payable will be 12.36% of Rs. 4,00,000 i.e. Rs. 49,440.

The contractor can avail Cenvat credit of Rs. 10,000.

If value of land is not shown separately, then service tax will be payable @ 40% of gross amount which will include value of land plus value of material and services supplied free by customer.

If the contract is covered under State Works Contract Tax, the service tax payable is 4.944% of Rs. 10,00,000 i.e. Rs. 49,440. He can avail Cenvat credit of Rs. 10,320. Thus, net tax payable is Rs. 39,120.

10.9

Valuation rules to determine sale price of works contract

So far, no specific provision was made in CST and hence 'sale price' was required to be determined on basis of definition of 'sale price' as contained in section 2(h) of CST Act. As per this definition, freight or delivery or the cost of installation is not includible when separately charged.

This definition is not sufficient to determine 'sale price' when the contract is an indivisible contract which comprises of both goods and services. In sales tax laws or VAT laws of many States, there is provision of 'composition scheme' to pay sales tax on gross value of contract on some ad hoc basis. So far, there was no similar provision in CST Act.

Now, proviso to section 2(h) (inserted w.e.f. 13th May 2005) provides that in case of transfer of property in goods (whether as goods or in some other form) involved in the execution of works contract, the 'sale price' of such goods shall be determined in the prescribed manner by making such deductions from the total consideration for the works contract as may be prescribed and such price shall be deemed to be the sale price for the purposes of section 2(h).

Thus, now 'sale price' in case of sale of 'goods involved in works contract' will be determined on the basis of rules that may be made by Central Government.

State valuation rules can apply if Central Government has not made rules - So far, Rules have not been framed by Central Government. In Mahim Patram P Ltd. v. UOI (2007) 7 STT 136 = 7 STR 110 = 6 VST 248 (SC), it has been held that in absence of rules, valuation can be made on basis of State Rules. It was also held that only because rules have not been framed under Central Act would not per se mean that no tax is leviable - followed in CVAT v. State of Haryana (2009) 1 GST 113 = 23 VST 10 (CSTAA).

In Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. State of Orissa (2007) 12 VST 31 (Ori HC DB), assessment of tax on works contract was held invalid as no rules were framed. Assessment was done only on basis of departmental circulars. However, it was held that fresh assessment can be made after rules are framed.

The Electricity Distribution Companies are procuring these services from the applicant in relation to a work entrusted to it by the State Government, which is supply of electricity to consumers and the fifth condition is also satisfied.[Para 11.7]

The contract is for construction, erection, commissioning, installation, completion of original works. The contract is a new construction involving erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures and hence the third condition is also satisfied.[Para 11.8] The issue under detailed discussion is whether the works are meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. The Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in selling of electricity to the consumers and are collecting consideration and electrical energy is considered as 'goods'. Hence the Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in the sale of goods or in general, supply of goods to the consumers for consideration. The Explanation clause inserted which provides that for the purposes of this item, the term 'business' shall not include any activity or transaction undertaken by the Central Government, a State Government or any local authority in which they are engaged as public authorities does not apply as they are not activities undertaken by the Central Government or State Government or a local authority.[Para 11.9]

Further, from the definition of business as defined in clause (17) of section 2 of the CGST Act, it is clear that any activity of trade, commerce, manufacture, etc. or any other similar activity is included in the definition of business and it is immaterial whether it is done for a pecuniary benefit, and any activity done in connection with or incidental or ancillary to such activity is also included in the scope of 'business'.[Para 11.11]

The Electricity Distribution Companies are involved in the supply of goods as already explained and hence they are involved in the business of supplying goods. They also receive consideration for the supply of electricity. The predominant activity of the Electricity Distribution Companies is to supply Electricity and the works executed by the applicant are used for this only predominant activity and hence are original works meant predominantly for use for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession. Hence, the contracts in question do not satisfy the fourth condition required for them to be covered under the Entry No.3(vij(a) of Notification No.11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate) as amended from time to time.[Para 11.12]

In view of the foregoing, it is ruled that the services provided by the applicant to the Electricity Supply Companies (wholly owned Government of Karnataka Undertakings) by way of construction erection, commissioning, installation, completion, etc, are not covered under entry 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No.12/2017- Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, or under entry 3(vi)(a) of the Notification No.8/2017-Integrated Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, as amended from time to time and consequentially are not eligible to be taxed at a lower rate of 12 per cent GST and hence are liable to be taxed at 18 per cent GST.[Para 12]

23.1-8 Redevelopment is subject to GST

Generally in re-development project, land is owned by a society, comprising members of the society with each member entitled to his share by way of an apartment. When it becomes necessary after the lapse of a certain period, society or its flat owners may engage a promoter (builder/developer) for undertaking re-construction. Society/individual apartment owners give 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) or permission to the promoter (builder/developer), for re-construction. The promoter (builder/developer) constructs apartments with same or different carpet area for original owners of apartment and additionally may also be involved in one or more of the following: (i) construct some additional apartments for sale to others (ii) arrange for rental accommodation or rent payments for society members/original owners for stay during the period of re-construction (iii) pay an additional amount to the original owners of flats in the society.

Under this model, the promoter (builder/developer) receives consideration for the construction service provided by him, from two categories of service receivers. First category is the society/members of the society, who transfer development rights over the land (including the permission for additional number of apartments), to the promoter (builder/developer). The second category of service receivers consist of buyers of apartments other than the society/members. Generally, they pay by cash.

In both the cases, GST is payable as in first case, the promoter receives consideration in form of TDR and in other cases, by cash.

23.1-9 GST on Slum Rehabilitation Programmes

In Slum Rehabilitation programmes, Government transfers TDR/FSI to promoter. The promoter supplies apartments to slum dwellers without monetary consideration. The apartments constructed in addition to apartments given free to the slum dwellers are sold.

In both the cases, GST is payable - FAQ (Part II) Nos. 8 and 9 issued by CBI&C vide circular F No. 354/32/2019-TRU dated 14-5-2019.

If the apartments fall within the definition of affordable residential apartments, GST rate will be 1% [0.5% CGST plus 0.5% SGST/UTGST]. Similarly, if such apartments are covered under specified schemes, the GST rate will be 1%

Purchaser of apartment is not liable to tax even if he sales before occupation or completion - The Purchaser of apartment is not liable to tax even if he sales before occupation or completion, for two reasons - (a) He is not supplying construction service, as deeming provision requires supply of construction service (b) He is not in the business of sale of apartments.

Introduction

1. If you have an open property interest or if you have purchased a property in Haryana or if you are a builder/Developer in Haryana, then you might be aware of a few frivolous issues viz, Assessment orders on Builders/Developers with heavy demands, penalties & interest, demand notice that the builders are raising on the buyers on account of additional Haryana VAT and recent case of Hon'ble Supreme Court of Larsen & Tubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka [2013] 41 STT 113/38 taxmann.com 98.

Judgment in the case L&T

2. The sales tax thrust on builders and developers has gained drastic momentum post the recent rulings of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Larsen & Tubro Ltd. (supra) which, in principle, accepts the law laid down in the earlier judgment in case of K. Raheja Development Corpn. v. State of Karnataka [2005] 2 STT 178 (SC) (Two Judge Bench) and lays a few essential laws as under :-

(a)

Any agreement entered into by the builder / promoter before the completion of construction tantamounts to works contract and, hence, is liable to Value Added Tax (VAT)/ sales tax.

(b)

When an agreement is entered into between the promoter/developer and the flat purchaser to construct a flat and eventually sell the flat with the fraction of land, it is obvious that such transaction involves the activity of construction inasmuch as it is only when the flat is constructed then it can be conveyed. The said activity will be covered by the term "works contract". The term "works contract" is nothing but a contract in which one of the parties is obliged to undertake or to execute works. Such activity of construction has all the characteristics or elements of a works contract.

(c)

In tripartite agreement between the owner of the land, the developer and the flat purchaser, there is nothing wrong if the transaction is treated as a composite contract comprising of both a works contract and a transfer of immovable property and levy sales tax on the value of the material involved in execution of the works contract.

Circular issued by Haryana VAT authorities based on Judgment in L&T's case

3. Based on above, Haryana VAT Authorities have released several circulars on back to back basis in this regard:-

(a)

Even prior to L&T's Judgment, the Haryana VAT Authorities (in conformity with K. Raheja Law) had released Circular No. 952/ST-1, dated 7th May, 2013:-

(i)

This circular clarified the assessment mechanism and various other issues as relevant for taxing such transactions related to agreements by developers/builders with prospective buyers.

(ii)

This circular categorically mentioned that where the builder/developer opts for composition scheme under Rule 49 then the value of taxable consideration shall exclude the land component, except in cases of joint development agreement.

(iii)

Currently, with no other clarification available or legal support under the specific scenario of civil works contract and their relevant ancillary issues like WCT, Valuation, procedural compliances and composition scheme (under Rule 49 as applicable to works contractors), the above said circular can be seen as only legal reference point for builder community.

(b)

Circular No. 693/ST-1, dated 26.3.2013 clarified that the VAT D-1 benefit is available only to manufacturer and lumpsum dealer under Rule 49. Hence, where a Builder/Developer does not opt for composition scheme the benefit of reduced rate under VAT D-1 shall not be available.

(c)

This was followed by another Circular No. 1166/ST-1, dated 4-6-2013 which clarified the limitation aspects in regard to both, the registered dealers and unregistered dealers under sections 15 and 16 of the HVAT, 2003 respectively. Further, the reassessment under section 17 and revision of original order under section 34 have been detailed.

(d)

Circular No. 41/ST-1, dated 14-1-2014 wherein it was clarified that the levy of additional tax @ 5% (i.e. surcharge) is applicable on all the composition rates except that of the retailers. Hence, the effective rate of tax for the works contract dealers / Builders and Developers shall be 4.2%.

(e)

Circular No. 259/ST-1, dated 10-2-2014 takes a stand exactly opposite to Circular No. 952/ST-1 in regard to valuation of taxable consideration under composition scheme. This circular amends the earlier circular to include even the value of land in the value of taxable consideration.

Works Contract - Divisible

Works contract can be divided into two separate contracts by legal fiction as provided in sub-clause (b) of clause (29A) of article 366 of the Constitution; (i) contract for the sale of goods involved in the said works contract, and (ii) for supply of labour and service. This division of contract can be made only if the works contract involved a dominant intention to transfer the property in goods and not in contracts where the transfer in property takes place as an incident of the contract of service. What is pertinent to ascertain what was the intention of the contract. [see Rainbow Colour Lab v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2000) 2 SCC 385]. The Supreme Court in Associated Cement Co. Ltd. v. CC (2001) 4 SCC 593 doubted this saying :

"The conclusion arrived at in Rainbow Colour Lab v. State of MP (2000) 2 SCC 385, in our opinion, runs counter to the express provision contained in article 366(29A) as also of the Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Builders Association of India v. Union of India (1989) 2 SCC 645".

The Supreme Court in BSNL v. Union of India [2006] 152 Taxman 135 agreed. However, the Supreme Court in C. K. Jideesh v. Union of India (2005) 8 SCALE 784 had held that aforesaid observations in Associated Companies Ltd.’s case were merely obiter and that Rainbow Colour Lab’s case was still good law.

In Hyundai Rotem Company, In re (2016) 55 GST 714 = 69 taxmann.com 391 = 91 VST 522 (AAR), the appellant had contract of testing, commissioning and trial runs of metro trains. It was held that rolling stock is 'plant' and its commissioning is covered under 'original works' and hence exempt.

Total amount - "Total amount" means the sum total of gross amount charged for the works contract and the fair market value of all goods and services supplied in or in relation to the execution of works contract, whether or not supplied under the same contract or any other contract, after deducting - (i) the amount charged for such goods or services, if any and (ii) the value added tax or sales tax, if any, levied thereon. - - Provided that the fair market value of goods and services so supplied may be determined in accordance with the generally accepted accounting principles.

In short, if customer (or any other person) supplies some goods or services free, its value will have to be added for calculating 'total mount'.

'Total amount' to include value of land also in composition scheme - Rule 2A of Service Tax (determination of Value) Rules, 2016 provided that 'total amount' shall include value of goods. However, the rule did not provide that the 'total amount' should include land or undivided share of land. In many states, contract with builder is for total value including value of land or undivided share of land. However, in some Southern States, two agreements are executed - one for undivided share of land and other for construction. Builders in those states where not including value of undivided share of land while calculating 40% of total value of contract.

Now, a retrospective amendment has been made w.e.f. 1-7-2010 to clarify that 'total amount' will include value of undivided share of land.

Now, valuation done in Northern States and Southern States is on equal footing.

However, the policy of Central Government has been consistent that no retrospective amendment shall be made. This amendment is against that declared policy of Central Government, though it cannot be said to be unfair.

Concept of fair market value - The concept of 'fair market value' will be highly relevant in cases where the customer supplies some material (like cement and steel) at lower than the fair market value. For example, if fair market value of cement is Rs. 350 per bag and the customer supplies cement to contractor free of cost, then Rs. 350 per bag will be added to 'total amount'. If the customer supplies the bag @ Rs. 250 per bag (and not free) Rs. 350 will be added to 'total amount' and deduction of Rs. 250 will be allowed. In effect. Rs. 100 per bag will be added to 'total amount' and then the percentage (40%/60%/70% as the case may be).

If fair market value of material supplied by service receiver is Rs. one lakh and if it is supplied free, then Rs. one lakh will be added to 'total amount'. If the material is supplied at Rs. 60,000 plus Vat of Rs. 3,000 (total Rs. 63,000), then Rs. 1,00,000 will be added to 'total amount' and Rs. 63,000 will be deducted. In effect, Rs. 37,000 will be added to 'total amount' and then the percentage (25%/30%/40%/60% as applicable) will be applied for calculating service tax payable.

The assessee had undertaken a contract for preparing and installing metal crash barriers. It paid tax at the rate of 2 per cent contending that it had undertaken the works contract for supply and fixing of metal tri beam crash barriers, which were in the nature of iron railings fitted on both the sides of the road for prevention of accidents.

The Commissioner rejected the contention of the assessee and levied tax on it at the rate of 12 per cent.

The Tribunal held that the supply and fixing of metal crash barriers amounted to civil works and, therefore, the assessee was liable to pay composite tax at the rate of 2 per cent.

With the above Circular No. 259 (to many it comes as a tyranny), the authorities have stirred a significant row of hue and cry, because it is felt that the circular has not only increased the tax burden drastically but has also not addressed other important ancillary issues that are bound to creep up because of this amendment. Some of them will be as under:-

(a)

Date of applicability of this Order. Whether it can substitute the relevant valuation mechanism with retrospective effect?

One of the astonishing aspect of the circular is that there is no specific date of applicability mentioned in the circular. It clearly means that the revenue will take the stand that the circular is clarificatory in nature and, hence, shall have retrospective effect. The stand is surely debatable and will enter into litigation sooner or later.

In case of Ranbir Singh Ram Gopal v. St. of Hr. [CWP No. 11994, dated 11-12-1996], it was held that the there shall be no retrospective enhancement in tax-rates by notification / circular. Revenue shall not initiate recovery of enhanced tax for erstwhile assessment periods. Same view was held in Rattan Bhatta v. St. of Haryana [2000] 16 PHT 487 (Punj. & Har.). Judgments in other indirect tax laws like service tax , excise can also be resorted to for this principle.

Note:- As per Rule 49(7), a lump sum contractor may, when rate of lump sum is revised, opt out of the scheme of payment of lump sum in lieu of tax payable under the Act by appearing before the appropriate assessing authority himself or through an authorised agent within ninety days of such revision and expressing in writing his intention to opt out of the scheme of payment of lump sum. Such contractor shall be liable to pay lump sum for the period before the revision in lump sum rate at the unrevised rate and in respect of transfer of property in any goods, whether as goods or in some other form, involved in the execution of the contract(s), thereafter he shall be liable to pay tax as a contractor not being a lump sum contractor.

(b)

Since many builders would have started paying without land component, can the burden of increased tax be passed on to the customer when composition scheme allows no additional tax recovery from the contractee?

Another problem the builder community faces is lack of proper burden passing on mechanism under the composition schemes of VAT. Under HVAT (similar to most of States) the tax cannot be collected separately on the strength of invoice where the dealer opts for composition scheme under rule 49.

(c)

Whether assessees can be re-assessed based on this Circular?

Another dilemma is that this circular is silent on whether this circular can be made as the basis for re-assessment or revision of orders under section 17 and section 34 respectively. Considering the broadness of Circular No. 1166 it is very much on the cards of the revenue to explore this aspect further.

(d)

Other issues still to be addressed and wanting the uber-attention of Law Makers and Law Administrators — No modus operandi has been identified in regard to WCT deduction by the customers, as they cannot be considered as structured as a 'normal contractee' to a normal works contract. Whether every customer is required to deduct WCT and seek registration under Haryana VAT Act?

There is major requirement to insert an exception to WCT deduction provisions to exclude flat buyers from WCT deduction liability. Ironically, a normal individual flat buyer today stand's on same footing as a well structured works contractee, though ground reality is exactly different. Individual flat owners cannot be expected to take registrations under sales tax, deduct WCT and deposit the same on behalf of Developers.

Note: - There is a discreet difference in Delhi VAT and Haryana VAT in regard to deduction of WCT. In Delhi, where the individual/HUF is the contractee, they are not burdened with WCT deduction liability (as per section 36A of DVAT Act), while as in Haryana the same is not the case, hence, even the individual / HUF shall be covered in the ambit of contractee and thereby liable to deduct WCT.

(e)

A Million Dollar Question - Can the burden of additional taxes be passed on to the customer or not? Will it affect the service tax liabilities ?

Another very interesting issue to arise here is that most developers enter into an agreement with prospective buyers according to which additional taxes are to be borne by the customers (as a part of space buyer's agreement).

But the governing section 9 of composition scheme mandates the contractor/developer not to issue any tax invoices. Hence, no tax can be collected on the strength of tax invoice.

The works are supply and installation of lines and equipments meant for telecommunication, signalling in the CMRL project and not related to any civil engineering work. Therefore, the supply of the applicant to Siemens is covered under SAC 9954, more specifically under SAC 995461 and the first requirement of the entry stands satisfied. [Para 11.1]

The second criteria to be satisfied is that the supply should be a 'Composite Supply'. In the case at hand from the purchase order furnished by the applicant, it is seen that there is supply of goods (equipments, goods, etc.) and services (installation, testing, etc.) for a particular cost center/Line and the work is considered to be done on that basis. Thus, there is a natural bundle of goods and services per cost center/Line and the supply is construed to be made when the entire supply of the line/cost center is made. Hence, the supply of the applicant is a composite supply and this criterion is satisfied. [Para 11.2]

The next criterion to be examined is whether the said composite supply is a 'Works Contract' as defined under section 2(119).

From the definition, a work shall be treated as Works Contract if that work is done for land or earth or for immovable property and there is transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such contract. Immovable property cannot be moved. It cannot be separated from the land or earth. If it is detached it shall have to destroy. In the case at hand, the 'Employer's Requirements, Particular Specifications-4B Telecommunication General Specification' - gives the outline summary of the various systems and sub-systems which are applicable to the Telecommunication scope and the outline description of the works said to be the works of the applicant. On going through same, it is observed that the work involves installation of the individual systems at platforms, stations, other select locations along the corridor and is integrated at the Operation Control Corridor (OCC) at Koyambedu and the Telecommunications Infrastructure implementation is to be synchronized with the civil construction phases. Further the scope of works of the applicant like Public Address and Voice Alarm System, CCTV System, Passenger Information Display System, Office Telephone System, etc. requires installation on specific locations, namely ceiling and the like and these goods once installed, may not necessarily be damaged while removing. The applicant has not established with documents that the works contracted to them are to be executed on immovable property as required under definition of 'Works Contract' given above. The applicant has stated that in the Pre-GST regime, under Service Tax, the applicant being a supplier of Works Contract Service relating to infrastructure project of railways, in capacity of sub-contractor was exempted from service tax and had claimed the benefit of entry 3(v) of Notification 11/2017 - C.T. (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 as above. The definition of 'Works Contract' as it existed in the 'Service Tax' law is different from that defined under section 2(119) of GST Act. Under GST, only those defined works carried out on any immovable property is covered under 'Works Contract'. Thus without documentary proof of the works contracted/undertaken like related diagrams/plans/schedules/Pictures/detailed write-up on the works, etc. in the absence of submission of the entire sub-contract agreement, it is not possible for this Authority to conclude that the works are done on the immovable property and once installed, the goods/equipments cannot be dismantled without damage so as to hold that the work undertaken is 'Works Contract' as per section 2(119) of the Act. As the applicant has stated that it will not be possible for them to furnish the entire sub-contract agreement which contains the requisite details, in the absence of the documentation works could not be said as 'Works Contract' as per section 2(119). [Para 11.3]

The other criteria to be satisfied are the supply should be by way of 'construction, erection, commissioning or installation of original works' pertaining to railways, including monorail and metro. Original work is defined in Para 2(zs) of the Notification No. 12/2017 - C.T. (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

From the submissions, it is seen that the work of the applicant includes Installation of the various systems on designing, manufacture and supply and therefore is 'Original work' as defined in the notification.

The work of the applicant is on the lines, stations and locations of land appurtenant and, therefore, this criterion is satisfied. [Para 11.4]

To summarize, the entry at 3(v) do not specify the class of service provider to whom it applies. The entry is specific to the composite supply of works contract pertaining to railways including monorail and metro. This view is fortified by the justification of the recommendation of the Fitment Committee to the 25th GST Council meeting (available in Volume-2 of the Agenda) after which the downward revision of the rate was effected.

The Fifth Contract termed as 'onshore Service Contract (VSC part) (NOA-V)' ('on shore Service Contract/Fifth Contract') provides for the subject package, for performance of all other activities inter alia including port handling of the plant and Equipment including mandatory Spares (except +320KV HVDC Cable and some of its associated items) to be supplied from abroad, loading, inland transportation and insurance for delivery at site, insurance, unloading, storage and handling at site, installation including civil works, testing and commissioning including Performance Testing in respect of all Plant and Equipment supplied under both 'First Contract' and 'Third Contract' and any other services specified in the Bidding Documents referred to hereinabove. The scope of work under this contract as referred in the Fifth Contract is as follows:

a.

Local transportation, insurance and other incidental services

b.

Installation charges

c.

Training charges

The appellant is entrusted with the responsibility of delivery of the goods at PGCIL's site. For this, the appellant engages local transporters who issue consignment notes to the appellant for such transportation of goods and issue their freight invoices on the appellant. The appellant discharges the GST liability under reverse charge mechanism on such freight amount being paid by it to these transporters as provided under Notification No. 13/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017. The appellant charges local transportation from the PGCIL as per the terms of the Service Contract. However, since the consignment note is already issued by the transporters engaged by the appellant, no subsequent additional consignment note is issued by the appellant. With respect to the local transportation charges recovered by the appellant under the aforesaid contract from the PGCIL without issuance of a consignment note, the appellant sought Advance Ruling on the applicability of tax exemption as provided under Serial No. 18 of the Notification No. 12/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017.

The Advance Ruling Authority observed that the First Contract including onshore Ex-works supply of all equipment and materials cannot be executed independent of the Second Contract which is for the onshore supply of services. The two contracts are linked by a cross fall breach clause deeming that any breach in either of the contracts is to be considered to be a breach of the other contract as well. Thus, it provides the recipient with an absolute right to either terminate both the contract or claim damages accordingly. That the 'cross fall breach clause', settles unambiguously that supply of goods, their transportation to the contractee's site delivery and related services are not separate contracts, but only form parts of an indivisible composite works contract supply, as defined under section 2(119), with single source responsibility. Thus, contracts are in nature of 'Composite Supply of Works Contract', therefore should be taxable at the rate of 18 per cent.

In a Post Budget Conference, R. Sekar, joint secretary, Ministry of Finance, has clarified that while accommodation in hotels has been excluded, commercial renting in hotels will attract service tax. Therefore, hotels leasing out shops and business centres will have to pay service tax. In real sense, this is the only service which can be called as a new service brought under service tax net. However, the proposal to include this one new service under the taxable services chargeable to service tax has not found favour with either the industry, real estate sector in particular, or the general public. The inclusion of this service in tax net could not have been proposed at a worse time. Last year, the prices for commercial property increased due to high demand and inadequate supply. Adding to the woes, the sealing drive undertaken by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi led to further escalation of rentals in and around the capital.

There are some issues involved with this service. Firstly, it can be argued that since the land and building are State subjects chargeable to State taxes (under Entry 49 of the Constitution, only States have the right to levy tax on land), it would be constitutionally incorrect to levy service tax, a Union tax, on such subjects. Secondly, the move will affect traders, retailers and export-oriented offices like BPOs the most. Since, they do not have any other service tax liabilities, it would not be possible for them to offset the service tax that will be levied on the rent. Retailers will increase prices as they have no option but to pass on this additional tax to the customer thereby fuelling the already high inflation. Thus, ultimately, the already costly services will end up getting costlier; digging a deeper hole in the customers’ pockets.

Finally, the most important issue is whether any service element is present in the renting of the property. However, Dr. Parthsarathy Shome, advisor to the Finance Minister, does not seem to buy this argument as he has said in a post budget interactive session that property rental whether horizontal or vertical are essentially services in nature and, therefore, have been brought into service tax net.

Service involved in the execution of a works contract

3. In a works contract, sales tax/VAT is levied on the transfer of property in goods involved in the execution of such works contract. Now, the Finance Bill, 2007 has proposed to levy service tax on the service element involved in the execution of a works contract. The proposed definition of works contract is an exhaustive one which covers only the following works contracts wherein transfer of property in goods involved in execution of such works contract is leviable to VAT/sales tax :—

(i)works contract for carrying out erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery, equipment or structures

(ii)works contract for commercial or industrial construction

(iii)works contract for construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof

(iv)works contract for completion and finishing services, repair, alteration, renovation or restoration of, or similar services, in relation to (ii) and (iii)

(v)works contract for turnkey projects including engineering, procurement and construction or commissioning (EPC) projects.

It is to be noted that works contracts in relation to specified infrastructure projects, viz., roads, airports, railways, transport terminals, bridges, tunnels and dams have been excluded from the definition of works contract, thereby excluding these types of works contract from the scope of the service tax levy.

The Finance Minister, P. Chidambaram, in his Budget speech has announced a composition scheme for the service providers involved in the execution of a works contact. The scheme would give an option to the assessee to pay 2 per cent of the total value of the works contract as service tax. The assessees opting for the composition scheme would not be entitled to avail CENVAT credit of capital goods, inputs and input services required for use in the works contract. The assessees who do not opt for this scheme would pay service tax on the taxable value of the works contract which is relatable to services provided in the execution of a works contract. Such value would be determined on actual basis based on the records maintained by the assessee. Separate rules for valuing works contracts will be notified later.

Mining service

Geological, geophysical or other prospecting, surface or sub-surface surveying or map-making services relating to location or exploration of deposits of mineral, oil or gas are subjected to service tax under ‘survey and exploration of mineral service’. Other services in relation to mining such as ‘site formation and clearance, excavation and earth moving’, drilling wells for production/exploitation of hydrocarbons (development drilling), etc., are also individually classified under the appropriate taxable services.

Now the Finance Bill, 2007 has proposed to bring services provided in relation to mining of mineral, oil and gas under a separate service. Thus, now services provided in relation to both exploration and exploitation of mineral, oil or gas would be covered under the service tax net.

It may be noted that unlike all other services where appropriate definitions have been provided in the Finance Act, the term ‘mining’ has not been defined. To ensure clarity and avoid ambiguity, it would be better if the term is defined appropriately.

Construction of cleaning and grading yards Question - We are establishing cleaning and grading yards at various places. These are to provide facility of cleaning and grading of farm produce to traders and farmers. After harvesting, the farmers or traders can bring the farm produce at these places. The cleaning and grading machinery installed at these places can be used by farmers. This will improve quality of the farm produce and fetch better price in market.

The construction work is done by contractors with their material. Is the service of construction of these cleaning and grading yards liable to service tax?

Answer - The work done by the contractors is 'works contract'.

As per Sr. No. 14(e) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012, services by way of construction, erection, commissioning, or installation of original works pertaining to mechanised food grain handling system, machinery or equipment for units processing agricultural produce as food stuff excluding alcoholic beverages are exempt from service tax.

Original works means - (i) all new constructions (ii) all types of additions and alterations to abandoned or damaged structures on land that are required to make them workable (iii) erection, commissioning or installation of plant, machinery or equipment or structures, whether pre-fabricated or otherwise - Explanation I(a) to Rule 2A of Service Tax (Determination of Value) Rules, 2006 - same definition adopted for exemption notifications as per definition clause 2(y) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Thus, construction service pertaining to machinery or equipment for units processing agricultural produce as food stuff is exempt from service tax.

Meaning of process - In CIT v. Tara Agencies [2007] 162 Taxman 337 (SC), Mamta Surgical Cotton Industries v. Assistant Commissioner (Anti Evasion) [2014] 44 GST 397/43 taxmann.com 237 (SC), following definitions were quoted with approval - process - A continuous and regular action or succession of actions taking place or carried on in a definite manner and leading to the accomplishment of some result - Oxford dictionary. A process is series of things which are carried out in order to achieve a particular result - Collins English Dictionary

Based on aforesaid judgments, it can be safely concluded that cleaning and grading is a 'process'.

Foodstuff - Foodstuff - any substance suitable as food - Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Food - a nutritious substance, esp. solid in form, that can be taken into an animal or a plant to maintain life and growth - - Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Foodstuff need not necessarily mean only the final food product which is consumed. It also include raw food articles which may after processing be used as food by human beings. - K Janadhan Pillai v. Union of India AIR 1981 SC 1485.

Thus, farm produce like wheat, rice etc. is 'foodstuff'.

Rule of purposive construction - This rule states that any statutory provision is to be interpreted considering the purpose behind the provision.

Based on aforesaid case law, it can be safely concluded that clearing and grading of farm produce by use of machinery is a 'process'. Further, it is one of the processes for preparation of foodstuff. Hence, service tax should be exempt.

If we apply the principle of purposive construction, the answer will be same i.e. exemption from service tax is available to the construction service, as that interpretation achieves the purpose of exemption.

Hence, in my view, the exemption from service tax is available to the service of construction of cleaning and grading yard in terms of Sr No. 14(e) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012.

Gitti obtained by breaking the stones/boulders

Only river sands and grit are mentioned in Entry 109 of the Schedule II, Part A. Under this entry the rate of tax 4% has been prescribed only on the sand and grit that flows with the river. Gitti of different sizes, according to use, is made by breaking the boulders in stone crushers or by hand. According to information received from the P.W.D., such gitti is used at different levels in the construction of roads. For example, from 63 mm to 40 mm gitti is used at the base and that 50 mm to 25 mm gitti is used at the upper level of the road. The grit obtained by breaking the boulders/stones is not included in this entry. Hence, the gitti obtained by breaking the boulders/stones in small sizes for use in the construction of road is not included in Entry 109, and it is taxable as unclassified goods at the rate of 12.5% under Schedule 5.
